# Detectors overview

[← Index](index.md)

Version 0.1 found four kinds of problem: N+1 queries, duplicate queries, slow queries and
requests with too many queries. Version 0.2 adds ten more, plus aggregate pages that look
across requests. This page is the map; each family has its own page.

Additional v0.3 development findings and their settings are described in [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md#additional-runtime-findings).

## Every issue kind

An *issue* is something the detectors found in one trace. Issues with the same identity
(kind, query or call, and callsite) are deduplicated across requests on the
[Issues](issues-and-endpoints.md#issues) page, with first seen, last seen and a count.

| Kind | Fires when | Default threshold | Page |
|---|---|---|---|
| `n_plus_one` | the same read from the same line, at least N times | `n_plus_one_threshold = 5` | [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md) |
| `duplicate_query` | identical SQL and parameters repeated | `duplicate_threshold = 2` | [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md) |
| `slow_query` | a query takes at least this long | `slow_query_ms = 100` | [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md) |
| `too_many_queries` | a request runs at least this many queries | `too_many_queries = 50` | [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md) |
| `blocking_in_async` | the event loop was stalled by synchronous work | `blocking_ms = 20` | [Blocking in async](async-blocking.md) |
| `long_transaction` | a transaction stayed open this long | `long_transaction_ms = 200` | [Transactions and locks](transactions.md) |
| `external_in_transaction` | an outbound HTTP call was made inside a transaction | any | [Transactions and locks](transactions.md) |
| `large_result` | a SELECT returned this many rows | `large_result_rows = 1000` | [Large and unbounded results](result-size.md) |
| `unbounded_query` | a SELECT with no `LIMIT` returned this many rows | `unbounded_rows = 200` | [Large and unbounded results](result-size.md) |
| `inefficient_count` | `len(qs)`, `if qs:`, `bool(qs)` or `.count() > 0` on a full-row query | pattern | [Count and exists](result-size.md#count-and-exists) |
| `slow_serializer` | a serializer takes at least this long | `slow_serializer_ms = 50` | [Slow serializers](serializers.md) |
| `slow_external` | an outbound call takes at least this long | `slow_external_ms = 500` | [External calls](external-calls.md) |
| `duplicate_external` | the same method and URL called twice or more | 2 | [External calls](external-calls.md) |
| `retry_storm` | three or more calls to one host with at least one failure | 3 | [External calls](external-calls.md) |
| `repeated_writes` | Repeated individual INSERT/UPDATE calls | 5 | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `deep_offset` | Large observed OFFSET | 10000 rows | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `database_round_trips` | Many queries with substantial cumulative cost | 10 queries and 100 ms | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `connection_pool_wait` | Long captured checkout wait | 50 ms | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `duplicate_llm_call` | Identical LLM prompt repeated in a request | 2 calls | [LLM-call observability](llm.md) |
| `serial_llm_calls` | LLM calls that ran back to back | 3 calls | [LLM-call observability](llm.md) |
| `llm_in_transaction` | LLM call while a transaction was open | always | [LLM-call observability](llm.md) |
| `llm_call_loop` | Many LLM calls in one request | 8 calls | [LLM-call observability](llm.md) |
| `uncached_large_prompt` | Large Anthropic prompt without prompt caching | 4000 characters | [LLM-call observability](llm.md) |
| `repeated_scan` | Distinct aggregates with matching predicate shape | 2 | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `large_response` | Response bytes exceed the threshold | 1000000 bytes | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `many_orm_instances` | Many model objects constructed or loaded | 500 | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `large_cache_entry` | Known binary cache payload size exceeds the threshold | 1000000 bytes | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `slow_cache_decode` | Explicitly instrumented cache decode exceeds the threshold | 50 ms | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `json_decode_hotspot` | Sampled standard-library JSON decoding cost | 50 ms | [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |

Severity is `info`, `warning` or `critical`. For most of the new detectors, a value at five
times its threshold is `critical`.

## Where the data comes from

The detectors read **spans**, and the new ones need new span kinds. The adapters and the
[integrations](integrations.md) create them.

| Span kind | Created by | Used by |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` (with `rows`, `has_limit`, `in_transaction`) | ORM and driver hooks | result-size detectors, N+1 |
| `serializer` | DRF, FastAPI response serialization, Marshmallow | `slow_serializer` |
| `resolver` | Strawberry, Graphene | N+1 over [GraphQL](graphql.md) |
| `transaction` | Django, SQLAlchemy | transaction detectors |
| `blocking` | the event-loop lag monitor, sync-driver hooks | `blocking_in_async` |
| `pool_wait` | SQLAlchemy connection checkout | shown in the timeline |
| `http_out` | httpx, requests integrations | external detectors |
| `cache` | Django cache, redis-py | the Cache page |

## Aggregate pages

Detectors look at one request. Some questions are about many requests, so Redline derives
small per-request summary tables at write time and the UI queries those:

| Page | Question | Source table |
|---|---|---|
| [Database](database.md) | Which SQL costs the most in total? Which index is missing or unused? | `trace_sql` |
| [Cache](cache-efficiency.md) | Which key patterns miss, are written but never read, or stampede? | `trace_cache` |
| [External calls](external-calls.md) | Which third parties are slow, duplicated or retried? | `trace_ext` |
| [History](history.md) | How did p95 change per release? What is new, resolved or regressed? | `rollups`, `issue_index` |

## Logs and exceptions

Two pieces of context are not issues but make every issue easier to understand: the **log
records** emitted during the request, and the **local variables** of the project frames in
an exception. See [Logs and exceptions](logs-and-exceptions.md).

## Tuning

Thresholds are ordinary [settings](settings.md#detectors). A noisy detector is usually a
threshold that is too low for your data: raise `large_result_rows` for a reporting app, or
`slow_external_ms` for a service that calls a slow vendor on purpose. There is no switch to
turn a single detector off; the registry is code (see [Extending](extending.md)).

All detectors run when a trace is **finished**, and only on kept traces, so a request that
is sampled out pays nothing for them. One detector raising an exception is logged and
skipped; it never fails the request.

---

# Performance checks and analysis tools

[← Index](index.md)

The v0.3 development build connects findings, response comparison and regression checks.
The UI exposes the same analysis engines as the command line. Open **More → Analysis**
for source analysis, recording health, suite coverage and suppressions.

## Try it in the UI

1. Run one of the demo shops and visit `/patterns/` (Django) or `/patterns` (the other
   shops). Open the recorded request's **Issues** tab. The original implementation runs
   four queries and deliberately repeats aggregates, uses deep OFFSET pagination and
   constructs full model objects.
2. Press **Try detector thresholds** to evaluate different thresholds against the recorded
   evidence. This preview does not change server settings or saved findings. Missing or
   truncated evidence cannot be reconstructed.
3. In **Analysis → Detector samples**, record the nine synthetic samples to inspect
   additional findings, including pool waits, large binary cache entries and sampled JSON
   decoding. Their operations and timings are illustrative, not application measurements;
   synthetic requests cannot be replayed as real endpoints.
4. Create a check suite with the rules below, record a baseline, then restart the shop with
   `SHOP_REFACTOR=1` and compare. The pattern endpoint drops from four queries to two and
   avoids full model construction. It deliberately reverses the response array and changes
   `total` by 0.005 to exercise the explicit comparison rules.

The demo settings explicitly enable check runs and source analysis from the UI. Keep
these development settings scoped to the demo. For test servers, use ports 8011 or higher.
The examples' existing READMEs explain the two terminals: the app directory for the server,
and the repository root for the commands.

For an in-process check of all four demos without opening server ports:

```bash
uv run --no-sync python scripts/check_demo_patterns.py
```

## Endpoint budgets and response rules

In **Checks → New suite**, each request has **Budgets and response rules**. Saving,
editing and exporting a suite preserves these rules.

```toml
name = "product report"
repeat = 20
warmup = 3
environment = { dataset = "shop-fixture-1", database = "SQLite fixture" }

[[requests]]
name = "performance patterns"
path = "/patterns"
array_keys = { items = "id" }
tolerances = { total = { absolute = 0.01 } }
budgets = { max_queries = 4, max_median_ms = 500, forbidden_issues = [] }
```

Use `/patterns/` for Django. Choose budgets for your environment; the example's latency
limit is illustrative.

| Rule | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `max_queries` | Maximum observed queries in any timed call; a whole number |
| `max_external_calls` | Maximum observed outbound HTTP calls in any timed call; a whole number |
| `max_median_ms` | Upper bound on the current run's client-side median latency |
| `max_p95_ms` | Upper bound on the current run's interpolated p95; use enough repeats |
| `min_samples` | Whole number ≥ 1. Latency budgets (`max_median_ms`, `max_p95_ms`) fail with "insufficient samples" instead of judging a run with fewer timed calls |
| `forbidden_issues` | Issue kinds that must not occur, for example `n_plus_one` |
| `array_keys` | Match elements at a configured JSON path by an identity field |
| `tolerances` | Allow a numeric difference at a configured JSON path |

Budgets are independent of improvement against the baseline. A slow baseline does not
make a budget pass. Missing required measurements, incomplete server metric collection,
and broken responses cannot pass a budget. Query counts remain usable when spans are
truncated; issue and external-call coverage require complete evidence.

Budget failures appear in the suite badges, report summary, per-request details, JSON,
Markdown, terminal output and JUnit. The default `--fail-on` includes `budget`; use an
explicit list or `none` to change that policy.

Array matching is opt-in: ordering may be part of an endpoint's contract. Every element
must have a unique non-null string or numeric identity; missing or duplicate identities
fail comparison. Added and removed elements remain differences. Paths within a matched
array refer to the aligned baseline order, so prefer wildcard ignore paths inside it.

Numeric tolerance accepts a difference no greater than
`max(absolute, relative * abs(baseline))`. Relative values are fractions: `0.01` means 1%.
Booleans, missing fields and type changes are not hidden by a numeric tolerance. Ignored
paths retain precedence. The report lists the configured comparison rules; a `same`
verdict under these rules means equivalent under those rules, not byte-identical.

## Environment and coverage

Kept requests record the target process's Python version, framework and installed
framework version when available. Check reports warn when observed target runtime
metadata changes or disappears. This is the application's runtime, not the runner's.

**Target environment labels** in the suite editor add dataset, database, Python, framework
and configuration labels. These are user declarations, not automatic database-version or
dataset verification. Hardware, data contents and shared-service state are not proven
equivalent by matching labels. Older baselines may lack metadata.

**Analysis → Suite coverage** compares a suite with the latest 500 retained traces. It
recognizes common Django, Flask, FastAPI and Litestar route parameters, shows missing and
single-input routes, and lists suite requests absent from observed traffic. Distinct
configured paths and headers count as different suite inputs. Unobserved routes and
unexercised branches remain unknown; this is not a completeness guarantee.

## pytest and no-query assertions

The core package registers a pytest plugin. Tests still need an installed adapter and an
instrumented in-process test client. The suite editor displays a pytest assertion snippet
for each request's query, outbound-call and issue policy.

```python
import pytest

@pytest.mark.redline(max_queries=5, max_external_calls=0, no_n_plus_one=True)
def test_products(client):
    assert client.get("/products").status_code == 200
```

Each captured request must meet the limits. No captured requests fails the assertion
rather than silently passing. Capture is context-local and includes sampled-out active
requests; it does not enable disabled instrumentation or ignored paths. Work in another
process or a thread that does not inherit context is outside this capture.

```python
from redline_core.testing import assert_no_queries

# Inside an active instrumented request, for example during serialization:
with assert_no_queries():
    result = serialize_preloaded_objects(objects)
```

Unexpected access raises with a callsite when available; an existing exception is
preserved. A route-wide no-SQL policy can also use `max_queries = 0` in a suite.

Stored test requests carry a `test_name` tag. Inspect them through **Analysis → Recording
health** and open the request for SQL, findings and exceptions. The UI configures and
explains policies; it does not execute arbitrary pytest or shell commands.

## Additional runtime findings

| Kind | Evidence | Setting and default |
|---|---|---|
| `repeated_writes` | Repeated individual INSERT/UPDATE statements; excludes executemany | `repeated_writes_threshold = 5` |
| `deep_offset` | Observed terminal OFFSET literal or integer bind | `deep_offset_rows = 10000` |
| `database_round_trips` | Many queries and substantial cumulative query cost | `round_trip_count = 10`, `round_trip_ms = 100` |
| `connection_pool_wait` | Captured connection checkout waits | `pool_wait_ms = 50` |
| `repeated_scan` | Distinct aggregates with the same table and predicate shape | `repeated_scans_threshold = 2` |
| `large_response` | Adapter-observed response bytes | `large_response_bytes = 1000000` |
| `many_orm_instances` | Django model construction or SQLAlchemy objects loaded into a session | `orm_instances_threshold = 500` |
| `large_cache_entry` | Known byte length of an already available binary value | `large_cache_bytes = 1000000` |
| `slow_cache_decode` | Explicitly instrumented decode block | `cache_decode_ms = 50` |
| `json_decode_hotspot` | Time attributed to standard-library JSON decoding in a profile | `json_decode_ms = 50` |

A zero threshold disables its corresponding rule. Counts are per request unless noted.
Round-trip findings avoid duplicating the existing count budget and repeated-query groups.
Similar aggregate shapes do not prove identical parameters or redundant work. Bulk writes
can change signals, validation and return behavior. Model counts do not prove objects are
unnecessary; Django includes newly constructed objects as well as database-loaded ones.
Response bytes do not measure network compression.

Redis reads and supported writes, and Django cache reads, can observe binary values
without copying them. Arbitrary objects and strings are not serialized or encoded just to
measure size. Network/cache operation time is not mislabeled as decode time. For a decode
block you control:

```python
import json
from redline_core.cache_payload import cache_decode

with cache_decode("reports:daily", payload=raw_bytes, backend="redis"):
    report = json.loads(raw_bytes)
```

Only size and duration are recorded, not the payload. Existing cache efficiency analysis
continues to report misses, unread writes and stampedes.

## Python source analysis

Use **Analysis → Python source** to paste or open a Python file, load the example, or scan
the configured `project_root`. Set `analysis_from_ui = true` explicitly, or leave it at
`"auto"` in framework debug mode. The production preset disables it; read-only mode refuses
the POST operations. The UI never accepts an arbitrary server filesystem root.

```bash
redline analyze ./app --json
redline analyze ./app --fail
# Explicit larger-project budget (defaults remain conservative):
redline analyze ./app --max-files 1000 --max-project-bytes 16000000 --json
```

Exit codes: `0` completed, `1` findings with `--fail`, `2` invalid/unreadable input or an
incomplete scan. Code is parsed and never imported or executed. Source inputs are capped
at 200 KB each; projects at 200 Python files, 2 MB and 20,000 visited entries. Dependency/generated directories
and symlinks are skipped. CLI users can raise the project budget with `--max-files`
(up to 10,000) and `--max-project-bytes` (up to 64,000,000). The same options are
available on `redline check-sql`; the per-file and 20,000-entry limits still apply.
UI scans keep the defaults. Errors, skipped files and limits remain visible.

Supported candidates include queryset operations inside loops, Python-side aggregation
and filtering, repeated fixed-range scans, repeated sorting, list membership inside loops,
and known blocking calls inside async functions. Queryset inference recognizes Django-style
chains and known SQLAlchemy Session/AsyncSession annotations or direct constructors;
Known `get`, `scalar`, `scalars`, `execute` and `query` calls are recognized.
Module-level local helpers are summarized through up to eight call edges; shadowed
helper names are excluded. A query in the first iterable is evaluated once and is
not classified as repeated by that loop; calls in later iterables can repeat.
Session identity-map hits, short-circuit branches and intentional chunking still need
runtime review. Helpers outside the scanned project, unknown factories and dynamic aliases may be missed. Findings are suggestions for review,
not proof of runtime evaluation, unused data or a safe transformation. Preserve null,
precision, duration rounding, hashing, ordering and mutation behavior when fixing them.

## On-demand database checks

Expand a request's **SQL** group and press **Inspect columns / indexes**. Redline reads
catalog metadata through the adapter's executor and reports selected TEXT/JSON/binary
columns, covering-index candidates for supported aggregate shapes, and an indexed
generated JSON expression that matches the query. Existing indexes are inspectable.

This first pass requires a single unqualified table and conservative expression matches.
Generated expressions are read for PostgreSQL/MySQL; SQLite column inspection does not
reconstruct generated expressions from DDL. Unsupported shapes remain explicit limitations.
No application query, DDL or index creation is executed by this inspection.

EXPLAIN additionally flags plans that actually discard many more rows than they return.
That evidence does not prove the planner selected the wrong index. Compare plans and
measured behavior before changing indexes; consider write cost and visibility effects.

## Evidence, impact and verification

The **Issues** page can sort by observed cumulative issue time or occurrences. These
describe retained traffic, reflect sampling and can overlap across findings; they are not
predicted savings. Each request's Issues tab shows supporting spans, thresholds and
evidence completeness.

**Verify a fix** opens a suite seeded from the affected real request, with that issue kind
forbidden. Record before the change and compare afterwards. Missing metrics cannot satisfy
the policy. Review response differences and measured gains alongside issue resolution;
absence from an incomplete observation is not proof of a fix.

**Analysis → Suppressions** accepts an exact route, fingerprint and/or callsite with an
issue kind, reason and optional expiry. Multiple selectors must all match. Suppressed
findings remain stored and can be shown on the Issues page. Expired rules stop matching.
Suppressions affect presentation; pytest assertions and check budgets still inspect raw
findings. Removing a suppression does not delete traces.

**Recording health** shows retained/drop counts, profiling availability and recorded test
requests. A request's **Time breakdown and recording health** partitions wall time into
database-only, external-only, pool-wait-only, cross-category overlap and remaining time.
Concurrent spans are not added twice. Remaining time is uninstrumented time, not measured
CPU. Truncated spans, dropped logs and profile errors remain visible.


### Project imports and SQL literal coverage

Project scans now follow explicit imports only between files included by the configured
scan budgets. Stable aliases, relative imports and package re-exports propagate query
helper summaries for up to eight project passes. The JSON `project_inference` field
reports the pass count, inferred helper exports and limitations. Exceeding the propagation
cap marks the scan incomplete. Wildcards, dynamic imports, unknown application factories
and class dispatch may still hide queries; single-file/pasted-source analysis cannot
follow imports into other files.

Known SQLAlchemy `Session`/`AsyncSession` annotations include Optional, Annotated and
bounded string forms. Known sessionmaker/async_sessionmaker factories and their
context-manager bindings establish session provenance without importing SQLAlchemy.
Arbitrary `get_sessionmaker()` functions and variable names are not assumed to be sessions.

`redline check-sql` recovers stable SQLAlchemy text clauses, literal wrappers, small pure
SQL templates and imported literal constants from the same bounded scanned set. It never
imports the application or evaluates arbitrary Python. Unknown ORM expressions and dynamic
SQL remain unresolved and cause exit 2. Runtime capture and isolated explicit compilation
remain necessary for those shapes; zero lint findings is not full SQL validation.

---

<!-- page: Real-world workflows -->

# Database failures, jobs and shared environments

These tools are part of the **0.5.0b1 development release**. They extend the existing
request profiler; they do not replace application tests, a database migration system or
production error monitoring. Recording does not start an exporter. Active load/check,
online compilation and export commands contact only their explicitly selected targets.
Production rollout is gated by the deployment-specific evidence described in
[Production](production.md).

## SQL failures that the application catches

An instrumented SQLAlchemy statement that raises now leaves a SQL span with its error
category, SQLSTATE/native code when available, duration and source location. A handler
may catch the exception and return HTTP 200; its recording still has a `sql_error` issue.
Failed statements are counted as attempted queries. A later successful statement does
not inherit the error. Sampling's error keep rule includes observed SQL failures, and a
span-limit overflow keeps a failure count with an incomplete-evidence finding.

Open **Requests → a recording → Issues**, then open the affected SQL span. The drawer
shows the driver error, raw rowcount and available connection evidence. Request search
also searches the configured request ID, user ID and job ID tags. Existing tag filtering
works through `GET api/traces?tag=request_id:example-id`.

`application_error` groups unhandled request/job exceptions by type and source location.
The existing Issues and release-history views can therefore compare those occurrences
across releases. Handled application exceptions outside database instrumentation are not
inferred automatically.

## Engine and connection coverage

Explicitly registered SQLAlchemy engines work as before. For engines created dynamically:

```python
settings = {"instrument_engines": "all"}
```

This installs process-level discovery hooks and lazily instruments engines used by an
active opted-in recorder. The mode must be enabled in each worker process that needs it.
`explicit` is the default; Flask-SQLAlchemy discovery continues to work in the Flask
adapter. `flask_sqlalchemy` is also accepted as a descriptive compatibility setting.
No database URL, password or connection string is used as an alias.

SQL evidence can include physical-connection age, observed statement number, pool recycle
and pre-ping settings, and bounded per-process hourly observations. `connection_churn`
requires at least 100 observed creations with recycling configured;
`fresh_connection_failure` requires three observed first-statement disconnects within five
seconds of creation in an hour. These are correlations, not diagnoses. Initial connections
or driver bootstrap statements made before observation can be unknown. Pool invalidation
is a separate `connection_failure`; it does not invent an executed SQL statement.
Per-process hourly gauges are also flushed to the store's `lifecycle_hourly` history as
max-per-hour rows, including for traces that sampling drops. `GET api/lifecycle` returns
them for dashboards. They are observed gauges, not a sum across processes, and carry no DSN
or credentials.

A raw rowcount of `-1` means unavailable. `dml_rowcount_unknown` on SQL Server can suggest
reviewing NOCOUNT, OUTPUT/returning results, batches and driver behavior; it does not prove
NOCOUNT is enabled or that a write failed. A 404 alone never establishes that cause.

`sql_retry_storm` groups attempts of the same statement and callsite inside one trace. It
requires at least three attempts after a transient, disconnect, deadlock or timeout failure
(the threshold is configurable). It reports the categories and total time; it never retries
or resets anything.

Direct session switches are observed without issuing probes or resets. SQL Server's
NOCOUNT/XACT_ABORT/ANSI/ARITHABORT switches, transaction isolation level,
`IDENTITY_INSERT`, language/date/timeout/deadlock settings and `sp_set_session_context`
keys are recognized alongside selected PostgreSQL `SET`/`set_config` options and MySQL
session/user variables. A checkin finding requires a configured expected value. The
default expectation is only `NOCOUNT = OFF`, and SQL Server context keys are declared
explicitly:

```python
settings = {
    "session_expected": {"NOCOUNT": "OFF", "XACT_ABORT": "OFF"},
    "session_expected_context": ["person_id", "endpoint", "request_id"],
}
```

Expected context keys are quiet when set with `@read_only = 1`; a leftover key set with
`@read_only = 0`, or a key outside the list, is reported as a lower-severity finding.
Values are stored as digests, never plaintext.

Generic string-valued options are stored as digests; expected values use the same SQL
value spelling. `SET LOCAL` is not treated as a persistent change, and observed PostgreSQL
transaction rollbacks restore tracked state. Stored procedures, raw driver cursors and
unobserved resets are unknown. Checkin findings require an active recording at checkin;
a connection returned after recording ends cannot retroactively amend a stored trace.
No automatic connection reset or query retry is performed.

## SQL Server plans and catalogs

SQLAlchemy's `mssql` dialect is recorded as `mssql`. On-demand estimated plans use a
dedicated connection, separate SHOWPLAN ON/query/OFF calls and rollback. If restoring the
session fails, the connection is invalidated. Permission failures are returned as EXPLAIN
errors; the database login needs SHOWPLAN and permissions on referenced objects.

The parser shows operators, estimated costs/rows, plan-affecting conversions and
missing-index candidates. Suggestions never create indexes. Catalog inspection supports
one simple `schema.table` reference, selected large column types, existing index columns
and visible enabled triggers. Unqualified names use `dbo`; workload catalog verification
is limited to `dbo`. Missing metadata permissions produce a limitation, not a clean bill
of health.

Actual XML plans are opt-in through `explain_analyze = true`, require a synchronous driver
with `nextset()`, execute the read query and roll back the transaction. Result consumption
is bounded to 100,000 rows and 5 MB of XML. STATISTICS IO summaries recognize English
messages only. Rollback cannot undo external side effects of database functions. Async
SQL Server actual-plan collection is not implemented. Estimated/actual driver behavior
still requires validation against a live SQL Server before claiming production support;
XML fixtures and fake executors are not that validation.

## SQL checks without importing an application

```bash
redline check-sql app/ services/ --dialect mssql
redline check-sql app/ --dialect mssql --json
redline check-sql app/ --dialect mssql --junit sql-results.xml
redline check-sql app/ --dialect mssql --write-baseline sql-baseline.json
redline check-sql app/ --dialect mssql --baseline sql-baseline.json
```

The AST extractor recognizes `text()`/`sqlalchemy.text()`, literal execute calls, module
constants and supported constant-only f-strings. Dynamic expressions, syntax errors and
scan limits are visible as unresolved input. Source is capped at 200 KB per file; a scan
is capped at 200 files, 2 MB and 20,000 filesystem entries. Dependencies and generated
folders are excluded, and symlinks are not followed. Local bindings that shadow constants
are not replaced with guesses.

Rules include bind-like text in comments, bare SQL Server OUTPUT, switches without a
reset in the same statement, INSERT SELECT star projections, and missing binds when the
parameter mapping is literal. They are conservative candidates: a reset in a separate
finally block is not currently proven. Bare OUTPUT does not prove a trigger exists.
Use a reviewed baseline or `-- redline: ignore[rule-name]` for accepted candidates.

Exit codes are 0 for no new findings, 1 for new findings, and 2 for invalid/unresolved
input. An empty finding list does not prove schema correctness.

**Analysis → SQL checker** uses the same offline engine on pasted source. It honors
`analysis_from_ui` and read-only policy. It accepts no filesystem root, DSN or online SQL.

## Explicit online compilation and schema drift

```bash
# Explicit Python files, isolated development database, optional SQLAlchemy dependency:
redline check-sql app/queries.py --dialect mssql --dsn "$DEV_DATABASE_DSN"
redline check-sql app/queries.py --dsn "$DEV_DATABASE_DSN" \
  --schema-snapshot schema-snapshot.json --json
```

Run the snapshot command after a migration to compare the default schema's column names,
types and nullability, plus SQL Server trigger and routine-parameter metadata. It updates
the local snapshot and, when a previous snapshot exists, recompiles only extracted
statements that reference an added, removed or changed table (including a table whose
triggers changed). An unchanged schema skips statement compilation; routine-parameter
changes recompile everything because those dependencies are not statically resolved. It
does not automatically run migrations or certify that all application SQL was extracted.
Snapshots are capped at 200 tables, 500 columns per table, 1000 triggers and 2000 routine
parameters.

Compilation uses SQLite EXPLAIN, PostgreSQL EXPLAIN without ANALYZE, MySQL server-side
PREPARE/DEALLOCATE, or SQL Server NOEXEC with cleanup on a dedicated connection. SQL
Server parameter types are read from `sp_describe_undeclared_parameters` and declared in
the NOEXEC batch; a single read statement also gets `sp_describe_first_result_set` so a
literal `row["col"]` read that the SELECT no longer returns is reported as a low-confidence
candidate. Only supported single statements are accepted. Parameter values are NULL
placeholders; type-dependent validity, temporary objects, stored procedures and runtime
permissions may remain unresolved. In particular, SQL Server NOEXEC supports deferred name
resolution. Use an isolated development login/database: server compilation can involve
extensions or planner functions. Driver messages and DSNs are not included in
machine-readable results.

### Watching a development schema

```bash
# One check (exit 1 on drift or a compile error), suitable for cron:
redline schema-watch app/queries.py --dsn "$DEV_DATABASE_DSN" \
  --snapshot schema-snapshot.json

# Poll every five minutes and raise a schema_drift Issue in the UI:
redline schema-watch app/queries.py --dsn "$DEV_DATABASE_DSN" \
  --snapshot schema-snapshot.json --interval 300 --store .redline/redline.db
```

The first run writes the baseline without alerting. Later runs compile only statements that
reference affected tables, and `--full` forces a complete pass. `--store` writes one
synthetic `TASK` trace carrying a `schema_drift` issue (affected table and routine names
only; no rows or SQL text). The command can also run from a Celery beat task or a CI job.
Exit `0` means no drift, `1` means drift or compile errors, and `2` means the watch could
not run (driver, DSN or permissions).

## Safer shared-development recording

```toml
preset = "shared-dev"
access = "token"
token_file = "/run/secrets/redline-token"
storage_path = "/var/lib/redline/{role}.db"
storage_role = "web"
instrument_engines = "all"

[redact]
profiles = ["credentials", "pii", "health", "payment"]
routes = { "POST /private/*" = "values", "PUT /medical/*" = "body" }
```

Generate a strong token and provide it through a private file or environment; do not put
it in a repository. The preset disables bodies, locals, SQL values, replay, load/check/UI
analysis and enables read-only UI behavior. Captured logs and free-text exception details are disabled; review
application logging separately because Redline does not suppress the application's own handlers. Explicit settings override preset defaults.

`capture_sql_params` accepts true, false or `reads_only`. False removes SQL literals and
parameters, omits source snippets associated with those SQL spans, withholds SQL error
messages that might echo values, and disables EXPLAIN for that recording. `reads_only`
retains values only for conservatively recognized read queries. SELECT parameters can
contain personal data too; shared-dev defaults to false.

Profiles are key/table-pattern starting points, not compliance guarantees. Add
`redact_keys`/`redact_tables` for application-specific patterns. Route rules match
`METHOD route-template` with shell-style wildcards. `values` preserves JSON structure
while masking values; `body` removes body contents. Both also mask SQL values, exception
messages/locals, captured log messages and query values before persistence. Free-form
text outside a known key cannot reliably be classified. Profile names are `pii`, `health`,
`credentials` and `payment`.

**Analysis → Redaction preview** uses current key/profile/route rules with invented JSON
samples. It sends the sample to this instance but does not save a trace. Capture switches
are separate from redaction. `redline audit-store --store /path/to/redline.db` reports
bounded possible unmasked-key counts without printing stored values.

`capture_loggers` and `ignore_loggers` accept logger-name glob patterns. With
`features.replay_writes = false`, the browser only offers GET/HEAD replay. This is a UI
control, not authorization for the application's own write endpoints.

## Request and user correlation

Configured request/response ID headers become a `request_id` tag; response IDs take
precedence at completion. Incoming IDs are available when a job is published. IDs are
labels, never authorization credentials. The default headers are X-Request-ID,
X-Correlation-ID and `traceparent`. A valid W3C `traceparent` also fills the OTel trace and
parent-span ids, and published jobs carry a child `traceparent`.

```python
from redline_core import tag
from redline_core.users import from_attr

settings = {"user_resolver": from_attr("state.user_id")}  # ASGI request state
# Django: from_attr("user.pk"); Flask: from_attr("person_id")
tag("operation", "daily-summary")  # no-op outside recording
```

Resolvers are synchronous Python callables invoked late in request handling. Return only
an identifier string/integer, not a name or e-mail. Errors are recorded as a resolver-error
tag and do not break responses.

## Jobs, stages and row outcomes

```python
from redline_core import Recorder, Settings, job, stage, row_outcome
from redline_core.storage import SQLiteStore

settings = Settings(storage_path="/var/lib/redline/worker.db", capture_locals=False)
store = SQLiteStore.from_settings(settings)
recorder = Recorder(settings, store)
with job("daily-import", recorder=recorder, task_id="run-123"):
    with stage("write"):
        row_outcome("succeeded")
    with stage("summary"):
        pass
store.flush()
```

A job is a TASK recording, searchable by its name/id and visible on **Jobs**. Stage spans,
SQL, outcomes and exception evidence use existing recording/issue views. Row outcomes are
bounded counters grouped by a digest of the reason; row IDs and samples are not stored.
An observed commit before a later failure is called out without claiming the whole job
completed. Nested jobs restore the outer recording context.

For Celery, install Celery in the worker environment and configure a recorder/store in
that worker process:

```python
from redline_core.contrib.celery import instrument_celery
integration = instrument_celery(celery_app, recorder)
# integration.uninstall() removes this instance's signal receivers.
```

Success, failure and retry outcomes are recorded. Publication can carry the current
request/parent trace ID. Arguments and results are not captured. Eager-mode tests require
no broker; prefork/broker behavior must be tested in the deployment. A task revoked before
it starts has no recording.

RQ (`instrument_rq`), Dramatiq (`instrument_dramatiq`) and FastAPI/Starlette background
tasks are recorded the same way, with trace-context propagation from the enqueuing request;
see [Integrations](integrations.md#rq). Their tests use fakeredis, `StubBroker` and a
TestClient, so real broker and process-model behavior must still be checked in deployment.

## Storage and mixed frameworks

Use private storage outside the repository, preferably a Docker named volume on a local
filesystem. Non-dev presets refuse an in-repository path unless
`allow_storage_in_repo = true`. Dev warns, and a `.redline` directory is ignored locally.
`{role}`, `{hostname}` and `{pid}` placeholders are supported; they do not replace a
filesystem/WAL compatibility check. SQLite remains unsuitable for arbitrary network shares.

Set `extra_stores` to existing worker store files to browse their request/job traces from
the web UI. Secondary files are opened read-only; they contribute browsing/profile lookup,
not history, aggregates, live-tail events or mutations. Files should have independent
trace IDs. Duplicate IDs are marked in lists; inspection, profiles and single-ID deletion
are unavailable for those IDs. Independent file reads are not an atomic snapshot.
EXPLAIN/catalog inspection of secondary traces is refused to avoid running a worker's SQL
through an unrelated web-process database binding.

For a Flask application mounted inside FastAPI, use the outer recorder/store:

```python
flask_redline.Redline(flask_app, recorder=outer_redline.recorder, mode="nested")
```

An active outer recording receives Flask route/view spans and errors rather than a second
trace. The adapter test uses the a2wsgi WSGI bridge and its copied context. It does not
claim equivalent behavior for every WSGI/ASGI bridge.

## Tests, import checks and explicit export

The pytest marker now defaults to rejecting SQL errors. It also accepts
`no_session_leaks`, `max_round_trips`, and existing query/outbound/issue budgets.
`no_sql_errors=False` is an explicit opt-out. `--redline-all` applies SQL-error assertions
to every test; a test that records nothing fails. Direct services can use
`recorder.recording()` inside `redline_capture()`. Truncation remains a failure for
assertions that require complete evidence.

`redline check-imports module:attribute` explicitly imports a development target in a
subprocess, loads each registered task's module and then the `import`/`from` statements
statically visible inside task functions, resolved against the same `sys.path`. It executes
module and lazy-import code; run it only in the intended development environment. Runtime
branches, dynamic imports and task execution are not covered. A missing lazy module is
listed by module name and makes the command exit `1`.

`redline check compare/run --ruff [PATH]` carries Ruff's JSON into the existing Markdown
and JUnit report; with no `PATH` it runs `ruff check --select F --output-format json`.
Redline is not a linter and does not fix findings.

```bash
redline export --store /path/to/redline.db             # OTLP JSON preview only
redline export --store /path/to/redline.db \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/traces --send      # explicit span transmission
redline export --store /path/to/redline.db \
  --endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/traces \
  --logs-endpoint http://127.0.0.1:4318/v1/logs --send
```

The exporter sends a root recording span plus sanitized SQL spans using `db.system`,
`db.operation`, `db.statement` (the normalized fingerprint unless `--include-sql` is
explicit; the raw statement is then redacted like the HTML export), `error.type` and
selected numeric/status attributes. It also builds OTLP log records for recorded issues,
with redacted titles. It omits bodies, parameter values, arbitrary tags and error
messages. A valid incoming `traceparent` supplies the exported trace id and parent span;
otherwise ids are derived from the recording id. It is not a production batching/retry
pipeline, and no exporter runs automatically during recording.

Routine CI and docs deployment run only on pushes to main, including merges. Package
publication follows a successful CI run on main only when the repository variable
`REDLINE_RELEASE_VERSION` opts in to the exact package version. The existing PyPI
environment approvals still apply. Tags and manual dispatch do not publish this release.
Local merges do not trigger remote jobs.


## Production validation targets

The production targets are Flask, FastAPI and Django with MySQL and SQL Server. Support
must be verified with the actual dialect/DBAPI and process model, not inferred from a
shared detector or SQLite demo.

| Combination | Required integration evidence |
|---|---|
| Flask + SQLAlchemy + MySQL | Handled errors, parameter style, counts, connection lifecycle, concurrency and shutdown |
| FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + MySQL | The same, with the actual sync/async driver and event-loop behavior |
| Django + MySQL backend | Native execute-wrapper failure metadata and row counts, transaction handling and framework middleware behavior |
| Flask/FastAPI + SQLAlchemy + SQL Server | pyodbc or the actual selected driver, code classification, session changes, reconnects and first-use failures |
| Django + SQL Server backend | The selected Django backend's vendor naming, native wrapper behavior and declared plan-executor capability |
| Celery worker, where used | Broker delivery, failure/retry signals, prefork/restart, SQL spans and correlation using explicit worker recorders |

The in-process demos exercise the common logic on disposable SQLite databases. Showplan
XML fixtures and fake cursor cleanup tests exercise parser/protocol behavior. Neither is
live SQL Server validation. Similarly, eager Celery execution does not prove broker or
prefork behavior. Keep those distinctions in the release validation report.

For production, record and inspect stored traffic with active tooling disabled. Do not
copy a demo's debug access, full sampling or active-job routes into a production codebase.
The detailed deployment and data-minimization recipe is on [Production](production.md).


### Native Django database evidence

Django's execute wrapper records caught database exceptions as failed SQL spans even
when the view returns HTTP 200. The trace retains a SQL failure count after its span
budget is exhausted, marking the resulting finding as incomplete evidence. Failed
statements cannot be explained. Native error codes are classified using the normalized
vendor; `microsoft`, `sql_server` and `sqlserver` identify SQL Server. Messages require
both `capture_error_details` and the SQL capture policy to allow them.

Fetch counting remains active when SQL parameter capture is disabled, so SQLite and
other cursors with unknown initial row counts can still report rows actually fetched.
Partially consumed results report only consumed rows. An uninspectable cursor leaves
rows unknown. Observation never consumes an `executemany` parameter generator.

Django's plan executor supports its existing PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite paths. The
Django SQL Server backend currently has **no estimated or actual plan executor**;
recording and structured SQL evidence do not imply EXPLAIN support. SQLAlchemy SQL
Server plan handling is a separate integration. Production disables plan execution by
default. Native SQL Server and MySQL driver/backend behavior still needs live validation
using the selected backend versions before rollout.


### Bounded capture in real workloads

Test oversized SQL, custom span data and tags as well as ordinary requests. Separate
`max_sql_bytes`, `max_span_data_bytes` and `max_tag_bytes` budgets limit captured values;
`max_trace_bytes` checks the completed serialized trace before save. Incomplete evidence
must be visible: preserved error counts do not reconstruct dropped SQL or parameters.
Include cycles, deep metadata, Unicode, uninspectable objects and a full writer queue in
the release checks. These limits complement privacy rules and deployment load tests.


The production preset uses tighter budgets than development: queue `64`, span count
`500`, SQL `16384`, span data `8192`, individual tags `2048` and completed trace `262144`
bytes. Use [the settings table](settings.md#capture-byte-budgets) for minimum values and
representation details. Incomplete SQL is not eligible for EXPLAIN; clients and tests must
keep the incomplete-evidence warning even when there are no retained error spans.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/database.md -->
<!-- page: Database -->

# Database

[← Index](index.md)

![The Database page: the slowest queries of the demo shop](assets/screenshots/fastapi-database-light.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-light }
![The Database page: the slowest queries of the demo shop](assets/screenshots/fastapi-database-dark.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-dark }

The request detail page tells you what *one* request did to the database. The **Database**
page answers the questions that only make sense across all of them:

- Which SQL costs the most in total, even though no single execution is slow?
- Where is a given table or column used?
- Which index would help the *workload*, rather than a single query?
- Which indexes does nobody use?

It has three tabs: **Queries**, **Index advisor** and **Unused indexes**, with a window
picker (1 h, 24 h, 7 d) applying to all of them.

## Queries: SQL search

Every kept trace is summarised by SQL fingerprint at write time (the `trace_sql` table:
one row per trace and fingerprint with its count, total and maximum time, and rows). The
Queries tab aggregates those rows.

Each row is one **fingerprint**, the normalised statement with literals replaced by `?`:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| SQL | the normalised statement. Click to open a sample request on its SQL tab |
| Executions | how many times it ran in the window |
| Requests | how many traces ran it |
| Total | summed time, the default sort. A cheap query run a million times beats a rare slow one |
| Mean, max | per execution |
| Mean rows | rows per execution, where the driver reports them |
| Routes | which endpoints run it |

The search box matches the **normalised SQL** as a case-insensitive substring, so you can
type a table (`shop_order`), a column (`customer_id`) or a keyword (`LEFT JOIN`). It is the
fastest way to answer "where do we query this table?" and "does anything still use that
column before I drop it?".

The request list has the same filter: `GET api/traces?sql=shop_order` returns only
requests that ran a matching statement.

!!! note "Normalised, not raw"

    Search runs over the normalised statement, so you cannot search for a literal value
    (`WHERE id = 42`). That is deliberate: it is what lets thousands of executions
    collapse into one row, and it keeps parameter values out of the aggregate table.

## Index advisor

The EXPLAIN drawer already suggests an index for a single query. The **advisor** looks at
the whole recorded workload instead, and proposes the indexes that would help the most
queries at once.

How it works, in order:

1. It takes the 100 SELECT fingerprints that cost the most time in the window and works out,
   per table, which columns they filter and sort on: equality columns first (`=`, `IN`,
   `IS NULL`), then one range column (`<`, `BETWEEN`, a prefix `LIKE 'abc%'`) or, without a
   range, the `ORDER BY` columns. A leading-wildcard `LIKE` or an `ILIKE` becomes a
   text-search suggestion (`pg_trgm`, FTS5 or `FULLTEXT`) instead of a B-tree.
2. It reads the database's catalog, through the same always-rolled-back connection EXPLAIN
   uses, and drops every requirement an existing index already serves.
3. It runs a plain `EXPLAIN` (never `ANALYZE`) for the 20 heaviest remaining queries to see
   which tables are read by a sequential or full scan. Catalog and EXPLAIN share a
   three-second budget; what does not fit is left unverified.
4. It picks the smallest set of indexes, up to 10, that covers the most query time.

Nothing here ever runs DDL. For each candidate you see:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Table, columns | the proposed index, with its columns in order |
| `CREATE INDEX` statement | ready to copy, for your database's dialect |
| Covers | the query fingerprints it would speed up |
| Executions | how often those queries ran in the window |
| Total time | what those queries cost in the window |
| Estimated saving | a heuristic: 80% of the covered time when EXPLAIN showed a scan of that table, 40% otherwise |
| Confidence | `high` when a scan was seen, `medium` for an unverified B-tree, `low` for text-search alternatives (not drop-in) and for queries that already avoid a full scan |

How to use it: take the top candidate, create the index on a **staging copy**, re-run the
[EXPLAIN](explain.md) for one of the covered queries, and compare. The advisor reads recorded
SQL, not table statistics, so it can suggest an index that the planner would not use
because the table is small or the column has few distinct values. Treat it as a ranked list
of things to check.

!!! warning "An index is not free"

    Every index slows down writes and takes disk. Do not create every suggestion.
    Prefer the ones that cover many queries, and look at the unused-index list before you
    add the tenth index to the same table.

If the store cannot compute the workload (a custom store without `sql_workload`), the tab
says the advisor is not available and the API answers `501 not_supported`.

## Unused indexes

On **PostgreSQL** and **SQL Server**, Redline lists indexes that have **never been scanned**
since the statistics were last reset (primary keys, unique indexes and indexes backing a
constraint are excluded). SQL Server additionally resets its usage counters when the
instance restarts:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Table, index | what it is |
| Scans | how many times the planner has used it (0) |
| Size | disk it occupies |
| Copy DROP | the `DROP INDEX` statement |

PostgreSQL reads `pg_stat_user_indexes`; SQL Server reads
`sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats` and sizes from `sys.dm_db_partition_stats`. For SQLite and
MySQL the page says the detection is not supported (`unused_supported: false` in the API).
If the database connection for the alias is missing or the statistics query fails on a
supported vendor, `unused_error` carries the reason.

The advisor result is cached for 30 seconds per window and database, because it runs
catalog reads and EXPLAINs. Add `refresh=1` to recompute at once; the response says
`"cached": true` when it was served from the cache.

Before dropping anything:

- Statistics **reset** on restart, failover or `pg_stat_reset()` (SQL Server also resets
  on restart). A freshly restarted database makes every index look unused.
- Check a **replica** and a **full business cycle**: month-end reports use indexes that
  nothing else touches.
- Unique and primary-key indexes enforce constraints even when they are never scanned. Do
  not drop them.

Redline only reads statistics. It never runs `DROP INDEX` for you.

MySQL is qualified against live servers with the pymysql, aiomysql and asyncmy drivers:
EXPLAIN findings, verified index suggestions and the recovery from a killed connection.

## Stored procedures

Calls to stored procedures are a query kind of their own. `EXEC`/`EXECUTE [schema].[proc] ...`
(SQL Server) and `CALL proc(...)` (MySQL, PostgreSQL, also the ODBC `{CALL proc(?)}` form)
are recorded with `query_kind: "procedure"` and the procedure name (`dbo.usp_orders`) on the
span. Their fingerprint is the procedure alone (`EXEC dbo.usp_orders`), so the SQL list and
the [index advisor](#index-advisor) workload aggregate per procedure whatever arguments it
was called with. Dynamic-SQL runners such as `sp_executesql` are not named and keep their
normal fingerprint.

Detectors treat procedure calls with care, because Redline cannot see whether a procedure
reads or writes:

- **N+1** still groups repeated calls from one line of code (`N+1: 24 queries calling
  procedure dbo.usp_item_for_order`) and suggests a set-based call.
- **Duplicate queries** report repeated identical calls as `info` only, never a warning.
- Procedures are never EXPLAINed.

### Ignoring session housekeeping

Statements that connection setup runs on every checkout (`EXEC sp_set_session_context ...`,
`SET search_path ...`, `SET NAMES ...`) would otherwise flood every trace and inflate query
counts. They are skipped by default through the [`ignore_sql`](settings.md) setting, a
list of regexes; a batch is only ignored when all of its statements match. Replace the
list to ignore more (`ignore_sql = ["^SET\\s", "^EXEC dbo\\.usp_audit_login"]`) or use `[]` to
record everything. Failed statements are always recorded, and
[session-state tracking](settings.md) still observes ignored statements.

## From the API

```text
GET api/sql?q=shop_order&window=24h&limit=100
GET api/indexes?window=24h
```

See [HTTP API](http-api.md#get-apisql) and [HTTP API: indexes](http-api.md#get-apiindexes).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/static-scan.md -->
<!-- page: Static N+1 scan -->

# Static N+1 scan

[← Index](index.md)

Runtime detection finds an N+1 only after something has run it, and only on a path your
test traffic reached. The **static scan** reads your templates (and, for Django, your
serializers) *without running anything*, and flags the patterns that are almost always an
N+1. Use it in CI to catch the problem before it ships.

```bash
python manage.py redline_scan          # Django
flask redline scan                     # Flask
```

## What it finds

### Template loops

A loop whose body reads a relation off the loop variable:

```django
{% for order in orders %}
  <tr>
    <td>{{ order.customer.name }}</td>        {# one query per order, unless prefetched #}
    <td>{{ order.items.count }}</td>          {# a COUNT per order #}
    <td>{% for i in order.items.all %}...{% endfor %}</td>
  </tr>
{% endfor %}
```

Each of `order.customer.name`, `order.items.count` and `order.items.all` costs a query per
iteration unless the view fetched the relation up front with `select_related` or
`prefetch_related`.

The scanner understands Django and Jinja syntax: comments (`{# #}` and
`{% comment %}`), `{% verbatim %}` and `{% raw %}`, nested loops, `{% with %}` and
`{% set %}` aliases, filters (`order.customer.name|upper`) and Jinja subscripts
(`order['customer'].name`). A template it cannot make sense of is **skipped with a
warning**, never an exception. It is dependency-free and best-effort.

### DRF serializers (Django)

A `ModelSerializer` with a nested relation serializer, used by a view whose queryset lacks
the matching `select_related` or `prefetch_related`. The check is on by default and skipped
with `--no-drf`.

## Fewer false positives in Django

Without help, any `x.a.b` in a loop could be a plain attribute. In Django the scanner asks
the app registry whether the **first hop is a real relation** (a foreign key, one-to-one,
many-to-many or reverse relation) and keeps only those chains. It also uses the relation's
kind to choose the right fix: `select_related` for a forward foreign key, `prefetch_related`
for a reverse or many-to-many relation. Flask has no model registry, so the Jinja dialect
cannot check that a hop is a relation and you triage its findings by hand.

## Running it

=== "Django"

    ```bash
    python manage.py redline_scan                    # every template directory
    python manage.py redline_scan templates/shop/    # specific files or directories
    python manage.py redline_scan --json             # machine-readable
    python manage.py redline_scan --fail             # exit 1 if anything is found
    python manage.py redline_scan --dialect jinja templates/jinja/
    python manage.py redline_scan --no-drf           # skip the serializer check
    ```

=== "Flask"

    ```bash
    flask redline scan [--json] [--fail]
    ```

    Runs the Jinja dialect over the template folders of the app and its blueprints (it takes
    no paths). Output and exit codes are the same.

Text output is an aligned table:

```text
LOCATION                      KIND      SEVERITY  CHAIN                SUGGESTION
shop/orders/list.html:14      template  warning   order.customer.name  select_related("customer")
shop/orders/list.html:17      template  warning   order.items.all      prefetch_related("items")
shop/api/serializers.py:22    serializer warning  items (nested)       prefetch_related("items") on OrderViewSet.queryset

3 possible N+1 finding(s).
```

`--json` prints `{"findings": [...], "warnings": [...]}` where each finding is:

```json
{
  "file": "shop/orders/list.html",
  "line": 14,
  "loop_var": "order",
  "chain": "order.customer.name",
  "kind": "template",
  "severity": "warning",
  "message": "...",
  "suggestion": "select_related(\"customer\")"
}
```

## In CI

```yaml
- name: Static N+1 scan
  run: python manage.py redline_scan --fail
```

`--fail` exits with status 1 when anything is found. Start by running it without `--fail`
to see the baseline, fix or accept what it finds, then turn it on so a new loop with a
relation inside cannot slip in.

## Limits

- It is **static**. It cannot know that the view already prefetched `customer`, so a
  finding is "check this", not "this is slow". The runtime detector is the confirmation.
- It reads templates and DRF serializers. Python code that does `for o in orders:
  o.customer.name` is what the runtime detector and its fix diff are for.

## Source analysis: cross-module helpers, dynamic SQL and precision

The template scan above has two Python-source companions, `redline analyze` (performance
patterns such as a query inside a loop) and `redline check-sql` (raw SQL lint). Neither imports
your code; both read the syntax tree within the usual file and byte budgets.

**Cross-module helpers.** `analyze` follows a helper that runs a query across files of the
scanned project: `from pkg.b import load_user`, `import pkg.b as b; b.load_user()`,
`from . import b` and re-exports through a package `__init__` all count. A loop in module A
that calls such a helper is reported as a `query_in_loop` candidate. Resolution is bounded
(a fixed number of propagation passes), has cycle protection, and only follows files included
in the scan; dynamic imports, wildcard imports and class dispatch may be missed.

**Dynamic SQL.** `check-sql` evaluates SQL text built from constants without running
anything: f-strings with constant parts, `+`, `%` and `.format()` on module-level constants,
`" ".join([...])` of literals, `+=` accumulation, and straight-line local reassignments inside
a function. Anything inside a branch, loop or `try`, a parameter, a call result or an
attribute stays unresolved. `.format()` fields with attribute or index access are refused.

Unresolved inputs are counted by reason in the report (`--json`):

```json
{"unresolved_by_reason": {"call": 2, "sqlalchemy_expression": 1, "unknown_name": 4}}
```

Each entry of `skipped` also carries a `category`. Categories: `unknown_name`, `call`,
`attribute_or_subscript`, `operand`, `unsafe_format`, `unsafe_helper`,
`sqlalchemy_expression`, `too_large`, `too_deep`, `limit`, `invalid_source`, `unreadable`,
`compilation` and `dynamic` (anything else).

**Measuring false positives.** `scripts/measure_static_precision.py` runs both analyzers over a
labelled corpus (`packages/redline-core/tests/fixtures/static_precision`) and prints
precision, recall and false-positive rate; a test keeps precision above a floor. Lines
marked `# expect: <kind>` are true positives; `# fp: <kind>` marks a shape the analyzer is
known to report wrongly (it counts against precision until fixed).

```bash
uv run python scripts/measure_static_precision.py          # the bundled corpus
uv run python scripts/measure_static_precision.py --json
```

On your own codebase:

```bash
uv run python scripts/measure_static_precision.py src/ > findings.txt   # lists finding ids
# review them; put the ids that were wrong into reviewed.json, e.g. ["a1b2...", "c3d4..."]
uv run python scripts/measure_static_precision.py src/ --false-positives reviewed.json --json
```

The result gives the false-positive rate overall and per finding kind for your code, which is
the number to use when deciding whether to gate CI on a rule.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/result-size.md -->
<!-- page: Large and unbounded results -->

# Large and unbounded results

[← Index](index.md)

A query can be perfectly indexed and still be the slowest thing in the request, because of
how much it returns. Fetching, building model objects and serializing 40,000 rows costs
far more than finding them. Three detectors cover the ways this goes wrong. They all read
two facts the adapters now record on every `sql` span: how many **rows** came back, and
whether the statement has a **`LIMIT`**.

| Kind | Fires when | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `large_result` | a SELECT returned at least this many rows | `large_result_rows = 1000` |
| `unbounded_query` | a SELECT with no `LIMIT` returned at least this many rows | `unbounded_rows = 200` |
| `inefficient_count` | a count or existence question answered by loading rows | a source-line pattern |

Severity is `warning`, and `critical` once the row count is five times the threshold.

## Large result

```text
Large result: 48,210 rows from shop_order   (shop/reports.py:31)
```

The detail says what to do: paginate, stream in chunks, or select fewer columns. Where
the adapter's fix suggester can tell which columns are wide (text, blob and JSON fields),
the issue lists them (`extra["wide_columns"]`), because dropping those is often the
cheapest fix:

```python
# Before: every column, including a 40 KB `notes` field, for 48,000 orders
orders = Order.objects.filter(status="open")

# After: only what the report needs, and a chunked iterator
orders = Order.objects.filter(status="open").only("id", "total").iterator(chunk_size=2000)
```

## Unbounded query

```text
Unbounded query: 1,350 rows, no LIMIT from shop_product   (shop/views.py:12)
```

The query has no `LIMIT`, `FETCH FIRST`, `TOP` or `ROWNUM`, and returned a lot. It is fast
today and keeps getting slower as the table grows, which is exactly why it is worth
flagging at 200 rows and not waiting for 200,000. `has_limit` is computed from the SQL
text; a limit inside a subquery does not count as the top-level limit.

Add pagination (`[:50]`, `.limit(50)`, keyset pagination) or, if you really do need all of
it, iterate in chunks.

## Count and exists

`inefficient_count` looks at the **source line** that issued the query (the callsite) and
recognises four idioms:

| Source line | What went wrong | Suggested |
|---|---|---|
| `len(orders)` | loaded every row to count them | `orders.count()` |
| `bool(orders)` | loaded every row to see if there are any | `orders.exists()` |
| `if orders:` | same, through truthiness | `orders.exists()` |
| `orders.count() > 0` (also `!= 0`, `>= 1`, `== 0`) | counted every match to compare with zero | `orders.exists()` |

```python
# Before
pending = Order.objects.filter(status="pending")
if pending:                      # SELECT every column of every pending order
    notify(len(pending))

# After
pending = Order.objects.filter(status="pending")
if pending.exists():             # SELECT 1 ... LIMIT 1
    notify(pending.count())      # SELECT COUNT(*)
```

When the source line can be located, the issue carries a one-line fix (`fix_line`) shown
as a diff. Severity is `info` for small tables and `warning` when the query returned at
least `unbounded_rows` rows or took at least `slow_query_ms`. A query that is already
bounded (`first()`, `get()`, a slice) is skipped.

The detector only inspects the callsite line itself, so `len([1, 2])` on a line that does
not run a query never fires. The `.count()` and `.exists()` names are Django ORM
spellings; for SQLAlchemy the hint is the same idea (`select(func.count())`,
`select(exists())`).

## Where the numbers come from

`rows` is the cursor's `rowcount` when the driver reports one, otherwise the number of rows
the ORM or driver has fetched so far (adapters update the span as rows are fetched, so a
lazily iterated queryset shows the rows actually read). When neither is known the span has
no `rows`, and these detectors skip it: they never guess.

The **Database** page ([Database](database.md)) shows mean rows per fingerprint across all
requests, which helps spot a query that returns a lot only occasionally.

## Settings

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `large_result_rows` | `1000` |
| `unbounded_rows` | `200` |

See [Settings](settings.md#detectors).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/transactions.md -->
<!-- page: Transactions and locks -->

# Transactions and locks

[← Index](index.md)

A database transaction holds a connection from the pool and, once it has written
anything, row locks that other requests can queue behind. The longer it stays open, the
worse both get. Redline records every transaction as a span and reports the two patterns
that hurt most.

## The `transaction` span

| Adapter | Where the span comes from |
|---|---|
| Django | `transaction.atomic` (the decorator, the context manager and `ATOMIC_REQUESTS`). The first atomic block entered while a trace is active opens the span; nested blocks (savepoints) only bump a depth counter |
| SQLAlchemy (FastAPI, Flask, Litestar) | the engine's begin, commit and rollback events |

The span's data:

| Key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `db_alias` | which database |
| `outcome` | `commit` or `rollback` |
| `queries` | statements run inside |
| `http_out` | outbound HTTP calls made while the transaction was open |

Empty transactions and control statements such as `SAVEPOINT` are not counted, so a
read-only request with `ATOMIC_REQUESTS` does not fill the timeline with noise. Queries
inside the transaction carry `in_transaction: true` in their span data.

## Long transactions

`long_transaction` fires when a transaction span lasts at least `long_transaction_ms`
(default 200). `critical` at five times that.

```text
Transaction open for 1,840 ms (12 queries, rolled back)   shop/services.py:88
```

Typical causes, in order of how often they show up:

1. **Work that does not need the transaction** inside it: rendering, serializing, sending
   an email, hashing a password.
2. **An outbound call** (see below).
3. **A loop of writes** that should be a bulk operation.
4. **Waiting on a lock** another transaction holds. The queries are fast; the time is spent
   waiting.

Fix by narrowing the `atomic` block (or the `with session.begin()`) to the statements that
must be atomic, and doing everything else before or after it.

## External call inside a transaction

`external_in_transaction` fires when a `transaction` span has `http_out > 0`:

```text
HTTP call to api.payments.example while a transaction was open   shop/checkout.py:41
```

This is worse than it looks. A slow or failing third party now holds your connection and
your locks, and a rollback cannot undo the call: you may have charged a card for an order
that no longer exists. The standard fix is to commit first and call afterwards, or to
record the intent in the transaction and let a background job make the call (the
*transactional outbox* pattern). Use `transaction.on_commit` in Django.

```python
# Before: the charge happens inside the transaction
with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    gateway.charge(order)               # http_out inside a transaction

# After: charge only once the order is safely committed
with transaction.atomic():
    order = Order.objects.create(...)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: gateway.charge(order))
```

## Pool waits

When SQLAlchemy checks a connection out of its pool and has to wait, Redline records a
`pool_wait` span if the wait is 1 ms or more. The data says which database, the pool size
and how many connections were already checked out:

```text
pool_wait  db_alias=default  pool_size=5  checked_out=5   waited 340 ms
```

A request that spends its time here is not slow because of its own queries. The pool is
exhausted: other requests hold connections too long (often *because* of a long transaction
or an external call inside one), or the pool is simply too small for the concurrency. Look
at the `long_transaction` issues first. In a [load test](load-testing.md), pool waits are
the typical shape of a knee: latency climbs while each individual query stays fast.

## Lock waits

Redline does not read `pg_locks`. A lock wait appears as a slow query or a long
transaction whose queries are individually trivial. The tell is a statement that is fast
under `EXPLAIN` (see [EXPLAIN](explain.md)) but slow in the trace, concentrated on the same
table or row from several requests. Reading `pg_locks` is on the [roadmap](roadmap.md).

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `long_transaction_ms` | `200` | Minimum open time reported as `long_transaction` |

There is no setting for `external_in_transaction`: any outbound call inside a transaction
fires it. To see outbound calls at all you must instrument the client
([Integrations](integrations.md)).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/graphql.md -->
<!-- page: GraphQL -->

# GraphQL

[← Index](index.md)

GraphQL is the natural home of the N+1: a query asks for `orders { customer { name } }`
and the default resolver loads each customer separately. The SQL is fine one query at a
time and bad in total, and the SQL alone does not tell you *which field* to fix.

Redline adds a `resolver` span for each non-trivial field resolution. SQL that runs inside
a resolver nests under that span, so the N+1 detector can name the field:

```text
N+1: 24 queries on shop_customer from resolver orders.*.customer
```

List indexes in the path are shown as `*`, so `orders.0.customer`, `orders.1.customer` and
so on are one issue. The path is also stored on the issue (`extra["resolver_path"]`).

## Strawberry

```python
import strawberry
from redline_core.contrib.strawberry import RedlineExtension

schema = strawberry.Schema(Query, extensions=[RedlineExtension])
```

Works for sync and async resolvers. Attribute resolvers that do no work are dropped, so the
trace shows resolvers that ran SQL or took time.

`strawberry-django` needs nothing extra: its resolvers run through the same hook, and the
Django adapter already records the ORM queries they issue.

The `redline-core[strawberry]` and `redline-core[graphene]` extras install the matching
GraphQL library if you want them pinned together.

## Graphene

```python
from redline_core.contrib.graphene import RedlineMiddleware

result = schema.execute(query, middleware=[RedlineMiddleware()])
```

Coroutine and promise results are handled.

## What it looks like

In the request's **Timeline** a resolver span (kind `resolver`) sits between the view and
its SQL, with `path`, `field` and `parent_type` in its data. In **Issues** the N+1 card
names the resolver path and, for a Django project, the usual `select_related` or
`prefetch_related` diff. For GraphQL the right fix is often a `DataLoader` rather than an
ORM change; the diff is a hint for the ORM-level fix when the resolver reads a model
relation directly.

| Span data | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `path` | `orders.*.customer` with list indexes as `*` |
| `field` | the field name |
| `parent_type` | the GraphQL type that owns the field |

## Tips

- **One endpoint, many operations.** All GraphQL requests hit `POST /graphql`, so they
  aggregate on the [Endpoints](issues-and-endpoints.md#endpoints) page as one route. The
  resolver paths in [Issues](issues-and-endpoints.md#issues) are how you tell operations
  apart.
- **Query size.** A deeply nested query can create thousands of resolver spans.
  `max_spans_per_trace` (default 2000) still applies: counts stay exact, spans beyond the
  cap are folded.
- **Load testing.** A scenario can POST a fixed query body:

  ```toml
  [[requests]]
  name = "orders"
  method = "POST"
  path = "/graphql"
  json = { query = "{ orders { id customer { name } } }" }
  ```

  See [Load testing](load-testing.md).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/async-blocking.md -->
<!-- page: Blocking in async -->

# Blocking in async

[← Index](index.md)

An `async def` handler runs on the event loop, one thread shared by every request. A
synchronous call inside it, `time.sleep`, `requests.get`, a sync ORM query, a big
`json.dumps`, does not just slow *that* request. It stops the loop, so every other
in-flight request waits too. It is the most common way to make an async service slow, and
it is invisible in a profiler that only times one request at a time.

Redline detects it and names the call.

## What you see

An issue of kind `blocking_in_async`:

```text
Event loop blocked 412 ms by requests.get   (shop/views.py:57)
```

with a `blocking` span in the Timeline at the moment of the stall, and the calling line as
the callsite. Spans with the same call and callsite are one issue, so `time.sleep` in a
loop is reported once with its count and total.

| Severity | When |
|---|---|
| `warning` | a stall of at least `blocking_ms` (default 20 ms) |
| `critical` | a stall at five times that or more |

## How it works

Both mechanisms are active **only while at least one request is in flight** on a loop. An
idle process pays nothing.

1. **A lag monitor.** A timer re-arms itself every 5 ms on the event loop
   (`loop.call_later`, no task) and measures how late it fires. A tick that is late by
   `blocking_ms` or more means the loop was stalled. The stall becomes a `blocking` span
   with `reason = "loop_lag"`.
2. **A watchdog thread.** One per process. When a tick is overdue by half of
   `blocking_ms`, it samples the loop thread's stack with `sys._current_frames()`. That
   sample gives the stall its callsite (the innermost project frame), the blocking call
   (`time.sleep`, `requests.get`, `sync ORM`, ...) and, through the running task, the
   request it belongs to.
A sample without a project frame keeps the culprit unknown. A sampled SQLAlchemy
   frame is labeled `SQLAlchemy work`: compilation/materialization can block even with
   an async driver, so the sample alone does not establish synchronous database I/O.
3. **Sync driver hooks.** When a synchronous database driver is called on the loop thread
   itself (a sync ORM query inside an `async def` view), the SQL hook marks it as a
   `blocking` span with `reason = "sync_call"`, so you see "sync ORM" even for a query that
   was individually fast.

If the culprit cannot be told apart from the other requests in flight, the stall is
attributed to every request that was running on that loop at the time, because each of
them really was blocked.

A stall that is still in progress when the request finishes (`time.sleep(1)` followed by a
`return`) is flushed when the trace is finished, so it is not lost.

## Fixing it

| Blocking call | Fix |
|---|---|
| `time.sleep(n)` | `await asyncio.sleep(n)` |
| `requests.get(...)` | `httpx.AsyncClient`, or `await asyncio.to_thread(requests.get, ...)` |
| a sync ORM or driver call | the async driver (`asyncpg`, `aiosqlite`), `AsyncSession`, or `sync_to_async` / `run_in_threadpool` |
| CPU-heavy work (hashing, parsing, image resize) | `await asyncio.to_thread(...)` or a process pool |
| a threading lock held on the loop | restructure; do not block the loop on a lock |

A plain `def` handler in FastAPI and Litestar (`sync_to_thread=True`) runs in a worker
thread, not on the loop, so it cannot cause this issue.

## Settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `detect_blocking` | `True` | Run the monitor in async adapters. Set it false to remove the monitor entirely |
| `blocking_ms` | `20` | Minimum stall that is recorded and reported |

The overhead is the timer callback, a few microseconds every 5 ms per busy loop. See
[Performance](performance.md).

## Which adapters

| Adapter | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| FastAPI | Lag monitor, watchdog and sync-driver hooks |
| Django on ASGI | Lag monitor and the sync ORM hook, for `async def` views |
| Litestar | Lag monitor (the app runs inside it while a request is recorded) |
| Django on WSGI, Flask | No event loop to watch: not applicable |

## Limits

- The lag monitor measures a loop that is *late*, which is the right signal but is not proof
  of a specific line. The sampled stack is the best available evidence.
- A stall shorter than `blocking_ms` is invisible by design. Lower the setting to see
  smaller ones, at the cost of more noise.
- Work in C extensions that release the GIL is not a stall; work that holds it is.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/serializers.md -->
<!-- page: Slow serializers -->

# Slow serializers

[← Index](index.md)

Turning objects into a response is real work. A Django REST Framework serializer with
nested relations, or a Pydantic response model over a few thousand items, can take longer
than the query that fetched the data, and a profiler that only shows "the view" hides it.
Redline times serialization as its own span kind and reports it when it is slow.

## The `serializer` span
