| Data key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `library` | `drf`, `pydantic`, `marshmallow` or `other` |
| `serializer` | the class or model name |
| `items` | how many objects were serialized, when known |
| `many` | whether it was a list |

Where each comes from:

| Library | How it is recorded |
|---|---|
| **DRF** (Django) | `BaseSerializer.data` for `Serializer`, `ModelSerializer` and `ListSerializer`. Only the outermost call is a span; nested serializers run inside their parent's `to_representation` and are part of its time |
| **Pydantic** (FastAPI) | `fastapi.routing.serialize_response`: response-model validation plus the dump, nested models included |
| **Marshmallow** | `Schema.dump`, if you call [`instrument_marshmallow()`](integrations.md#marshmallow); the outermost dump only |

Serializers built by hand inside a `SerializerMethodField` are covered by the parent
serializer's span.

## The `slow_serializer` issue

`slow_serializer` fires when a serializer span takes at least `slow_serializer_ms`
(default 50 ms). It is `critical` at five times that. Spans of the same serializer class
from the same callsite are one issue, with the run count and the total.

```text
Slow serializer: OrderSerializer took 340 ms for 1,200 items   (shop/api.py:44)
```

The item count tells you whether the cost is **per item** or a fixed cost: 340 ms for 1,200
items is 0.28 ms each, and the fix is to return fewer items or cheaper ones; 340 ms for
three items is something pathological inside the serializer.

## Usual causes and fixes

| Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| A nested serializer or a `SerializerMethodField` that runs a query per item (this will also be an [N+1](n-plus-one.md), and the serializer span *contains* those SQL spans) | `select_related` / `prefetch_related` on the view's queryset, or `selectinload` |
| Returning every row | paginate; see [Large and unbounded results](result-size.md) |
| Heavy per-item Python (date formatting, computed fields) | compute in the database (`annotate`), cache, or do it once outside the loop |
| Validating a response model for data you built yourself | `response_model_exclude_unset`, a lighter model, or return the model instance directly |

The static [N+1 scan](static-scan.md) also checks DRF serializers for nested relations whose
queryset lacks the matching `select_related` or `prefetch_related`, before you ever run the
code.

## In the UI

A serializer span appears in the Timeline in its own colour, between the view and the
response. Its drawer shows the library, the class and the item count. The span's SQL
children, if any, nest under it.

## Settings

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `slow_serializer_ms` | `50` |

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/external-calls.md -->
<!-- page: External calls -->

# External calls

[← Index](index.md)

Most backends spend more time waiting on other services than on their own database. The
payment gateway, the email API, the search cluster, a partner's REST endpoint: each is an
`http_out` span in the trace, and together they are a page of their own.

## Recording them

Outbound calls are recorded once you instrument the client you use
([Integrations](integrations.md)):

```python
from redline_core.contrib.httpx import instrument_httpx
from redline_core.contrib.requests import instrument_requests

instrument_httpx()
instrument_requests()
```

A span records method, URL (query-string secrets masked), status and duration. In the
Timeline it is purple and named `GET api.example.com/v2/users/42`.

## Detectors

Three detectors read `http_out` spans in one request:

| Kind | Fires when | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| `slow_external` | a call takes at least `slow_external_ms` (default 500), grouped by method, URL without query string, and callsite | `critical` at 5x |
| `duplicate_external` | the same method and **full URL** is called twice or more | `warning` at 5 copies, or when together they exceed `slow_external_ms` |
| `retry_storm` | the same method and **host** is called three or more times with at least one failure | `critical` at 6 calls |

A *failure* here means a 5xx, a 429, or no status at all (timeout, connection error). A
group that is already a retry storm is not reported again as a duplicate.

```text
Retry storm: 5 calls to api.mailer.example, 3 failed          (shop/notify.py:19)
Duplicate external call: GET api.rates.example/usd ×4         (shop/pricing.py:62)
Slow external call: POST api.payments.example/charge, 1.8 s   (shop/checkout.py:41)
```

Common fixes: cache the response for the duration of the request (a duplicate), cap the
retries and add jitter (a storm), set a short timeout and move the call off the request
path (slow), and never call out inside a transaction
([Transactions and locks](transactions.md#external-call-inside-a-transaction)).

## The External page

Across requests, **External calls** groups every outbound call by method, host and a **URL
pattern**: digit runs, UUIDs and hex strings of eight or more characters become `*`, so
`/v2/users/42` and `/v2/users/77` are one row, `/v2/users/*`.

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Method, Host, URL pattern | the group |
| Calls | total calls in the window |
| p95, max | latency. p95 is taken over each request's *mean* for the pattern (exact when a request calls it once) |
| Errors, error rate | 5xx, 429 and status-less calls |
| Duplicates | requests that called this pattern two or more times |
| Retries | requests with three or more calls and at least one error |

The window picker (1 h, 24 h, 7 d) and the sort let you find the slowest dependency first.
The same data is served by `GET api/external?window=`
([HTTP API](http-api.md#get-apiexternal)). It is derived from the `trace_ext` table, so it
reflects *kept* traces: with sampling, counts are of the sample.

## Settings

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `slow_external_ms` | `500` |

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/cache-efficiency.md -->
<!-- page: Cache efficiency -->

# Cache efficiency

[← Index](index.md)

A cache that nobody checks tends to rot: keys that always miss, values written and never
read, a hot key that expires and sends fifty requests to the database at once. The
**Cache** page looks across recorded requests for those three things.

## Recording

| Source | How |
|---|---|
| Django cache framework (any backend) | recorded by `django-redline` automatically |
| redis-py, sync and asyncio | [`instrument_redis()`](integrations.md#redis) |

Each operation is a `cache` span with `op`, `key`, `backend` and, for reads, `hit`.

For the aggregate, keys are reduced to **patterns**: digit runs, UUIDs and hex strings of
eight or more characters become `*`, but digits glued to a preceding letter or digit are
kept. So `user:42:profile` and `user:77:profile` are both `user:*:profile`, while `v2`
stays `v2`.

Which commands count:

| Class | Commands |
|---|---|
| Reads | `get`, `get_many`, `get_or_set`, `has_key`, `mget`, `hget`, `hmget`, `hgetall`, `exists`, `getex`, `getdel` (and Django's async `a...` variants) |
| Writes | `set`, `add`, `set_many`, `setex`, `psetex`, `setnx`, `mset`, `hset`, `hmset`, `incr`, `decr`, `incrby`, `decrby` |
| Deletes | `delete`, `delete_many`, `del`, `unlink`, `hdel`, `clear` |

Spans with no key (a Redis pipeline is one keyless span) are skipped.

## The page

One row per backend and key pattern:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Gets, hits, misses | reads, and how they resolved |
| Hit rate | `hits / (hits + misses)`. Blank when the backend does not say (a plain `EXISTS`) |
| Sets, deletes | writes and invalidations |
| Unread sets | writes to a pattern that had **no reads at all** in the window |
| Stampedes | bursts of three or more requests that missed the **same pattern within one second** |

### Reading it

- **Low hit rate on a hot pattern.** The TTL is too short, the key includes something that
  varies (a timestamp, a random id), or the data is never reused. A pattern that is read
  often and hits rarely is wasted round trips.
- **Unread sets.** You pay to compute and store a value that nothing ever fetched. Delete
  the write, or find the reader that uses a different key spelling.
- **Stampedes.** The classic *thundering herd*: a popular key expires and every concurrent
  request recomputes it. Add a lock around the recompute, stagger expirations with jitter,
  refresh before expiry, or serve stale while one worker refreshes.

## API

`GET api/cache?window=` returns the same rows. See [HTTP API](http-api.md#get-apicache).

## Limits

- Statistics come from *kept* traces. With `sample_rate = 0.1` they describe a 10% sample;
  rates are still meaningful, absolute counts are not.
- Stampede detection uses request **start times** and a one-second window, so it can miss
  a stampede spread over several seconds and can flag requests that merely arrived together.
- A key built from a short alphanumeric id (`user:ab12`) is not collapsed, so such patterns
  stay separate rows.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/logs-and-exceptions.md -->
<!-- page: Logs and exceptions -->

# Logs and exceptions

[← Index](index.md)

A slow or failing request is a story, and the SQL timeline is only half of it. The other
half is what your own code said while it ran: the `logger.warning("retrying payment")` two
lines before the 500, and the value of `order` at the moment it raised. Redline now keeps
both with the trace.

## Logs

Every record your application logs **during a recorded request** is filed under that
request. Open a request and choose the **Logs** tab.

```text
  +12.4 ms  INFO     shop.cart       Loaded cart for user 42            shop/cart.py:31
  +96.0 ms  WARNING  shop.payments   Gateway slow (retry 1)             shop/payments.py:77
 +311.8 ms  ERROR    shop.payments   Gateway timeout, giving up         shop/payments.py:84
```

Each row has the time since the request started, the level, the logger name, the message
and the file and line of the log call (project-relative, clickable if
[open in editor](the-ui.md#open-in-editor) is configured).

### How it is captured

Redline does not add a logging handler or change any logger's level. The first recorder
with `capture_logs` wraps the log record factory (`logging.setLogRecordFactory`, keeping
whatever factory was installed before), so your own `logging.basicConfig(...)`,
`dictConfig(...)` or `basicConfig(force=True)` work exactly as without Redline, before or
after it is configured. Each record is filed under whichever request is active in the
current `contextvars` context, so concurrent requests and threads do not mix. Outside a
request a record costs a single `ContextVar.get()`. Records from Redline's own `redline`
loggers are ignored so it can never recurse.

Python only creates a record when the logger is enabled for its level, so capture follows
**your** logging levels and `log_level` is an additional minimum on top. To capture INFO
your loggers must be at INFO: Django's default `LOGGING` and most configured apps are. An
app that never configured logging has its root logger at WARNING, so only WARNING and above
are captured there (call `logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)` to get INFO too).

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `capture_logs` | `True` | Master switch |
| `log_level` | `"INFO"` | An extra minimum level for stored records, on top of your loggers' own levels. `"WARNING"` is a good production value |
| `max_logs_per_trace` | `200` | Cap per request. Extras are counted in `logs_dropped` and the UI says how many were dropped |

Messages are formatted, **redacted** and capped at 2,000 characters. Redaction looks for
`key=value`, `key: value` and `"key": "value"` pairs whose key matches `redact_keys`
(`password=...`, `"token": "..."`) and masks the value; passwords inside URLs
(`https://user:password@host`) and secret query-string values are masked too. It is the same key-based rule as everywhere else,
so a secret that appears bare in a sentence ("the code is 4821") is **not** masked. See
[Security](security.md#logs-and-locals).

!!! tip "Logs in the trace list"

    The **Logs** tab on a request shows only records from that request. To find requests
    that logged a particular problem, open the request that raised it and follow the
    linked issue; logs are not searchable across requests (that is a job for your log
    pipeline).

## Exceptions with locals

When a request raises an unhandled exception, the trace's `error` has always held the type,
message and traceback. With `capture_locals` (on by default) it also keeps the **project
frames** of the traceback together with the local variables in each, which is usually the
fastest way to see *why*:

```text
OrderError: no stock for sku 'A-77'
  shop/services.py:58  in reserve
      item   = <OrderItem 913: sku='A-77' qty=3>
      stock  = <Stock sku='A-77' on_hand=2>
      order  = <Order 4410 status='pending'>
  shop/views.py:21  in checkout
      request = <WSGIRequest: POST '/checkout/'>
      cart    = {'A-77': 3, 'B-10': 1}
```

Open the request and choose the **Exception** tab: each frame is expandable, with the
source line, the variables, and an open-in-editor link.

### What is kept

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| Frames | project code only (library frames are not captured), innermost last, at most 20 |
| Locals per frame | at most 30 |
| Each value | its `repr`, truncated at 300 characters |
| Names starting `__` | skipped |
| Unprintable objects | shown as `<unrepresentable>` |

### What is masked

A local whose **name** matches `redact_keys` (`password`, `token`, `api_key`, `session`,
`card`, ...) is replaced by `[redacted]`. A local that is a dict or other mapping has its
secret-looking **keys** masked before it is printed.

This is key-based, so it has the same blind spot as the rest of redaction: a secret held in
a variable with an innocent name (`x = request.headers["Authorization"]`), or inside a
model's `repr`, is shown as it is. Locals can contain personal data too: an `order`
object's `repr` may include a customer's name or email. If that is a concern,
turn the feature off and keep the traceback:

```python
REDLINE = {"CAPTURE_LOCALS": False}
```

The `production` [preset](configuration.md#presets) does exactly that. The `locals` and `logs`
[feature switches](access-control.md#feature-switches) turn the two features off from the
access-control side.

### Settings

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `capture_locals` | `True` |

## Cost

Logs: one `ContextVar.get()` per record outside a request; inside, building one small
object (message formatting, redaction and a callsite lookup). Locals are captured **only
when a request raises**, from the traceback, so the happy path pays nothing.

## Correlating your own logs and error reports

Redline's recordings, your log files and your error tracker can all point at the same
request through the Redline trace id.

```python
import logging
from redline_core.correlation import TraceIdFilter

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.addFilter(TraceIdFilter())          # a handler filter sees every record
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(asctime)s [%(redline_trace_id)s] %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger().addHandler(handler)
```

`redline_trace_id` is the id of the request or job being recorded, `-` outside one. The
filter never drops a record. `install_log_filter()` adds it to the root logger's existing
handlers. Search the id in the UI (`/_redline/#/requests/<id>`).

**Sentry.** Without importing anything from Sentry at module level, Redline can tag events
that happen inside a recording and add an "Open in Redline" link:

```python
import sentry_sdk
from redline_core.correlation import chain_before_send

sentry_sdk.init(
    dsn=...,
    before_send=chain_before_send(None, base_url="https://dev.example.com"),
)
```

The event gets the tag `redline_trace_id` and a `redline` context with `trace_id` and
`open_in_redline`. `base_url` defaults to `$REDLINE_PUBLIC_URL`; pass `mount="..."` when the UI
is not at `/_redline`. Pass your existing hook as the first argument to keep it.
`tag_sentry_scope()` sets the same tag and context on the current scope instead (a no-op when
`sentry_sdk` is not installed). Remember that Redline is for development and staging: only
link to a UI that exists where the event happens.

**OpenTelemetry.** Exported spans (`redline export --send`) carry the attribute
`redline.trace_id`, next to the W3C trace id, so a collector can link back to the recording.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/agents.md -->
<!-- page: Working with agents -->

# Working with AI agents

Redline is built so a coding agent can find a performance problem, fix it and prove the fix,
using recorded data instead of guesses. Everything here is read-only unless stated.

## Machine-readable docs

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`/llms.txt`](llms.txt) | Index of every page with a one-line summary ([llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) format) |
| [`/llms-full.txt`](llms-full.txt) | All pages in one file, for loading into a context window |
| [`/reference/settings.schema.json`](reference/settings.schema.json) | Every setting with its type and default (JSON Schema) |
| [`/reference/cli.json`](reference/cli.json) | Every command and flag |

They are generated by `scripts/build_llms.py`; CI fails when they are stale.

## Give your agent the instructions

```bash
redline agent-skill --write ~/.claude/skills        # a Claude skill: .../redline/SKILL.md
redline agent-skill --format agents --write .       # AGENTS.redline.md to merge into AGENTS.md
```

The text covers how to find problems, fix them and verify, and the rules below.

## MCP server

```bash
redline mcp --store .redline/redline.db [--audit .redline/agent-audit.jsonl]
```

It speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio (line-delimited JSON-RPC) and opens the store
read-only. Example client entry:

```json
{ "mcpServers": { "redline": { "command": "redline", "args": ["mcp", "--store", ".redline/redline.db"] } } }
```

| Tool | Returns |
|---|---|
| `list_issues` | Findings ranked by sampled impact, each with `why`, callsite and suggestion |
| `explain_issue` | One finding in full |
| `get_trace` | A bounded request summary: timings, issues, slowest spans (no bodies or logs) |
| `instrumentation_report` | What redline cannot see: inactive integrations, truncated traces, drops |
| `verify_fix` | gone / still_present / inconclusive from a saved compare report |
| `llm_summary` | Sampled LLM-call tokens and counts per route and model |

Bad input produces an error result the model can read; the server keeps running. Output is
bounded in size. With `--audit`, each call is appended as a JSONL record containing the tool
name, argument *names* and timing, never argument values. The file is created with mode 0600.

## The fix loop

```bash
redline fix-prompt ISSUE_ID --store .redline/redline.db > brief.md   # evidence + constraints
redline check record check.toml                                      # baseline, before editing
# ...the agent edits the code...
redline check compare check.toml --json report.json
redline check verify report.json --kind n_plus_one                   # exit 0 only when gone
```

`verify` answers `gone`, `still_present` or `inconclusive`. A finding is only `gone` when it
was in the baseline, is absent now, responses are equal, and the run had enough samples with
complete server metrics. If it says `inconclusive`, collect more samples; do not declare
success. See [Refactor check](refactor-check.md#verify-a-fix).

## Reviewing agent-written code in CI

```yaml
- run: redline check compare check.toml --json report.json --fail-on slower,changed,broken,budget
- run: redline check findings report.json --new-only --json > findings.json   # exit 1 if any
```

`findings` lists issues that are new relative to the baseline and includes a fix brief for
each, which an agent step can consume. Pair it with the pytest markers
(`@pytest.mark.redline(max_queries=…, no_n_plus_one=True)`) and the `redline check ratchet`
query-count ratchet so a change cannot quietly add queries.

## AI-assisted diagnosis

```bash
redline diagnose ISSUE_ID --store .redline/redline.db          # preview only, nothing is sent
redline diagnose ISSUE_ID --store .redline/redline.db --send   # opted in: really sends
```

Off by default. The default run prints the exact request (destination, model and body) and
exits. Sending needs three things together: `--send`, `ai_diagnosis = true` in the settings,
and the key in the `REDLINE_AI_API_KEY` environment variable. The destination host is fixed
for the provider (`api.anthropic.com`); it cannot be redirected. The body is an allowlist of
finding fields (kind, title, evidence, SQL *shape* with literals replaced, file, line,
function and one line of source) passed through the redactor. Request and response bodies,
logs and LLM prompt text are never part of it. Errors report the HTTP status only, never the
key or the provider's response body. Agents must not enable this themselves.

## Rules for agents

- Never capture, log or paste prompt or completion text, tokens, passwords or request bodies.
- Do not delete traces or run EXPLAIN ANALYZE against a production store.
- Do not weaken a test, threshold or budget to make a finding disappear.
- Do not push, tag or publish without the owner's approval.
- Do not enable `ai_diagnosis` or set `REDLINE_AI_API_KEY`; only the owner opts in.

## Safe deployment recipe

Run the app with `read_only = true` and `explain_analyze = false`, point `redline mcp` at a
*copy* or read-only mount of the store, and keep `--audit` on. The MCP process cannot write to
the store at all.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/llm.md -->
<!-- page: LLM-call observability -->

# LLM-call observability

Redline records calls to the Anthropic and OpenAI SDKs as `llm_call` spans, next to the SQL
and HTTP spans of the same request, and flags patterns that waste time or money.

**Privacy.** Only metadata is stored: provider, model, token counts, status, whether the call
streamed, a 16-character hash of the prompt and its length. Prompt text, completions, tool
arguments and exception messages are never recorded.

## Turn it on

```python
from redline_core.contrib.anthropic import instrument_anthropic
from redline_core.contrib.openai import instrument_openai

instrument_anthropic()   # Messages.create and AsyncMessages.create
instrument_openai()      # chat.completions.create, sync and async
```

Both return `False` when the SDK is not installed, are idempotent, and leave the SDK's
behaviour and exceptions unchanged. Calls made outside a traced request cost one context-variable
read. `redline instrumentation` lists them under integrations.

**Streaming.** A streamed call is recorded with `stream: true` and no token counts, because
usage is only known when the stream ends. Totals therefore undercount when you stream.

## Findings

| Kind | Fires when | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `duplicate_llm_call` | The same model got an identical prompt (same hash) repeatedly in one request | 2 calls |
| `serial_llm_calls` | Calls ran back to back with no overlap | 3 calls |
| `llm_in_transaction` | A call started while a database transaction was open | always |
| `llm_call_loop` | One request made many calls (agent loops, per-item calls) | 8 calls |
| `uncached_large_prompt` | A large non-streamed Anthropic prompt used no prompt-cache tokens | 4000 characters |

Settings: `llm_duplicate_threshold`, `llm_serial_min`, `llm_loop_calls`,
`llm_prompt_cache_chars`. A value of `0` disables that detector.

Limits worth knowing:

- `serial_llm_calls` is a candidate, not a verdict. A trace shows timing, not whether a later
  prompt needs an earlier answer.
- `duplicate_llm_call` compares hashes of the prompt-bearing arguments (system, messages,
  tools, input). Model output may legitimately differ between identical prompts.
- `uncached_large_prompt` only looks at Anthropic, whose caching is opt-in. OpenAI caches
  automatically.
- Hashes are computed over at most the first two million characters of the arguments.

## Usage summary

```text
GET api/llm?window=24h
```

Returns sampled calls, errors, streamed calls, `input_tokens`, `output_tokens`,
`cache_read_tokens` and `cache_creation_tokens` per route and model, with totals. Agents get
the same data from the `llm_summary` MCP tool. Prices are not included because they change;
multiply the token counts by your own rates. Only the newest 300 traces in the window are
scanned and counts are labelled sampled.

```python
PRICE_PER_MTOK = {"claude-x": (3.0, 15.0)}          # your own numbers: (input, output)
cost = sum(PRICE_PER_MTOK[r["model"]][0] * r["input_tokens"] / 1e6
           + PRICE_PER_MTOK[r["model"]][1] * r["output_tokens"] / 1e6
           for r in data["items"] if r["model"] in PRICE_PER_MTOK)
```

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/load-testing.md -->
<!-- page: Load testing -->

# Load testing

[← Index](index.md)

Load testers such as Locust, k6 and Gatling see an application from the outside. They can
tell you the p95 doubled at 150 requests per second. They cannot tell you **which query**
went from 3 ms to 410 ms. Redline's profiler sees the inside, one request at a time. The
load tester joins the two: it drives your app at a controlled rate, tags every request, and
then shows, per step of the test, **what got slower inside the server**.

```text
Bottlenecks                      10 rps     50 rps    100 rps   150 rps    growth
SELECT ... FROM shop_order ...    3.1 ms     4.0 ms    62 ms    410 ms     132x
GET /api/orders                    18 ms      24 ms    120 ms   690 ms      38x
```

It ships in `redline-core`. Install the `load` extra (it needs `httpx`):

```bash
pip install "redline-core[load] @ git+https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline#subdirectory=packages/redline-core"
```

The command is `redline`.

## Concepts

You can skip this section and use the [quickstart](#quickstart), but the three ideas below
decide whether a load test tells you the truth.

### Open versus closed model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph closed["Closed model: N users in a loop"]
        direction LR
        u1[user] --> s1[send] --> w1[wait for response] --> t1[think] --> u1
    end
    subgraph open["Open model: fixed arrival rate"]
        direction LR
        clock(["clock: R requests per second"]) --> s2[send] --> srv[server]
        clock --> s3[send] --> srv
        clock --> s4[send] --> srv
    end
```

A **closed** model runs N virtual users in a loop: send a request, wait for the response,
think, send the next. When the server slows down, the users slow down too, so the offered
load *falls* exactly when you most need it to hold. The test politely stops hurting the
server it is meant to stress.

An **open** model sends requests at a fixed arrival **rate**, whether or not earlier ones
have finished, the way independent users on the internet behave. When the server slows
down, requests pile up, queues grow and latency climbs, which is what happens in
production. Redline uses the open model: you choose requests per second, not users.

### Coordinated omission

A load generator that waits for each response before sending the next one measures the
wrong thing: if one request stalls for two seconds, it silently *omits* the requests it
should have sent in that time, and the slow period is under-counted. This is **coordinated
omission**, and it makes latency charts look much better than reality.

Redline schedules each arrival on a timetable and measures latency from the **scheduled**
time, not from when the request was finally sent. If the generator was late, or the
connection pool was busy, that waiting counts. Arrivals that cannot even be started
because too many requests are already in flight are counted as **dropped** and shown in
the results, never hidden.

### The knee

Plot achieved throughput and p95 latency against offered load. For a while the server keeps
up: latency is flat, throughput follows the target. Then, at some load, it bends: latency
shoots up, errors appear, or throughput stops following the target. That bend is the
**knee**, and the load just before it is your **maximum healthy rate**.

Redline finds the knee for you in a ramp or step test. It is the first complete step where
any of these is true:

- p95 is more than **2x** the first step's p95;
- the error rate is above **1%**;
- the achieved rate is below **90%** of the target.

The p95 rule compares with the first step, so the first step can only be the knee through
errors or a missed target. A step cut short by a stop is reported but never decides the
knee.

## Quickstart

1. Start your app (with Redline mounted, so the run can be correlated; see below).
2. Generate a scenario from what Redline already knows:

   ```bash
   redline load init --from-traces -o scenario.toml
   ```

   or from an OpenAPI schema:

   ```bash
   redline load init --from-openapi http://localhost:8000/openapi.json -o scenario.toml
   ```

3. Open `scenario.toml`, check the `base_url` and the request list, and set weights.
4. Run a step test:

   ```bash
   redline load scenario.toml --steps 10:100:10 --step-duration 20s
   ```

   That is 10, 20, ... 100 requests per second, 20 seconds each.

5. Read the table, then open the run in the UI (the link is printed at the end as
   "Open the run in Redline: …") to see the chart and the bottlenecks. The link uses
   `--ui-url`, else the scenario's `ui_url`, else `mount_path` from your project's Redline config,
   else `/_redline`; with Django (mounted where your URLconf puts it, often `/redline/`) pass
   `--ui-url /redline` or set `ui_url` in the scenario.

```text
redline load: browse → http://127.0.0.1:8000
run 7c1e...: steps 10 to 100 rps by 10, 20s each
step   target  achieved    sent      ok    err   drop      p50      p95      p99      max   err%
   1     10.0      10.0     200     200      0      0     12ms     21ms     38ms     64ms   0.0%
   2     20.0      20.0     400     400      0      0     13ms     23ms     41ms     70ms   0.0%
   ...
   7     70.0      69.8    1396    1390      6      0     41ms    190ms    420ms    910ms   0.4%
   8     80.0      71.2    1424    1380     44      0    210ms    1.40s    2.10s    3.50s   3.1%

total: sent 6420  ok 6370  errors 50  dropped 0  p50 38ms  p95 410ms  p99 1.80s
knee: step 8 – error rate 3.1% > 1%
max ok rps: 69.8
verdict: saturated (knee at step 8 (80 rps): error rate 3.1% > 1%)
```

!!! warning "Test an environment you own"

    A load test is an attack on whatever it points at. Run it against your own local,
    staging or review environment. Never point it at a production system, a shared
    dependency or someone else's service. In a shared staging environment, tell the
    people who use it.

### Correlating with the app

Every request carries a header `X-Redline-Run: <run_id>;step=<n>`. A Redline-instrumented
app turns it into the trace tags `run_id` and `step`, as long as that run is in the app's
store and running (or ended less than a minute ago): a made-up header tags nothing, and a
run with `--no-store`, or written to another store, does not tag the app's traces. The
**bottleneck** analysis joins
those tags with the per-query summaries, so the app must be recording the load. Remember
[sampling](production.md#sampling): in a profile that keeps 5% of requests you still get
enough traces at high rps, but at 5 rps you may get none. Raise `sample_rate` on the
instance under test.

The run itself (its steps and latency histograms) is written to the same store the app
uses. The default is `.redline/redline.db` in the working directory, and `--store` points
elsewhere, so run the command from the app's directory or pass the path. The UI then lists
it under **Load**.

## Profiles

A profile says how the rate changes over time.

| Mode | Shape | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `constant` | one step at a fixed rate | `rps`, `duration_s` |
| `ramp` | the rate rises (or falls) linearly | `start_rps`, `end_rps`, `duration_s`, `step_duration_s` (default 5 s) |
| `steps` | a staircase | `start_rps`, `end_rps`, `step_rps`, `step_duration_s` (default 30 s) |

Results are reported **per step**. A ramp is reported in steps too (each at the ramp's
rate at the step's midpoint), so the knee finder works on it. Prefer `steps` when looking
for a knee: each step is long enough for a stable p95, and "the server held 70 rps and
broke at 80" is a sentence you can act on.

`stop_on` ends the run after the first step that breaches a limit, so a test does not keep
hammering a server that has already fallen over:

```toml
[profile]
mode = "steps"
start_rps = 10
end_rps = 200
step_rps = 10
step_duration_s = "20s"
stop_on = { error_rate = 0.05, p95_ms = 2000 }
```

Arrivals are evenly spaced by default. `poisson = true` (or `--poisson`) uses random
inter-arrival times with the same mean, which is closer to independent real users and
produces burstier queues.

## Scenario reference

A scenario is a **TOML** file (Python 3.11 or newer, or the `tomli` package), a **JSON**
file, or a **Python** file that defines `SCENARIO = {...}`.

```toml
name = "browse"
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
headers = { Accept = "application/json" }
timeout_s = 10

[[requests]]
name = "orders"
path = "/api/orders/?page={random_int:1:20}"
weight = 3

[[requests]]
name = "order detail"
path = "/api/orders/{random_int:1:500}/"
weight = 5

[[requests]]
name = "add to cart"
method = "POST"
path = "/api/cart/"
json = { sku = "A-1", qty = 1 }
expect_status = [200, 201]

[profile]
mode = "steps"
start_rps = 10
end_rps = 100
step_rps = 10
step_duration_s = "20s"
stop_on = { error_rate = 0.05, p95_ms = 2000 }
```

### Top-level keys

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | file name | Shown in the UI |
| `description` | | Free text |
| `base_url` | required, here or with `--base-url` | `http://` or `https://` root of the app. Requests use paths only |
| `headers` | `{}` | Sent with every request |
| `timeout_s` | `10` | Per-request timeout. A timeout is an error |
| `requests` | required | A non-empty list. At least one needs `weight > 0` |
| `profile` | constant 10 rps for 30 s | See [Profiles](#profiles) |
| `workers` | min(CPUs, 8) | Worker **processes** |
| `connections` | `64` | Keep-alive connections per worker |
| `max_inflight` | `1000` | In-flight cap per worker; arrivals beyond it are counted `dropped` |
| `seed` | random | Integer seed for placeholders and request choice, for repeatable runs |
| `ui_url` | config `mount_path`, else `/_redline` | Where the Redline UI is mounted (path on `base_url`'s host, or a full URL); only used for the printed link |

Durations accept a number of seconds or strings such as `"20s"`, `"2m"`.

### Request keys

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | method and path | Label in results |
| `method` | `GET` | `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE` |
| `path` | required | Must start with `/`. May contain placeholders |
| `weight` | `1` | Relative frequency. `0` keeps the request in the file but never sends it |
| `headers` | `{}` | Added to the top-level headers |
| `json` | none | A JSON body; sets `Content-Type: application/json` |
| `body` | none | A raw string body |
| `expect_status` | any status below 400 | A list of acceptable status codes. Anything else counts as an error |

### Placeholders

Rendered separately for every request:

| Placeholder | Result |
|---|---|
| `{random_int:A:B}` | a random integer from A to B, inclusive |
| `{random_choice:a\|b\|c}` | one of the listed values |
| `{uuid}` | a fresh random UUID (32 hex digits, no dashes) |

Any other `{...}` in a path is an **error**, so an OpenAPI path such as `/orders/{id}` can
never be sent by accident.

### Authentication

Put credentials in `headers`. Do not commit tokens: read them from the environment in a
Python scenario.

```python
# scenario.py
import os

SCENARIO = {
    "name": "authenticated browse",
    "base_url": "http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    "headers": {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['LOAD_TOKEN']}"},
    "requests": [{"path": "/api/orders/", "weight": 1}],
    "profile": {"mode": "constant", "rps": 50, "duration_s": 30},
}
```

## CLI reference

`redline load SCENARIO [options]`. Options override the scenario:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--rps N` | constant rate |
| `--ramp A:B` | ramp from A to B rps over `--duration` |
| `--steps A:B:STEP` | steps from A to B rps, STEP apart, each `--step-duration` |
| `--duration 60s` | total duration (default 30 s for constant and ramp) |
| `--step-duration 30s` | length of each step |
| `--poisson` | Poisson arrivals instead of evenly spaced |
| `--workers N` | worker processes |
| `--base-url URL` | override the scenario's `base_url` |
| `--ui-url PATH\|URL` | where the Redline UI is mounted, for the printed link (overrides the scenario's `ui_url`) |
| `--name TEXT` | run name |
| `--store PATH` | store to write the run to (default `.redline/redline.db`) |
| `--no-store` | do not write to a store |
| `--json OUT` | also write the results as JSON |
| `--fail-p95-ms X` | exit 1 if the run-wide p95 exceeds X ms |
| `--fail-error-rate Y` | exit 1 if the error rate exceeds Y (`0.01` or `1%`) |
| `--quiet`, `-q` | only print the final table |
| `--ui-url URL` | the Redline UI address printed in the "See bottlenecks in the Redline UI at ..." line after the run. Default: the scenario's host plus the `mount_path` setting (from `redline.toml` or `REDLINE_MOUNT_PATH`), else `/_redline` |

`--rps`, `--ramp` and `--steps` are mutually exclusive. `redline load init` writes
scenarios; see [Generating scenarios](#generating-scenarios).

Exit codes: `0` ok, `1` a `--fail-*` threshold was breached or the run failed, `2` usage or
scenario error, `130` interrupted with Ctrl-C (the partial results are still saved).

### Workers

The generator runs as several **processes** (asyncio and httpx in each), not threads, so
that the Python GIL in the generator does not cap the rate it can offer or distort the
latency it measures. Each worker sends per-second histograms to the parent. All workers
follow the same precomputed plan from a shared start time, so step boundaries line up
without any messaging. The number of workers never exceeds the target rate.

For a high rate, raise `--workers` up to your core count, leaving one for the app if it
runs on the same machine. A generator on the same machine competes with the app for CPU;
for numbers you trust, run it from another host.

## Reading the results

![A load run: steps, latency chart, the knee and the bottlenecks found under load](assets/screenshots/fastapi-load-light.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-light }
![A load run: steps, latency chart, the knee and the bottlenecks found under load](assets/screenshots/fastapi-load-dark.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-dark }

### The step table

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `target`, `achieved` | the offered rate, and what was actually completed per second |
| `sent`, `ok`, `err` | requests started, successful, failed |
| `drop` | arrivals that could not start because the in-flight cap was reached. Non-zero means the **generator** or the server's queue was saturated |
| `p50`, `p95`, `p99`, `max` | latency, from the *scheduled* time |
| `err%` | errors divided by completed requests |

An error is a status outside `expect_status`, a timeout, or a connection failure; the
final summary breaks them down (`timeout x12, 503 x31`).

The verdict is one word:

| Verdict | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `healthy` | no knee in the tested range. Raise the top of the range to find it |
| `saturated` | a knee after at least one good step. `max ok rps` is the last good step |
| `failing` | the very first step is already the knee. Lower the starting rate |
| `no data` | no complete step |

### Bottlenecks

The **Bottlenecks** table in the UI answers "what got slower". It joins the traces tagged
with the run, step by step, with their per-fingerprint and per-route summaries:

| Item kind | Compared |
|---|---|
| `sql` | mean time per execution of each query, by step |
| `route` | mean time per request of each endpoint, by step |

Each item shows its mean and p95 at every step and a **growth** factor: the last step's
mean divided by the first's (floored at 0.01 ms to avoid dividing by nothing). Items are
sorted by growth, so the top row is the thing that degraded most as load rose. Click one
to open a sample trace, with its callsite.

### What a bottleneck usually means

| Pattern | Usually |
|---|---|
| One SQL statement's time grows 100x | a missing index or a lock; run [EXPLAIN](explain.md) on a sample |
| Every statement grows together; routes grow | the database or its pool is saturated. Look for `pool_wait` spans ([Transactions and locks](transactions.md#pool-waits)) |
| SQL flat, routes grow | the app itself: CPU, GIL, [blocking in async](async-blocking.md), or a downstream call |
| `dropped` rises with flat server latency | the generator is the limit. More workers, or another machine |
| Errors with no matching traces | requests are rejected before the app records them (proxy, worker queue) |

## CI usage

`--fail-p95-ms` and `--fail-error-rate` turn a run into a gate. The exit code is `1` on a
breach, with the reason printed:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/perf.yml (excerpt)
- name: Start the app
  run: |
    python manage.py migrate
    python manage.py runserver 8000 &
    sleep 5
- name: Smoke load test
  run: |
    redline load scenario.toml --rps 30 --duration 30s \
      --fail-p95-ms 400 --fail-error-rate 1% \
      --json load-result.json --no-store
- uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
  if: always()
  with:
    name: load-result
    path: load-result.json
```

Notes for stable CI numbers:

- Shared CI runners are noisy. Use **generous** thresholds, or compare against a stored
  baseline rather than an absolute number. Use `constant` at a rate comfortably below the
  knee: the goal is to catch a regression, not to find capacity.
- The gate checks the **whole run**, not each step.
- `--json` writes the full per-step results for archiving. `--no-store` skips the SQLite
  file when there is no UI to view it in.

## Starting a run from the UI

With `load_from_ui = True` the **Load** page has a form that starts a run against the app
that serves the UI. It is **off by default** (`403 load_disabled`) and needs
`redline-core[load]`, a file-backed SQLite store, and a store the background process can
write to. It is also blocked by `read_only` (`403 read_only`) and the `load` feature
switch (`404 feature_disabled`), and the `production` preset keeps it off. Turn it on only
in environments where load is welcome. See [Security](security.md#load-from-the-ui).

**Where the run goes.** The request list can contain only paths (a single leading `/`; no
scheme or host), so the form cannot aim the server at somebody else. The target is the
`base_url` setting when you set it. Otherwise it is `127.0.0.1` on the port the server is
**listening** on (ASGI `scope["server"]`, WSGI `SERVER_PORT`), plus the script root; the
`Host` header is never used, so a request cannot aim the run at another service on the
machine. When the port is unknown (the app listens on a unix socket), or the app is not
reachable on `127.0.0.1` (it listens on one specific interface, or behind a container
port mapping), `POST api/runs` answers `400 invalid_body` or the run fails to connect: set
`base_url`:

```toml
# redline.toml
base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"      # the application's own address
```

A `base_url` or `workers` key in the request body is ignored.

**Limits.** Runs started from the UI are capped more tightly than the CLI: at most one
hour, 5 000 requests per second and 200 steps; the body needs a `name`, a non-empty
`requests` list, and a `profile` with a `mode` (`constant`, `ramp` or `steps`), a positive
`duration_s` and the rates that mode needs. A run goes through the same scenario
validation as a file. It runs in a detached `redline load` process, writes into the same
store, and is listed with status `running`, then `done`, `stopped` (you stopped it) or
`failed`. The run's stored config has secret-looking header values, body keys and URL secrets masked (the raw scenario lives in a mode 0600 file that is deleted when the run ends).

The same actions are in the API: `POST api/runs` (`202`), `POST api/runs/{id}/stop`,
`DELETE api/runs/{id}` (`409 run_active` while it runs) ([HTTP API](http-api.md#runs)).

## Generating scenarios

Writing a scenario by hand is fine for a handful of endpoints; for a real app, generate a
starting point and edit it.

| Source | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAPI** (FastAPI, Litestar, Django Ninja) | `redline load init --from-openapi URL_OR_FILE` | Path parameters get example values. Operations with required query or header parameters, and all non-GET operations, are written with `weight = 0` so you opt in after reviewing |
| **Captured traffic** | `redline load init --from-traces` | Takes the busiest endpoints from your store (`--top`, `--window`), picks a concrete sample path for each, weights GETs by their share of traffic. Bodies are never copied |
| **Django URLconf** | `python manage.py redline_scenario [-o FILE] [--base-url URL] [--force]` | Every GET route; routes without parameters get `weight = 1`. A parameterised route (`<int:pk>`) is filled with a concrete path from a recent trace of that route, and left out when there is none. The `admin` namespace and Redline's own URLs are skipped. Django Ninja and DRF routes are included. Prints to stdout without `-o` |
| **Flask `url_map`** | `flask redline scenario [-o FILE] [--base-url URL] [--force]` | The same rule over the `url_map` (static files and Redline's own routes skipped). Default base URL `http://127.0.0.1:5000` |

`redline load init` options:

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--from-openapi URL\|FILE` | an OpenAPI 3 or Swagger 2 document |
| `--from-traces` | captured traffic in `--store` |
| `--store PATH` | for `--from-traces` (default `.redline/redline.db`) |
| `--window 24h` | how far back to look |
| `--top 10` | endpoints to keep |
| `--include-writes` | also include POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE (written with `weight = 0`) |
| `--base-url URL` | set `base_url` |
| `-o, --out PATH` | output file; `.toml` or `.json`; `-` prints to stdout (default `scenario.toml`) |
| `--force` | overwrite an existing file |

The generator validates its own output, so a scenario it writes can be run. Write requests
are always disabled by default: a load test that POSTs and DELETEs against a real
database is something to choose deliberately.

## Limits

- It tests **HTTP endpoints over the network**. It does not model browsers, WebSockets or
  think time.
- Latency is as measured by the generator, including the network and the generator's own
  event loop. Distrust sub-millisecond numbers.
- Correlated bottlenecks need the app to record the load; with strong sampling, or a
  store the app is not writing to, the table is empty.
- Run records live in the Redline SQLite store and are subject to
  [history retention](history.md#retention).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/history.md -->
<!-- page: History and releases -->

# History and releases

[← Index](index.md)

Redline keeps individual traces for a few days. That is the right window for debugging a
request, and the wrong one for the question you ask after every deploy: **did this release
make anything slower?**

The **History** page answers it. It keeps small, hourly summaries of every endpoint for 90
days, remembers which release was running, and compares any two releases or time ranges
side by side, with a verdict per endpoint and the issues that appeared or went away.

## How it works

Three things are stored, all written in the same transaction as the trace itself, and all
kept for `history_retention_days` (default 90) regardless of how soon the traces are
pruned:

| Table | What it holds |
|---|---|
| **rollups** | per hour, release, route and method: request count, errors, summed duration, a mergeable latency **histogram**, summed queries and query time, issue count |
| **releases** | each release name, when it was first and last seen, and how many requests it served |
| **issue index** | every issue ever seen: kind, severity, title, route, first and last seen, first and last release, occurrences. It **survives trace pruning** |

The latency histogram is log-linear (HDR-style, about 1% relative error from 1 microsecond
to an hour). Because histograms merge exactly, p50, p95 and p99 over a week are computed
from the hourly rows, not averaged from percentiles (which would be wrong).

History reflects **kept** traces. With `sample_rate = 0.1` it is built from a 10% sample
(plus every slow request and error), so counts are the sample's, and percentiles are
representative. Requests that are ignored or dropped are not included.

## Releases

A trace is stamped with a release when it is recorded. Redline resolves the name once, at
configure time, from the first of:

1. the `release` setting;
2. the environment variable `REDLINE_RELEASE`;
3. `GIT_SHA`, `SOURCE_VERSION`, `RENDER_GIT_COMMIT` or `HEROKU_SLUG_COMMIT`, which most
   platforms already set;
4. `git rev-parse --short HEAD` in `project_root`, run once with a one-second timeout;
5. nothing. History still works, grouped as one unnamed release.

```python
REDLINE = {"RELEASE": os.environ.get("APP_VERSION")}   # or set it in CI
```

Use something that changes on every deploy and is meaningful to you: a git SHA, a version,
a build number. The release markers on the timeline are placed where each name is first
seen.

## The History page

![The History page with release markers](assets/screenshots/fastapi-history-light.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-light }
![The History page with release markers](assets/screenshots/fastapi-history-dark.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-dark }

Choose an endpoint (or the whole app) and a window. Four charts share one time axis, with
a vertical marker at each release:

- **Latency percentiles**: p50, p95 and p99.
- **Request count.**
- **Error rate.**
- **Average queries per request.**

Buckets are one hour for windows up to two days, otherwise one day. Only non-empty buckets
are drawn, and time is UTC-aligned. The same series is served by
`GET api/history` ([HTTP API](http-api.md#get-apihistory)).

## Before and after: comparing periods

A period is a **release** or a **time range**:

| Form | Example |
|---|---|
| a release | `release:3f9c2ab` |
| a range | `range:1761400000-1761486400` (start and end, epoch seconds) |

Pick a baseline (**A**) and the period under test (**B**) and Redline compares them
endpoint by endpoint. Each row carries both periods' request count, error rate, p50, p95,
p99, average duration and average queries, the p95 change, and a **verdict**:

| Verdict | Rule |
|---|---|
| `regressed` | p95 up **20% or more and 5 ms or more**, or average queries up by 1 or more |
| `improved` | the mirror image: p95 down 20% and 5 ms, or average queries down by 1 |
| `same` | none of the above |
| `new` | the endpoint exists in B only |
| `gone` | the endpoint exists in A only |

Rows are sorted regressed, new, improved, gone, same, so the problems are on top. The
double condition on latency (a relative *and* an absolute change) stops a 0.3 ms endpoint
doubling to 0.6 ms from being a headline. Compare two real releases that each served a
meaningful amount of traffic; an endpoint with a handful of requests is noise.

### Issues: new, resolved, persisting

Below the table, the same two periods' **issues** are diffed:

| Group | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **New** | present in B, not in A. Candidates for "this release introduced it" |
| **Resolved** | present in A, gone in B. Did the fix work? |
| **Persisting** | present in both, with B's occurrence count |

Each links to a sample request while its traces still exist. The issue index itself
outlives the traces, so you can still read "N+1 on `/orders/`, first seen in `3f9c2ab`,
last seen in `a81d0e4`" months later.

### A typical use

1. Deploy `release B`. Let it serve traffic for an hour or a day.
2. Open **History**, choose A = the previous release, B = the new one.
3. Read the regressed endpoints and the new issues. Open a sample trace for each.

For the same comparison on two single requests, use [Compare](the-ui.md#compare-two-requests).
For a comparison in your CI pipeline, see the [roadmap](roadmap.md) (v0.3).

## Retention

| Setting | Default | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `history_retention_days` | `90` | rollups, issue index, releases, load runs |
| `max_age_days`, `max_rows` | `7`, `10000` | individual traces (and their `trace_sql`, `trace_ext`, `trace_cache` summaries) |

The two are independent: traces can be pruned after a week while the hourly rollups live
for 90 days. `0` or `None` for `history_retention_days` keeps history forever.

When pruning runs it deletes rollup hours that ended before the cutoff, releases and issue
index entries last seen before it, and load runs (with their steps) created before it, but
never a run that is still running. **Clear all** and `manage.py redline_clear` delete
traces but **keep history**; the API and store can wipe history too
(`clear(history=True)`). See [Storage](storage.md#history-tables).

## Upgrading an existing store

A store written by 0.1 is migrated in place the first time 0.2 opens it. The new tables are
created and **backfilled from the traces still in the file**, in one transaction, so history
starts from whatever was there (at most the retained week) rather than from zero. If several
workers start at once, the migration runs once. See [Storage](storage.md#the-schema).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/django.md -->
<!-- page: Django -->

# Django

[← Index](index.md)

`django-redline` adds Redline to a Django project: one app, one middleware and one URL
mount. It supports Django 5.2 (LTS), 6.0 and 6.1 on Python 3.12 and later, under both WSGI
and ASGI, with sync and async views.

```python
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [..., "django_redline"]

MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "django_redline.middleware.RedlineMiddleware",     # as high as possible
    ...,
]

# urls.py
urlpatterns = [..., path("redline/", include("django_redline.urls"))]
```

Install it as described in [Getting started](getting-started.md#install). There are
**no migrations** and no models: Redline never touches your database.

## The pieces

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| `"django_redline"` in `INSTALLED_APPS` | `RedlineConfig.ready()` installs the SQL, cache, template and view hooks, and registers the system checks |
| `django_redline.middleware.RedlineMiddleware` | starts and finishes a trace per request; sync and async capable |
| `include("django_redline.urls")` | serves the UI at the mount and the [JSON API](http-api.md) under `api/`. The URL namespace is `redline` (`redline:index`, `redline:asset`, `redline:api`) |
| `REDLINE = {...}` | optional settings; see the [reference](settings.md) |
| `django_redline.span` | re-export of [`redline_core.span`](custom-spans.md) |

## Middleware placement

Put `RedlineMiddleware` **near the top**, because the time of everything *below* it is part
of the trace and everything above it is not.

```python
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    # "django.middleware.gzip.GZipMiddleware",       # keep above Redline if you use it
    "django_redline.middleware.RedlineMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.common.CommonMiddleware",
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",
    "django.contrib.messages.middleware.MessageMiddleware",
]
```

| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| **Below** `GZipMiddleware` | otherwise Redline sees compressed bodies (check `W002`) |
| **Above** session, common, CSRF, auth and messages middleware | so their time is in the trace (check `W003`) |
| After `SecurityMiddleware` | its redirects need no tracing |

The whole stack under Redline appears as a `middleware` span, with the `view` span inside
it.

## The URL mount

```python
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("redline/", include("django_redline.urls")),
]
```

Any prefix works: the UI uses hash routing and relative URLs. The **trailing slash
matters**: `/redline` redirects to `/redline/` through `APPEND_SLASH`. Requests under the
mount are **never recorded**; the middleware resolves the mount with
`reverse("redline:index")`.

If you mount it behind a `path("internal/", ...)` that your auth already protects, you get
that protection **in addition to** Redline's own permission check.

## Settings

```python
REDLINE = {
    "SAMPLE_RATE": 1.0,
    "SLOW_QUERY_MS": 50,
    "IGNORE_PATHS": ["/static/", "/media/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health"],
    "PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.can_view",
}
```

Every key is a [core setting](settings.md) (case-insensitive) except `PERMISSION` and
`STORE`. What Django adds:

| Behaviour | Detail |
|---|---|
| `SAMPLE_RATE` default | `1.0` with `DEBUG = True`, **`0.1` with `DEBUG = False`** |
| `STORAGE_PATH` default | `<BASE_DIR>/.redline/redline.db` when `BASE_DIR` is defined |
| `PROJECT_ROOT` default | `BASE_DIR`. It decides which stack frames count as your code |
| Errors | An unknown key or a bad value raises `ImproperlyConfigured` carrying the core message, and the system check `django_redline.E001` reports it |
| Paths | `STORAGE_PATH` and `PROJECT_ROOT` accept a string or a `pathlib.Path` (`BASE_DIR / ".redline" / "redline.db"`) |
| `STORE` | Where traces are kept, like FastAPI's `install(store=...)`. See [Custom store](#custom-store) |

The runtime (settings, store, recorder, API) is built **lazily on first use**, not in
`AppConfig.ready()`, so management commands like `migrate` never create `.redline/`. It is
rebuilt when `REDLINE`, `DEBUG` or `BASE_DIR` change through `setting_changed`, which is
what makes `override_settings(REDLINE=...)` work in tests.

## Custom store

`REDLINE["STORE"]` replaces the default `SQLiteStore.from_settings(settings)` with any
object implementing the [`Store` protocol](extending.md#the-store-protocol). It accepts:

| Value | Used as |
|---|---|
| a callable or a class, e.g. `MyStore` | called with the core `Settings`; the result is the store. Rebuilt (and the old one closed) whenever the runtime is rebuilt |
| a ready instance | used as-is. It outlives runtime rebuilds (`override_settings` only flushes it) and is closed at process exit |
| a dotted path to either, e.g. `"myproject.redline.make_store"` | imported, then as above |

```python
# myproject/redline.py
from redline_core.storage import SQLiteStore

class MirroringStore(SQLiteStore):
    def __init__(self, settings):
        super().__init__(
            settings.storage_path,
            queue_size=settings.writer_queue_size,
            max_rows=settings.max_rows,
            max_age_s=settings.max_age_s,
        )

    def save(self, trace):
        super().save(trace)
        send_somewhere_else(trace)                          # must not block

# settings.py
REDLINE = {"STORE": "myproject.redline.MirroringStore"}
```

An import error, or a value that does not produce a `Store`, raises
`ImproperlyConfigured` (and the system check `django_redline.E001`).

## What 0.2 adds for Django

| Feature | Where to read |
|---|---|
| `transaction.atomic` recorded as `transaction` spans (with `ATOMIC_REQUESTS`), long-transaction and external-call-in-transaction detection | [Transactions and locks](transactions.md) |
| DRF serializers timed as `serializer` spans | [Slow serializers](serializers.md) |
| Row counts on queries, large and unbounded results, `len(qs)` vs `.count()` / `.exists()` | [Large and unbounded results](result-size.md) |
| A sync ORM call inside an `async def` view reported as blocking the event loop | [Blocking in async](async-blocking.md) |
| Django's cache framework analysed per key pattern | [Cache efficiency](cache-efficiency.md) |
| Strawberry and Graphene resolvers (and `strawberry-django`) | [GraphQL](graphql.md) |
| Django Ninja | [Django Ninja](django-ninja.md) |
| `manage.py redline_scan` (templates and DRF) | [Static N+1 scan](static-scan.md) |
| `manage.py redline_scenario`, then `redline load` | [Load testing](load-testing.md) |
| `Server-Timing`, the floating badge (when `DEBUG`), live mode, snapshots | [Server-Timing and the badge](server-timing-badge.md) |
| `REDLINE["PRESET"]`, `redline.toml`, `REDLINE_*` | [Configuration](configuration.md) |

The badge is `"auto"` by default, which in Django means **on when `DEBUG` is true**. Nothing
changes in `MIDDLEWARE` or `urls.py`.

## Access control

Django's default access policy is `framework`: the permission check below, and it stays the
default under the `production` preset (a preset does not change it). The other policies
(`token`, `basic`, IP allow-lists, `read_only`, ...) are available through the same `REDLINE`
dict and are described on [Access control](access-control.md). When `ACCESS` is not
`"framework"`, `PERMISSION` is not consulted.

Every view, page, assets and API, first checks `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (it calls
`request.get_host()`, so this holds even without `CommonMiddleware`, a defence against
[DNS rebinding](security.md#dns-rebinding)) and then the access gate, with
`REDLINE["PERMISSION"]` as the framework hook. Top-level files such as `badge.js` skip
`PERMISSION` but not the network rules.

| | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| Who | active superusers: `user.is_active and user.is_superuser` | changed in 0.2 (was staff) |
| Anonymous, on the page | redirected to `admin:login` (or `LOGIN_URL` if the admin is not installed), with `?next=` | |
| Signed in without access, on the page | `403` plain text | |
| On the API | `403` JSON `{"error": {"code": "forbidden", ...}}` | |

!!! warning "Changed in 0.2: superusers, not staff"

    Until 0.1 any active **staff** user could open Redline. Staff status is often given
    for the admin of a single model, while Redline shows every user's requests (headers,
    SQL, bodies), so the default now asks for a superuser. To keep the 0.1 rule:

    ```python
    REDLINE = {"PERMISSION": "django_redline.conf.staff_permission"}
    ```

Override it with a callable `(request) -> bool`, or its dotted path:

```python
# myproject/redline.py
def can_view(request):
    user = request.user
    return user.is_active and user.groups.filter(name="performance").exists()
```

```python
REDLINE = {"PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.can_view"}
```

- A string that cannot be imported, or a value that is not callable, raises
  `ImproperlyConfigured` (and `E001`).
- An exception raised **inside** your callable **denies access** (fails closed).
- The check needs `request.user`, so keep `AuthenticationMiddleware` in `MIDDLEWARE`.
  Redline's own middleware does not need it.

See [Security](security.md) for the wider picture.

## CSRF

The page and `GET` calls need nothing. The mutating calls, `DELETE` (a trace, or all of
them) and `POST api/explain`, are protected by Django's own CSRF check, which Redline runs
on **every** API request **even if `CsrfViewMiddleware` is not in `MIDDLEWARE`**:

- the token must arrive in the CSRF header (`X-CSRFToken`, or whatever `CSRF_HEADER_NAME`
  says);
- on HTTPS Django's Origin and Referer checks also apply;
- a failure is a **JSON** `403` with code `csrf_failed`, not Django's HTML page.

The served page embeds a fresh token in `<meta name="redline-csrf" content="..."
data-header="...">`, and the SPA sends it back. Because the token is in the page and
not read from a cookie, this works with `CSRF_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = True` and with
`CSRF_USE_SESSIONS = True`.

Scripts calling the API must log in, keep the session cookie, and send the token. The
exception is `ACCESS = "token"`: a request carrying `Authorization: Bearer <token>` skips
Django's CSRF check. The gate's own CSRF rule (`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` or `same-site`,
or a mismatched `Origin`, refused with `403 csrf_failed`) applies as well.

## How it hooks in

Everything is installed once from `AppConfig.ready()` and is a single `ContextVar.get()` and
`None` check when nothing is being recorded.

| What | Hook | Span |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL** | a `connection.execute_wrapper` appended to **every** connection's `execute_wrappers`, through the `connection_created` signal and for connections already open | `sql` |
| **Cache** | the backends that `django.core.cache.caches` creates get their public methods wrapped | `cache` |
| **Templates** | `django.template.base.Template.render` (top-level templates and `{% include %}`) and the Jinja2 backend | `template` |
| **View** | `BaseHandler.make_view_atomic`, called by both the sync and the async handler right before the view | `view` |
| **Middleware** | the middleware itself wraps the rest of the stack | `middleware` |

Details worth knowing:

- Redline's own store is a separate `sqlite3` file, **not a Django connection**, so it can
  never record itself. Queries run by [EXPLAIN](explain.md) are explicitly suppressed.
- **Cache** spans carry `op` (`get`, `set`, `add`, `delete`, `touch`, `incr`, `decr`,
  `has_key`, `get_or_set`, `get_many`, `set_many`, `delete_many`, `clear`), the `key`
  (cut at 200 characters, or the first five keys plus a count for the `_many` calls),
  `hit` (for `get`, `get_many`, `has_key`) and `backend` (`default (LocMemCache)`). A cache
  backend object you instantiate **yourself**, not through `caches`, is not instrumented.
- **Template** spans are named after the template; queries run during rendering nest under
  them, which is how an N+1 in `{% for item in order.items.all %}` is attributed to the
  render.
- **View** spans are named by the dotted path (`shop.views.order_list`, or the class for
  class-based views) and carry `{"async": true|false}`.
- Queries issued from **library code** (a generic `ListView`, DRF, a lazily rendered
  `TemplateResponse`) have no project frame in their stack. They are attributed to the
  **project view** that handled the request, using the view's definition site. When the
  stack does not pass through the view (a serializer called by a DRF viewset), the view
  is added as the outermost frame so the [fix suggester](n-plus-one.md#how-the-fix-is-found)
  can find its queryset.

## What the middleware records

| Recorded | Notes |
|---|---|
| Method, path, **route template** (`/orders/<int:pk>/`), view | from `request.resolver_match` after the response |
| Request headers, query string | redacted before storage |
| Request body | read up front only if it is **not multipart**, has a `Content-Length` above 0 and at most `max_body_bytes`. Otherwise Redline does **not** read it (the view may stream it), and picks up whatever the view itself read |
| Response status, headers | `Set-Cookie` values from `response.cookies` are included, then redacted |
| Response body | only for non-streaming responses; **streaming and file responses are never consumed**. The size comes from `Content-Length` |
| Exceptions | `process_exception` remembers a view's exception for the trace and returns `None`: it **never handles or swallows** it. It becomes the trace's `error` only when the final response is a 5xx: `Http404`, `PermissionDenied`, `BadRequest` and friends turn into 4xx responses and are **not errors** (no `error` on the trace, not kept by `ALWAYS_KEEP_ERRORS`). An exception that escapes the stack is recorded as a 500 and re-raised |
| `X-Redline-Run` | becomes `run_id` and `step` tags (kept only for a run that is running in the store) |
| `?_redline=profile` (or `1`, `true`, `yes`, `on`) / `X-Redline-Profile: 1` | starts the [profiler](flamegraphs.md); the same values as FastAPI. Honoured with `DEBUG = True`, or when the request carries Redline credentials under `token`/`basic` (a `PERMISSION` cannot run in the middleware) |

With `DEBUG = True`, a **kept** response gets an `X-Redline-Trace: <trace id>` header so you
can find it. It is never sent in production.

## Async views

`RedlineMiddleware` declares `sync_capable` and `async_capable`. Django adapts it to the
stack automatically: under ASGI with async middleware chain it runs its async path
(`__acall__`), under WSGI its sync path. In both, state is carried by `contextvars`.

```python
async def summary(request):
    n = await Order.objects.acount()          # recorded, attributed to this line
    return JsonResponse({"orders": n})
```

- Async ORM calls (`acount`, `aget`, `async for`) are recorded; they run through the same
  connection wrapper, via `sync_to_async`, which copies context.
- Concurrent async requests do not mix (there is a test for it).
- The view span of an async view has `async: true`.

## Django REST Framework

DRF views are ordinary Django views, so they are traced like any other. The extra value is
in the fix suggester: when a **serializer** reads a relation for every object it
serializes, the suggested diff targets the **view's** `queryset` or `get_queryset()`, and
the summary says which serializer does it:

```diff
 class OrderViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
-    queryset = Order.objects.all()
+    queryset = Order.objects.prefetch_related("items")
     serializer_class = OrderSerializer
```

(Shape only: illustrative, not output copied from a run.)

!!! note "How well tested is the DRF support?"

    The repository's tests exercise this with a small stand-in for `Serializer` and a
    viewset-shaped class, not with `rest_framework` itself, and the demo shop does not use
    DRF. The mechanism looks at class names ending in `Serializer` and at the view's
    `queryset`/`get_queryset`. It should hold for real DRF; it has not been run against it.

## Multiple databases

Every connection gets the wrapper, and each SQL span stores its `db_alias` (`default`,
`replica`, ...) and `vendor`. EXPLAIN runs on `connections[db_alias]`. If the span's alias
no longer exists, or the connection's vendor differs from the recorded one, EXPLAIN answers
`501 explain_unavailable`. Vendors other than PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite record SQL but
cannot be explained.

## System checks

`manage.py check` (and `runserver`) run these.

For filesystem store paths, the storage check uses effective process permissions:
creates/writes/removes its own temporary probe in the nearest existing parent, and
opens an existing target for writing without truncating or modifying it. It does not
initialize the database. Root may legitimately write through restrictive mode bits;
read-only mounts and refused filesystem operations still produce `E002`.

| ID | Level | Problem | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| `django_redline.E001` | Error | `REDLINE` is invalid: an unknown key (with a "did you mean"), a bad value, a bad `PERMISSION` | Fix the setting |
| `django_redline.E002` | Error | The storage location cannot be created or is not writable | Point `STORAGE_PATH` somewhere writable |
| `django_redline.W001` | Warning | `RedlineMiddleware` is not in `MIDDLEWARE`, so nothing is recorded | Add it near the top |
| `django_redline.W002` | Warning | `GZipMiddleware` is **after** Redline, so bodies are compressed | Move Redline below it |
| `django_redline.W003` | Warning | Redline is listed **after** session, common, CSRF, auth or messages middleware, so their time is not traced | Move Redline above them |
| `django_redline.W004` | Warning | `django_redline.urls` is not mounted, so the UI is unreachable | Add the `include()` |
| `django_redline.W005` | Warning | `DEBUG` is false and `SAMPLE_RATE` is `1.0` | Lower it, or leave it unset for `0.1` |

All are registered under the `compatibility` tag. `E002` and `W005` are only checked when
Redline is enabled; the others always run.

## Management commands

| Command | Does |
|---|---|
| `manage.py redline_clear [--noinput]` | Deletes every recorded trace. Asks for confirmation (`Delete all N Redline traces? [y/N]`) unless `--noinput` or `--no-input` |
| `manage.py redline_prune [--max-age-days N] [--max-rows N]` | Applies [retention](storage.md#retention) now. Defaults to the `MAX_AGE_DAYS` and `MAX_ROWS` settings. `0` disables that rule for this run (it never deletes everything: that is `redline_clear`). Negative values are an error |
| `manage.py redline_scan [PATHS] [--json] [--fail] [--dialect django\|jinja] [--no-drf]` | [Static N+1 scan](static-scan.md): templates that read a relation in a loop, and DRF serializers whose queryset lacks the matching `select_related` / `prefetch_related`. `--fail` exits 1 on findings |
| `manage.py redline_scenario [-o FILE] [--base-url URL] [--force]` | Writes a [load-test scenario](load-testing.md#generating-scenarios) from your URLconf (stdout without `-o`) |

`redline_clear` and `redline_prune` build the runtime, flush pending writes, and print how
many traces they removed. `redline_clear` keeps [history](history.md). Run
`redline_prune` from cron if your app is idle for long stretches (the writer prunes as
it writes, so an idle app does not prune on its own).

```console
$ python manage.py redline_prune --max-age-days 1
Pruned 4120 trace(s); 880 left.
```

## Under test

`override_settings(REDLINE={...})` rebuilds the runtime. To keep test runs from writing a
file, use an in-memory store, and set `PROJECT_ROOT` to the code under test so test
functions themselves do not count as "your code":

```python
REDLINE = {
    "STORAGE_PATH": ":memory:",
    "SAMPLE_RATE": 1.0,
    "PROJECT_ROOT": str(BASE_DIR / "myapp"),
}
```

To assert on traces, read the store:

```python
from django_redline.runtime import get_runtime

rt = get_runtime()
rt.store.flush(5.0)
trace = rt.store.get(rt.store.list(None, limit=1).items[0]["id"])
assert not [i for i in trace.issues if i.kind == "n_plus_one"]
```

A pytest marker for this (`@pytest.mark.redline(no_n_plus_one=True)`) is planned for
[v0.3](roadmap.md).

## Deployment notes

- **WSGI (gunicorn, uWSGI)**: the runtime is built lazily in each worker, after the
  fork, and the store is fork-safe even if something built it before the fork
  (`--preload`). Each worker writes to the same file; see
  [Production: process models](production.md#process-models).
- **ASGI (uvicorn, daphne, hypercorn)**: nothing special.
- **Behind a proxy**: the Django permission uses your session, not the client address, so
  the FastAPI proxy caveat does not apply. `ALLOWED_HOSTS` and `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS`
  must include your host as usual.
- **Containers**: `.redline/` must be writable. With a read-only root filesystem point
  `STORAGE_PATH` at a mounted volume or `/tmp`.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| `manage.py check` warns `W001` | the middleware is missing |
| The UI says 404 at `/redline` | use `/redline/` (trailing slash), or `APPEND_SLASH = False` |
| 403 for a superuser | your `PERMISSION` callable returned false or raised (it fails closed). Test it in a shell |
| `403 csrf_failed` from a script | send the `X-CSRFToken` header and the session cookie |
| No requests appear | path in `IGNORE_PATHS`; `ENABLED` false; `SAMPLE_RATE` below 1 (default `0.1` with `DEBUG = False`) |
| Empty callsites | `PROJECT_ROOT` is not an ancestor of your code (set it as a string) |
| `ImproperlyConfigured: settings.REDLINE: ... must be a string` | a `Path` in `STORAGE_PATH` or `PROJECT_ROOT`: wrap it in `str()` |
| Queries from a thread missing | a bare `threading.Thread` does not carry the trace; use `contextvars.copy_context().run` |

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/django-ninja.md -->
<!-- page: Django Ninja -->

# Django Ninja

[← Index](index.md)

[Django Ninja](https://django-ninja.dev) apps are served by `django-redline`; there is no
separate package. Install and mount Redline exactly as in [Django](django.md), and your
Ninja endpoints are recorded like any other Django view, with two Ninja-specific
improvements.

## What you get

Ninja registers **one Django view per path** and dispatches to the operation inside it.
Left alone, every Ninja request would look like `ninja.operation.view_wrapper` with a route
template that is the same for every HTTP method. Redline looks inside:

| Trace field | Without the Ninja support | With it |
|---|---|---|
| `view` | `ninja.operation.view_wrapper` | `shop.api.list_orders`, your endpoint function |
| `route` | the Django URL pattern for the path | the same, resolved per operation, so `GET /api/orders/{order_id}` and `DELETE /api/orders/{order_id}` aggregate separately on the [Endpoints](issues-and-endpoints.md#endpoints) page |

Nothing is imported unless Ninja is already loaded in the process, so non-Ninja projects
pay nothing.

## Setup

```python
# settings.py
INSTALLED_APPS = [..., "django_redline"]
MIDDLEWARE = [
    "django.middleware.security.SecurityMiddleware",
    "django_redline.middleware.RedlineMiddleware",
    ...,
]
```

```python
# urls.py
from django.urls import include, path
from ninja import NinjaAPI

api = NinjaAPI()

urlpatterns = [
    path("api/", api.urls),
    path("redline/", include("django_redline.urls")),
]
```

Your Ninja routes do not change. Sync and `async def` operations are both supported; the
async rules from [Django: async views](django.md#async-views) apply.

## Schemas and serialization

Ninja serializes with Pydantic. The `serializer` spans come from [DRF](serializers.md)
and from [FastAPI](fastapi.md); Ninja's response building is not hooked separately, so a slow
one shows up as time in the `view` span. Wrap
the suspect code in a [custom span](custom-spans.md) if you need to isolate it.

## Load testing a Ninja API

Ninja publishes an OpenAPI document, so scenarios can be generated from it:

```bash
redline load init --from-openapi http://localhost:8000/api/openapi.json -o scenario.toml
redline load scenario.toml --steps 10:100:10 --step-duration 20s
```

See [Load testing](load-testing.md#generating-scenarios).

## N+1 in Ninja endpoints

The Django fix suggester works unchanged, because Ninja endpoints use the Django ORM: an
N+1 inside `list_orders` is reported with a `select_related` or `prefetch_related` diff at
the queryset line. See [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md).

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/fastapi.md -->
<!-- page: FastAPI -->

# FastAPI

[← Index](index.md)

`fastapi-redline` adds Redline to a FastAPI (or plain Starlette) application with
SQLAlchemy. One function, `install()`, does everything.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine

from fastapi_redline import install

app = FastAPI()
engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite:///app.db")

# access="local": localhost only (unset, Redline answers 404 outside debug mode)
install(app, engine=engine, settings={"access": "local"})  # UI at http://localhost:8000/_redline/
```

Requirements: Python 3.10+, FastAPI 0.110+ (below 1.0), SQLAlchemy 2.x, and
`redline-core` at the exact version the adapter pins. Install as shown in
[Getting started](getting-started.md#install).

Since 0.2 the SQLAlchemy and httpx hooks live in `redline_core.contrib` and are shared with
the Flask and Litestar adapters; `fastapi_redline` re-exports them (`instrument_engine`,
