    ```python
        "RELEASE": os.environ.get("GIT_SHA"),
        "IGNORE_PATHS": ["/static/", "/media/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health"],
        # the token itself comes from REDLINE_TOKEN in the environment
    }
    ```

=== "FastAPI"

    ```python
    install(app, engine=engine, settings={
        "preset": "staging",
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
        "release": os.environ.get("GIT_SHA"),
        "ignore_paths": ["/static/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health"],
    })
    ```

=== "Flask"

    ```python
    app.config["REDLINE"] = {
        "preset": "staging",
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
        "release": os.environ.get("GIT_SHA"),
        "ignore_paths": ["/static/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health"],
    }
    Redline(app, engine=engine)
    ```

=== "Litestar"

    ```python
    RedlinePlugin(engine=engine, settings={
        "preset": "staging",
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
        "release": os.environ.get("GIT_SHA"),
        "ignore_paths": ["/static/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health"],
    })
    ```

## Checking your setup

```bash
redline config        # the effective configuration, its sources and any warnings
redline doctor        # checks: storage writable, UI bundle present, access policy, token, sessions, proxies, retention
```

Run `redline doctor` as a deploy-time check. See the [CLI reference](cli.md).

## Which layer should I use?

| You want to... | Use |
|---|---|
| Set thresholds the whole team shares | `redline.toml` in the repo |
| Differ per environment without code changes | `REDLINE_*` variables |
| Supply a secret | environment variable or `token_file` |
| Pass a Python object (a `Store`, a callable) | the framework settings (it cannot be written in a file) |
| Make production safe in one line | `preset = "production"` |

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/access-control.md -->
<!-- page: Access control -->

# Access control

[← Index](index.md)

The Redline UI shows SQL, request and response bodies, headers, source lines and exception
locals. Treat it like a database console. Who may open it is decided by **one policy**,
the same for every framework: `redline_core.access.check(request_info)` returns a decision,
and each adapter just asks it.

Two things always apply, whatever policy you pick: the **CSRF check** on every request
that is not a `GET`, `HEAD` or `OPTIONS` (login and logout included) and
**`X-Frame-Options: DENY`** on Redline's own responses. The CSRF check refuses
`Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` **and `same-site`**, and any `Origin` (the literal `null`
too) whose host and port differ from the host the request was addressed to; a request with
no `Origin` is not a browser and is allowed. It runs after the policy, so outsiders get the
policy's refusal first.

The order of the checks is: `ui_enabled` (off: `404`), the effective client address
(`trusted_proxies`), the network rules, the policy, feature switches and `read_only`, then
CSRF.

## Policies

Set `access` to one of:

| `access` | Who gets in | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| `local` (default, see below) | loopback clients using a loopback `Host`, plus anything in `allowed_ips` | your laptop |
| `token` | a request with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, or a browser that logged in with the token | staging, production, a shared server |
| `basic` | a user from `basic_users` (`Authorization: Basic`, or the login form) | a small team, behind a proxy that cannot do SSO |
| `framework` | the framework's own check: Django superusers or `PERMISSION`, FastAPI `dependencies`, Flask `permission`, Litestar `guards` | you already have an admin login |
| `custom` | whatever your `access_check(request_info) -> bool` returns | anything else |
| `open` | everyone | **refused** unless `REDLINE_ALLOW_OPEN=1` is also set |

The default is `local` for FastAPI, Flask and Litestar. In Django the default is
`framework`, meaning active **superusers** (staff in 0.1; see
[Django: access control](django.md#access-control)). Passing a native hook (a non-empty
FastAPI `dependencies=` or Litestar `guards=` list, a Flask `permission=` callable) switches
the default to `framework` for you, unless you set `access` yourself in the file, the
environment or the framework settings (a preset does not count). An empty list is the same
as no hook.

!!! warning "Set `access` explicitly (FastAPI, Flask, Litestar)"

    While `access` is not set anywhere (code, `redline.toml`, `REDLINE_ACCESS`), Redline
    serves the `local` default **only when the framework is in debug mode** (`app.debug`,
    for example `FastAPI(debug=True)`, `flask --debug run` or `Litestar(debug=True)`).
    Otherwise every Redline URL answers `404` and an error is logged at startup. The
    reason: a reverse proxy on the same host that adds no `X-Forwarded-For`
    (`proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8000;` with no `proxy_set_header`) makes every visitor a
    loopback client addressing a loopback `Host`, so `local` would let the whole internet
    in. Choose: `access = "token"` or `"basic"` on any server, or `access = "local"` on a
    development machine where you accept that risk.


### Local

Only loopback clients (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`) that address the server by a
loopback name (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `[::1]`, any port) are served. The
`Host` check defeats DNS rebinding: a malicious page cannot make your browser talk to
`evil.example`, resolve it to `127.0.0.1`, and read your traces. `allowed_ips` adds client
networks, and `allowed_hosts` adds accepted `Host` values (ports are ignored).

If a loopback peer sends `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP` or `Forwarded` and is **not** in
`trusted_proxies`, the request is refused with `403 forbidden`, and `api/config` carries a
warning. A reverse proxy running on the same host would otherwise make every visitor look
local. Set `trusted_proxies` (see [Network restrictions](#network-restrictions)) or use
`token`.

A **unix-socket** peer (the app listens on a socket, so there is no client address) is not
local: a proxy on the same machine is the usual reason for one. Set
`trust_unix_socket = true` if only you can reach that socket.

### Token

```bash
REDLINE_ACCESS=token
REDLINE_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)       # or token_file=/run/secrets/redline_token
```

Clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. In a browser, the UI shows a **login screen**
when the API answers `401 login_required`; you paste the token once, and Redline sets an
HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict cookie (`Secure` when the effective scheme is https, see
`cookie_secure`) scoped to
its own mount path, valid for `session_ttl_s` (12 hours by default). The token is compared
as SHA-256 digests in constant time and is never logged or shown, not even on the Settings
page. The page shell and its assets (and `badge.js`) are public because they hold no data;
**every `api/` call needs credentials**.

Outside the `dev` preset the token must be at least 24 characters, or Redline refuses to
start and prints a command to generate one. A `token_file` is read once at startup; keep its
permissions to the owner only (`redline doctor` warns otherwise).

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDLINE_TOKEN" https://staging.example.com/_redline/api/meta
```

A failed credential (login body, Bearer or Basic) counts against the client address (an
IPv4 address, or the IPv6 /64 it belongs to). After `max_login_attempts` (10) within 300 seconds, further credential attempts from that
address answer `429 too_many_requests` with `Retry-After`; a success resets it, and
requests carrying a valid session cookie are never limited. The counters are in memory and
per process; a full table evicts expired and unblocked entries before blocked ones.
For an unknown Basic user name the password is still hashed with the same iteration count
as the configured users, so response time does not reveal which names exist. Behind a proxy without `trusted_proxies` all clients share one bucket
(`redline doctor` warns).

!!! warning "Several worker processes need `secret_key`"

    Login cookies are signed with `secret_key`. When it is unset each process generates a
    random key, so a login only works on the worker that issued it and every restart logs
    everyone out. Set `secret_key` (16 characters or more, for example
    `REDLINE_SECRET_KEY`) for any multi-worker deployment. Rotating the key, the token or
    a password revokes all sessions. Logout clears the cookie **and revokes that session**
    in the process that answered: the cookie is refused there until it would have expired.
    The revocation list lives in memory, so with several worker processes another worker
    still accepts a copy of the cookie until it expires (or until you rotate
    `secret_key`).

`cookie_secure` decides the cookie's `Secure` attribute: `"auto"` (default) sets it when
the request is https, which includes `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` from a peer in
`trusted_proxies`; `true` always sets it (use it when TLS ends at a proxy you have not
listed); `false` never does.

A refused API call answers `401 login_required` (no credentials) or `401
invalid_credentials` (wrong ones). Both carry a `WWW-Authenticate` header, unless the
request has `X-Redline-UI: 1` (the UI and `badge.js` send it) so browsers do not pop up
their own dialog.

### Basic

```bash
redline hash-password            # prompts, prints a PBKDF2-SHA256 hash
```

```toml
# redline.toml
access = "basic"

[basic_users]
alice = "pbkdf2_sha256$..."      # the output of redline hash-password
```

Passwords are stored only as hashes: `pbkdf2_sha256$<iterations>$<salt>$<hash>`, 600 000
iterations by default (`redline hash-password --iterations N`; 1 000 is the minimum
accepted, and `redline doctor` warns below 100 000). A plain password in `basic_users` is
rejected at startup. Unknown users still cost a hash computation, so response time does
not reveal which users exist. The browser UI shows a username and password form; scripts
may send `Authorization: Basic`. Use it behind HTTPS only: basic credentials are sent on
every request, and sessions need `secret_key` with several workers, as for tokens.

### Framework

Use your application's existing authentication and let Redline defer to it. With no hook
configured the request is refused (`403 forbidden`). Each framework exposes its native hook,
and passing it implies `access = "framework"`:

=== "Django"

    ```python
    REDLINE = {"ACCESS": "framework", "PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.can_view"}
    ```

    Default: `user.is_active and user.is_superuser` (staff before 0.2). See [Django: access control](django.md#access-control).

=== "FastAPI"

    ```python
    install(app, engine=engine, dependencies=[Depends(require_admin)])
    ```

    See [FastAPI: access control](fastapi.md#access-control).

=== "Flask"

    ```python
    Redline(app, permission=lambda request: current_user.is_admin)
    ```

=== "Litestar"

    ```python
    RedlinePlugin(guards=[require_admin])
    ```

### Custom

```python
def can_view(request_info) -> bool:
    return request_info.headers.get("x-internal-user") in ALLOWED

REDLINE = {"ACCESS": "custom", "ACCESS_CHECK": can_view}   # or "myproject.redline:can_view"
```

`request_info` has `method`, `path` (relative to the mount), `client_ip` (after
`trusted_proxies`), lower-cased `headers`, `cookies`, `host`, `scheme` and `mount`. If
your function raises, the error is logged and the request is refused.

### Open

`access = "open"` serves the UI to everyone. Without `REDLINE_ALLOW_OPEN=1` in the
environment every request is answered `403 open_refused` and an error is logged at
startup. With it, Redline serves the UI and logs a warning at startup and then at most
once a minute. It exists for
sealed environments (a throwaway container, a network you control completely). Do not use
it on anything reachable from the internet.

## Network restrictions

These apply **in addition to** the policy:

| Setting | Effect |
|---|---|
| `allowed_ips` | IPs and CIDRs (v4 or v6). With `local` it **widens** access: loopback plus these (for example a VPN range `10.8.0.0/16`). With `token`, `basic`, `framework`, `custom` and `open` it **restricts**: when non-empty the client must also be in it, and loopback is not implicit |
| `allowed_hosts` | extra `Host` values accepted by `local`'s DNS-rebinding check |
| `trusted_proxies` | IPs and CIDRs of reverse proxies. **Only** requests whose TCP peer is in this list have `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` believed |

`trusted_proxies` matters. If you do not set it, the forwarding headers are ignored, so a
client cannot claim to be `127.0.0.1` by sending one. If you do set it, list only the
proxies you operate: `X-Forwarded-For` is read from the right, skipping trusted hops, and
the first untrusted address is the client. `Forwarded` (RFC 7239) is not parsed.

## Read-only mode

`read_only = True` refuses every state-changing `api/` call (anything but `GET`, `HEAD` and
`OPTIONS`) with `403 read_only`: deleting traces and runs, `POST api/runs`, stopping a run.
Login, logout and `POST api/explain` still work, but an `EXPLAIN` with `analyze: true` is
refused with `403 read_only`. Reads, plain EXPLAIN, search and exports still work. The
`production` [preset](configuration.md#presets) turns it on. `GET api/meta` reports
`access.read_only`, and the UI hides Clear all, ANALYZE and the run controls.

## Feature switches

`features` turns individual capabilities off. All default to on. A disabled feature's
routes answer `404 feature_disabled`, and the UI hides the matching controls (from
`GET api/meta`). Unknown names are an error.

| Switch | Turns off |
|---|---|
| `explain` | `POST api/explain` and the EXPLAIN drawer |
| `profile` | `api/traces/{id}/profile`, and the profile is left out of snapshots |
| `replay` | the Replay button (replay has no server route; it is a UI feature) |
| `snapshot` | `GET api/traces/{id}/snapshot` and the download button |
| `load` | the Load page and everything under `api/runs` |
| `checks` | the Checks pages and everything under `api/checks` ([Refactor check](refactor-check.md)) |
| `logs` | log capture (the trace's `logs` is `[]`) and the Logs tab |
| `locals` | exception local variables (not captured, dropped from responses) |
| `sse` | `api/stream`; Live mode is hidden |

```toml
[features]
explain = false
replay = false
```

## Other access settings

| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `ui_enabled` | `True` | If false, every Redline URL answers `404`; Redline **captures but does not serve** the UI or API |
| `mount_path` | `None` (then `/_redline`) | Where FastAPI, Flask and Litestar serve the UI when `prefix` / `url_prefix` / `path` is not passed. Django ignores it |
| `session_ttl_s` | `43200` | Login cookie lifetime |
| `max_login_attempts` | `10` | Failed credential attempts per client IP per 300 seconds |
| `secret_key` | `None` | Signs login cookies (see above) |
| `base_url` | `None` | Where load runs and refactor checks started from the UI go; see [Load testing](load-testing.md#starting-a-run-from-the-ui) |
| `checks_from_ui` | `"auto"` | Whether baseline and compare runs may be started from the UI. `auto` = only in the framework's debug mode; `true`/`false` force it; the `production` preset sets `false`. Every `POST`, `PUT` and `DELETE` under `api/checks` is also refused under `read_only`, and the whole tree answers `404 feature_disabled` when the `checks` feature is off. See [Refactor check](refactor-check.md#settings-and-access) |

## Login and API

![The login screen of a token-protected instance](assets/screenshots/fastapi-login-light.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-light }
![The login screen of a token-protected instance](assets/screenshots/fastapi-login-dark.png){ .rl-shot .rl-only-dark }

| Endpoint | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `POST api/login` | body `{"token": "..."}` or `{"username": "...", "password": "..."}` (4 KiB at most); answers `200 {"ok": true, "expires_at": <epoch>}` and sets the cookie. Never redirects. `400 invalid_json` / `invalid_body`, `401 invalid_credentials`, `429 too_many_requests`; `404` under other policies |
| `POST api/logout` | answers `200 {"ok": true}` and clears the cookie, under any policy |
| `GET api/config` | `{preset, file, settings, sources, groups, warnings}`: the effective configuration with secrets as `***`, where each value came from, and risky-combination warnings |

An unauthenticated request to a `token` or `basic` instance gets `401 login_required`. The
UI reacts by showing its login screen. See [HTTP API](http-api.md#authentication-and-csrf).

## Recipes

### Local development

Run the app in debug mode and the default `local` policy serves
`http://localhost:8000/_redline/` to you and nobody else. Without debug mode (for example a
plain `uvicorn main:app`), set it yourself:

```python
install(app, engine=engine, settings={"access": "local"})   # or REDLINE_ACCESS=local
```

### Behind a VPN

You run a shared dev or staging box that only VPN users can reach. Add the VPN range:

```toml
access = "local"
allowed_ips = ["10.8.0.0/16"]
allowed_hosts = ["devbox.internal"]
```

Anyone on the VPN can open the UI with no login. If the VPN is wider than the people who
should see request bodies, use a token as well.

### Token in staging

```bash
REDLINE_PRESET=staging          # token access, 25% sampling, no locals
REDLINE_TOKEN=...               # from your secret store
```

Share the token with the team through your password manager. Rotate it by changing the
variable and restarting.

### Production, read-only

```bash
REDLINE_PRESET=production
REDLINE_TOKEN=...
```

Read-only, token-protected, 5% sampling plus slow requests and errors, no bodies, no
locals, no badge. Reach it through your VPN or an SSH tunnel as well; a token is a second
lock, not the only one. See [Production](production.md).

### Behind a reverse proxy

The proxy terminates TLS and forwards to the app. Without help, every request appears to
come from the proxy. Tell Redline which proxy to believe:

```toml
access = "token"
trusted_proxies = ["10.0.0.0/8"]       # your load balancer's network, not "0.0.0.0/0"
```

The proxy must set `X-Forwarded-For` and overwrite any value the client sent. Also set
`X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host` (or pass the original `Host`) so the CSRF
`Origin` comparison sees the public host name and the login cookie gets `Secure` (or set
`cookie_secure = true`). Set
`secret_key` when you run several workers. Optionally, restrict `/_redline/` at the proxy to your office or VPN range, so the
app's check is the second line of defence:

```nginx
location /_redline/ {
    allow 10.8.0.0/16;
    deny  all;
    proxy_pass http://app;
}
```

### Kubernetes

Do not expose Redline through a public Ingress. Options, safest first:

1. **`kubectl port-forward`**. Reach it from your machine only, with `access = "local"`
   (set explicitly):

   ```bash
   kubectl port-forward deploy/shop 8000:8000
   # http://localhost:8000/_redline/
   ```

   `port-forward` makes the connection arrive from the pod's own loopback side, so the
   `local` policy lets you in as long as the app is not behind a proxy that adds
   forwarding headers. If the client address is not loopback, add it to `allowed_ips`.

2. **An internal Ingress or Service** reachable only from the cluster or VPN, with
   `access = "token"` and `trusted_proxies` set to the ingress controller's pod CIDR.

Keep the token in a `Secret`, mounted as `token_file`:

```yaml
env:
  - name: REDLINE_PRESET
    value: production
  - name: REDLINE_TOKEN_FILE
    value: /run/secrets/redline/token
volumeMounts:
  - { name: redline-token, mountPath: /run/secrets/redline, readOnly: true }
```

Remember that the store is a SQLite file **per pod**: use a volume if you want it to
survive restarts, and note that each replica has its own data
([Production](production.md#process-models)).

## What to read next

[Security](security.md) covers what is stored and the full threat model;
[Configuration](configuration.md) covers how these settings are supplied.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/production.md -->
<!-- page: Production -->

# Production deployment

Redline's next release targets production recording across several codebases. Readiness
is established for a particular combination of framework, driver, process model, traffic
and storage; passing a SQLite unit test does not establish SQL Server or broker-worker
behavior. The release must retain its development status until the required deployment
checks below have evidence.

<a id="the-production-preset"></a>

## Start with recording and stored-data inspection

Use a separate configuration and private storage directory for **each application and
environment**. Do not point a profiler store at the application's database. For an initial
production canary, make active tools unavailable explicitly:

```toml
preset = "production"
access = "token"
cookie_secure = true
token_file = "/run/secrets/redline-token"
# Supply REDLINE_SECRET_KEY separately through the deployment secret provider.
storage_path = "/var/lib/redline/myapp-production/{role}.db"
storage_role = "web"
release = "myapp-release-identifier"

sample_rate = 0.01
always_keep_errors = true
always_keep_slower_than_ms = 500
max_rows = 5000
max_age_days = 2
history_retention_days = 7
writer_queue_size = 64
max_spans_per_trace = 500
max_sql_bytes = 16384
max_span_data_bytes = 8192
max_tag_bytes = 2048
max_trace_bytes = 262144

capture_request_body = false
capture_response_body = false
capture_sql_params = false
capture_locals = false
capture_logs = false
capture_error_details = false
read_only = true
profile = "off"
badge = false
server_timing = false
load_from_ui = false
checks_from_ui = false
analysis_from_ui = false
explain_analyze = false

[features]
explain = false
profile = false
replay = false
replay_writes = false
load = false
checks = false
logs = false
locals = false
```

Supply `secret_key` through `REDLINE_SECRET_KEY` or the application's secret provider
instead of committing it to a file. Use a randomly generated signing key of at least
32 characters and a strong token of at least 24 characters. Length checks do not verify
randomness. Different codebases and
environments should have different tokens/signing keys and storage access permissions.
A signing key is shared only among workers intentionally serving the same Redline UI.

The count/byte controls above match the production preset: queue `64`, span count `500`,
SQL text `16384`, span data `8192`, tag value `2048` and completed trace `262144` bytes.
The sample, trace/history retention and always-keep rules shown are canary choices.
The production preset is a starting point; explicit settings override it. Inspect the
resolved configuration with `redline config`, and run `redline doctor` in the deployment's
working directory. A configuration file alone is not evidence that the intended workers
loaded it. Confirm through the UI's effective configuration and recording health.

For Flask, FastAPI and Litestar, pass this settings mapping to the existing adapter. Django
maps the same settings from `REDLINE`, with its framework permission policy retained when
configured. An explicit native permission hook must authorize the intended operator, not
ordinary application users. Authentication details are in [Access control](access-control.md).

## Data minimization and privacy

Disabling SQL values withholds bound parameters, normalizes inline literals and removes
associated SQL source/fix snippets. This also makes EXPLAIN unavailable for those recordings.
`reads_only` is an explicit opt-in, not a privacy boundary: SELECT parameters can contain
personal data too.

Bodies, locals and logs are separate capture surfaces. Keep all three off for the first
production canary. Exception type and structured database codes are useful without treating
free-form exception messages as safe. Follow [Security](security.md) for the exact captured
surfaces and the current exception-detail controls. Profiles and route rules are pattern
matching, not a guarantee that arbitrary clinical notes, identifiers or secrets are absent.

Before rollout, use invented sentinel values in the actual application's headers, query
strings, routes, SQL, logs and exceptions. Inspect the stored trace, issue data, source
snippets and exported snapshot, then scan the disposable store. `redline audit-store`
reports bounded key-pattern candidates without printing values; it is not a complete
privacy audit and does not prove an existing store is clean. With
`capture_error_details = false`, Redline retains error types and structured database
codes without formatting exception messages or tracebacks; project exception locals
are also disabled. This preserves failure counts while reducing free-text exposure.

## Refuse to attach in production

Each adapter has an `install_if_dev` entry point that attaches Redline only when the process
does not look like production. It returns `None` (and logs a warning on the `redline`
logger) when `REDLINE_ENV`, `APP_ENV`, `ENV`, `ENVIRONMENT`, `FLASK_ENV` or `DJANGO_ENV` is
`prod` or `production`, and, for Django, when `DEBUG` is false. `REDLINE_ALLOW_PRODUCTION=1`
overrides it (also logged).

```python
from fastapi_redline import install_if_dev   # flask_redline: install_if_dev(app, ...)
install_if_dev(app, engine=engine)

from litestar_redline import install_if_dev  # returns the plugin, or None
plugin = install_if_dev(engine=engine)
app = Litestar([...], plugins=[plugin] if plugin else [])

# Django: settings.py, then urls.py
from django_redline import install_if_dev, urls_if_dev
install_if_dev(globals())                    # adds the app and middleware
urlpatterns += urls_if_dev("redline/")       # [] when refused
```

This is a safety net, not access control: it does not replace the `access` settings, and
production recording is still configured with the [production presets](#start-with-recording-and-stored-data-inspection).

## Network and operator access

Expose the application normally, but place the Redline mount behind the intended operator
network/authentication boundary. Use TLS. Configure `trusted_proxies` with the actual proxy
peers; do not trust every address for convenience. Set `cookie_secure = true` when the
operator entrypoint is always HTTPS and the proxy is configured correctly.

`access = "local"` can fail behind a Docker bridge, or accidentally accept a same-host
proxy. Use the token/framework policy instead of switching to open access. Test unauthenticated,
wrong-token, insufficient-role and cross-origin requests against every worker.

Read-only API policy does not govern the application's own endpoints. Replay is a browser
request to that application, so disabling `features.replay` is part of recording-only mode.
Estimated plans and catalog inspection also contact a database and are separate from reading
stored traces; they remain off in the recipe. Load generation, refactor-check runs, source
scans, online compilation and actual plans belong in an isolated development environment.

<a id="process-models"></a>

## Storage and process models

Use local disk or a local-filesystem Docker named volume with private directory/file
permissions. Do not share a writable SQLite file through NFS/SMB or an arbitrary remote
filesystem. WAL being available is necessary, but does not prove the underlying volume is
safe under multiple containers. A writable store refuses a non-WAL result. Non-development
presets refuse an in-repository store unless explicitly overridden.

Run `redline doctor` **inside the actual container**, with the same mount and working
directory as the app. Its `storage WAL` check creates a throwaway database beside the store
and requires `journal_mode=wal` to work; its `filesystem` check warns on Linux mount types
commonly used by network/virtual shares. The check does not write to the configured store.
The test suite also writes to one file from two independent OS processes, but only your
deployment's volumes and process model prove your topology.

`{role}`, `{hostname}` and `{pid}` path placeholders help choose separate files. They are not
an application namespace automatically added to a shared store. Use an application/environment
prefix yourself. Files from unrelated codebases must not be mixed accidentally.

| Deployment | Intended storage arrangement | Validation needed |
|---|---|---|
| One application, one process | One private local file | Retention, shutdown, disk errors and normal traffic |
| Several workers on one host | The shared PostgreSQL store, or a local shared file only after a concurrent-writer test, or per-worker files | Contention, busy timeout, pruning, loss and shutdown |
| Web and task workers | The shared PostgreSQL store, or explicit web/worker roles with separate files | Worker initialization, fork behavior and correlation |
| Several replicas/hosts | The shared PostgreSQL store (`storage_url`), or a private local file per replica | Database reachability and credentials; with files, replica-local inspection and no network-file sharing |
| Several independent codebases | Separate processes, settings, credentials and store paths | No cross-application traces or operator access |

The SQLite writer starts lazily and has fork/PID handling, but validate the actual gunicorn,
uWSGI, ASGI or task-worker start model. Database engines must also follow the database
library's fork lifecycle. Redline's storage handling does not make an inherited application
connection pool safe.

Multiple applications in one interpreter need explicit per-application recorders and
integration tests. The default recorder and some integration hooks are process-wide; do not
assume that repeatedly calling `configure()` provides application isolation. Queue-independent
`job()` accepts an explicit recorder. Initialize Celery instrumentation in the intended worker
lifecycle and confirm actual broker delivery, retries and prefork behavior.

`extra_stores` provides read-only request/job/profile browsing from existing worker files.
It does not combine history, aggregates, live-tail events or mutations. Independent files
should use independent trace IDs. Duplicate IDs are marked in request/job listings;
inspection, profiles and single-ID deletion are refused rather than choosing another
store's evidence. Cross-file reads are not an atomic distributed snapshot. Secondary
EXPLAIN/catalog requests are refused because a web process cannot establish the worker's
database binding. This is not a distributed store.

### Multi-worker deployments

A SQLite file is a single-host store. Several gunicorn/uvicorn workers can write one local
file (WAL plus a busy timeout), but their writes queue on one file lock, and as soon as there
is more than one host or container each keeps its own traces. For any of these, set
`storage_url` to a PostgreSQL database ([Storage: a shared PostgreSQL
store](storage.md#a-shared-postgresql-store)):

```bash
pip install "redline-core[postgres]"
REDLINE_STORAGE_URL=postgresql://redline:...@db.internal:5432/redline
```

Every worker and host then writes the same store, and the UI of any of them shows all
traffic. The store opens its connection lazily per process, so gunicorn `--preload` and
forked task workers are safe; give it its own database or schema and a role that owns only
that.

`redline doctor` flags the risky shapes. It reads the worker count from `WEB_CONCURRENCY`,
`--workers`/`-w` in `GUNICORN_CMD_ARGS` and `UVICORN_WORKERS` (or `--workers N` when the
count lives elsewhere, such as a process manager's command line) and warns when more than one
worker would share a SQLite file; it also warns for a SQLite store on a network filesystem.
In a deployment pipeline run it with `--strict`, which turns both warnings into failures:

```bash
redline doctor --strict --workers 4
```

<a id="sampling"></a>

## Capacity and failure behavior

Sampling is applied when a recording finishes. Unretained requests still pay the span,
fingerprint and callsite cost. A sample rate of 1% is not 1% of the instrumentation overhead.
Slow/error keep rules can retain much more than the nominal sample during an incident.

The writer queue is bounded and drops/counts traces rather than blocking request code when
full. SQL text, span data and tags have separate byte budgets, and the completed serialized
trace is checked against `max_trace_bytes` before saving. Budget enforcement may shorten
or discard evidence; keep truncation/drop notices visible and inspect preserved failure
counts. See [Settings](settings.md#capture-byte-budgets) for defaults and scope.

These controls do not establish an absolute process-memory or disk-size ceiling. Active
requests, application objects, analysis, serialization and writer batches also consume memory.
Measure representative large traces as well as the median request. Retention runs
periodically, so a configured row cap is not an instantaneous disk-size guarantee.

Measure and monitor:

- Application throughput, median/tail latency, CPU and memory with recording disabled and enabled.
- Queue drops, writer failures, storage growth and time spent draining at shutdown.
- SQL-heavy requests, large results, errors, retries, streaming and concurrent jobs.
- Full disk, unwritable directories, SQLite contention and sudden process termination.

Use `GET api/meta` recording/drop indicators and the `redline` logger. SQLite's
`storage.dropped` includes queue overflow, closed-store loss and failed writer batches;
it does not distinguish all those causes. `flush()` signals that queued work was processed,
not that every trace persisted successfully: check loss counters and verify expected
recordings. Recorder-side capture/sink failures must also be checked in operational
logs and independent monitoring. Do not treat sampled
endpoint percentiles as an unbiased application SLO. Keep application monitoring independent
so a profiler failure cannot hide an application incident.

FastAPI/Litestar shutdown hooks and Flask/Django exit hooks flush pending traces. Give the
process enough graceful-shutdown time and verify that the hook runs in the deployment.
A forced kill can lose queued traces; state the acceptable loss window before rollout.

## Production release gate

The complete Compose baseline passed on 2026-10-29 (run
`20261029T052447Z-caaef5f7`): 2,120 Python tests, zero failures/errors/skips, plus frontend,
demo, docs and packaging checks. Main CI and the actual production topology
still require their own evidence; an environment restriction is never a passing assertion.

| Area | Confirmed baseline | Still required for the target deployment |
|---|---|---|
| Capture boundaries | Cycle/Unicode/custom-object/size-limit and safe-fallback tests | Representative memory/latency at intended concurrency and payload sizes |
| Privacy and storage loss | Sentinels, effective-write probes, deterministic queue/writer failures and worker shutdown | Actual disk exhaustion, permissions, storage volume and sustained concurrency |
| Framework SQL recording | Live Django backend and Flask/FastAPI SQLAlchemy sync/async cases on MySQL, SQL Server and PostgreSQL | Exact deployed backend/driver versions, reconnect behavior and deployment topology |
| SQL Server tooling | Live estimated/actual plans, catalogs, compilation nonexecution and setting cleanup | Least-privilege production-like permissions; Django SQL Server EXPLAIN remains unsupported |
| Jobs | Redis-delivered Celery prefork success/failure/retry, correlation and shutdown-drain checks | Actual broker/deployment, restart and expected worker concurrency |
| Browser | Real Chromium Jobs/detail, SQL checker, privacy and mobile overflow checks | Full accessibility review and target-browser coverage |

The Compose baseline uses Python 3.13, Django 5.2 and the driver versions recorded in the
run summary. It does not certify all supported versions; the broader matrix runs in main
CI. SQL Server's supported container qualification requires native Linux amd64, even if
an emulated local run succeeds. Record server/process versions with deployment results.

A production recommendation requires evidence for each target deployment:

1. Exact supported Python/framework/driver/queue versions and the process/storage topology.
2. Unit and adapter suites, installed-wheel tests, UI checks and documentation build passing.
3. Live driver tests for failed statements, reconnects, parameter styles and session cleanup;
   SQL Server plan/compile tests only against an isolated database with appropriate permissions.
4. Broker-worker success/failure/retry, prefork/restart, correlation and graceful shutdown tests.
5. Concurrent writers, retention, backpressure and fault-injection tests under expected traffic
   (`redline doctor --strict` passing for the storage topology).
6. Sentinel privacy checks across stored traces, issues, callsites, logs and exports.
7. A low-traffic canary with an immediate `enabled = false` rollback and independent monitoring.

The [full-stack Compose test project](testing.md) supplies a repeatable baseline for
these checks. Its current report must be green; merely adding its test files is not
qualification. Validate deployment-specific conditions as well.

Once these pass, expand one codebase at a time. Keep active tools disabled on production even
when the development demo exercises them. See [Real-world workflows](real-world-workflows.md)
for individual feature setup and [Performance](performance.md) for measurement limitations.


## Enforce the recording-only configuration before deployment

From **inside the deployment container**, with the same config/environment/working
location as the app, run:

```bash
redline doctor --production --strict --json
```

`--production` validates the configuration you supplied; it does not switch presets or
make an unsafe configuration safe. `--strict` returns nonzero for warnings as well as
failures. This gate checks recording-only settings, private persistent storage and
retention, authenticated operator access, explicit secure cookies and restricted proxy
trust. It keeps provider/auth/storage probes from ordinary `doctor`. Application-defined
access hooks remain warnings because a CLI cannot prove their authorization behavior.
Use a token-backed configuration for an automated strict gate, or review the hook and its
warning explicitly. Never print real token/signing values in deployment logs.

If settings are overridden in application code, this CLI cannot see those overrides.
Confirm the worker's effective configuration and test its access boundary as well. A
successful configuration gate does not validate TLS, real database drivers, disk failure
behavior, concurrency or the contents of actual captured data.

## Monitor profiler health independently

Poll the protected `GET <mount>/api/health` endpoint with your operator credentials.
A healthy supported process returns HTTP 200. Degraded, closed, disabled or unavailable
recording health returns 503. It reports:

- queue depth/capacity and writer-started/alive state;
- completed-recording capture/sink failures separately from storage loss;
- cumulative dropped items by reason, writer/flush/shutdown failures and written count;
- shutdown completion and the serving process PID.

Do **not** use this endpoint as the application's load-balancer readiness probe. A profiler
problem should alert operators without taking a healthy application out of service.
The snapshot does not query the initialized trace database, so it remains useful while
SQLite queries are blocked or the connection has closed. It is authenticated, contains
no trace payload, storage path or exception message, and uses the same access policy as
the other operator endpoints. The UI's Recording health panel shows the same information.

Counters are process-local and cumulative, including historical failures; a degraded
status can persist after recovery. Monitor counter increases/rates and individual workers,
not just the last status response. Unsupported custom health providers are reported as
unknown. Queue depth includes markers and lifecycle work; written counts describe write
processing rather than an fsync/durability guarantee. Continue independent application
monitoring and inspect truncated evidence too.

## Verify graceful shutdown and failure behavior

The SQLite writer stops admission before its stop marker. `close(timeout=10)` reports
whether shutdown completed. If the deadline expires, queued items may be discarded and
counted, while an in-flight batch may still finish later. A live writer retains ownership
of its connection until it stops. This improves isolation; it does not make forced kills
lossless. Adapters still perform their normal flush/close lifecycle, so size the server's
grace period to include both and test it in the actual process topology.

Deterministic tests cover full queues, dead writers, injected write failure/recovery,
thread-start failure, failed logging and concurrent save/close accounting. Validate actual
volume permissions, disk exhaustion, worker restarts and intended concurrency in staging.
Read `flush()` success together with loss counters: barrier completion is not proof that
every trace persisted. Emergency rollback remains `enabled = false`, followed by normal
application restart/reconfiguration; no production traffic generator is enabled by this work.

The close timeout bounds admission/queue/join/lock waits. It is not a hard real-time
bound on operating-system filesystem calls. Let the process manager enforce the final
grace deadline and document the acceptable loss on forced termination. Worker processes
without a web endpoint can expose `recorder.operational_health()` and
`store.operational_health()` through their existing private metrics/logging integration;
the library does not start a monitoring server or aggregate those counters automatically.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/upgrading.md -->
<!-- page: Upgrading -->

# Upgrading

Redline is pre-1.0: the public API may change between minor versions, and every change is
listed in the [changelog](changelog.md). The five packages (`redline-core`, `django-redline`,
`fastapi-redline`, `flask-redline`, `litestar-redline`) are versioned in lockstep, so upgrade
them together.

## Steps

1. Read the [changelog](changelog.md) entries between your version and the target, in
   particular the *Changed* and *Security* sections.
2. Upgrade the framework package and `redline-core` in the same command:

    ```bash
    pip install --pre --upgrade django-redline   # or fastapi-redline, flask-redline, litestar-redline
    ```

3. Run the configuration check. It loads your settings without changing them and reports
   anything deprecated or unsafe for recording-only deployments:

    ```bash
    redline doctor --production --strict
    ```

4. Restart every worker. The recorder is per process; mixed versions against one store work
   but report their own version in the Meta tab.
5. Open the UI and confirm new traces arrive.

## The trace store

The SQLite store migrates itself in place the first time a newer version opens it, in one
transaction, so concurrent workers start safely. Older traces stay readable. A store written
by a newer version is never opened by an older one; if you must roll back, point the older
version at a fresh `store_path` or delete the file. See [Storage](storage.md) and
[History and releases](history.md#upgrading-an-existing-store).

## Pre-releases

Beta builds are published as pre-releases and need `--pre`. Pin an exact version in
production (`django-redline==X.Y.ZaN`) and upgrade deliberately. Anything marked experimental
in [API stability](api-stability.md) can change without notice.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/operating.md -->
<!-- page: Operating Redline -->

# Operating Redline: its own logs, metrics and health

[← Index](index.md) · [Production](production.md)

When Redline runs anywhere other than a laptop, you want to know when *it* is unhealthy:
dropping traces, failing to write, or misconfigured. This page lists the signals it gives
about itself.

## Logs

Redline uses the standard library `logging` module and never configures handlers itself;
records go wherever your application sends logs.

| Logger | What it reports | Typical level |
|---|---|---|
| `redline` | startup warnings (open access, uninstrumented integrations with `auto_instrument="warn"`, a refused `install_if_dev` in production), writer failures, dropped lifecycle data | `WARNING`, `ERROR` |
| `redline.check` | refactor-check runs that could not store a result or read traces | `ERROR` (with traceback) |
| `redline.load` | load-test sink failures | `ERROR` (with traceback) |
| `redline.scan` | static-scan limits reached | `WARNING` |

Messages start with `Redline` (or the command name) and never include captured request
data, SQL parameters or credentials: they name the operation and the exception *type*.
Debug-level records (catalog reads, executor lookup) are off unless you enable `DEBUG` for
`redline`.

A JSON log pipeline needs nothing special. With `python-json-logger`, for example:

```python
import logging
from pythonjsonlogger.json import JsonFormatter

handler = logging.StreamHandler()
handler.setFormatter(JsonFormatter("%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s"))
logging.getLogger("redline").addHandler(handler)
logging.getLogger("redline").setLevel(logging.WARNING)
```

To stamp *your application's* log lines with the id of the recording they belong to, add the
`TraceIdFilter` from `redline_core.correlation` (see [Logs and exceptions](logs-and-exceptions.md)).

## Metrics

`GET {mount}/api/metrics` returns Prometheus text format, behind the same access policy as
the rest of the API (so scrape it with the Redline token, or from an allowed network):

| Series | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `redline_writer_queue_depth` / `redline_writer_queue_capacity` | traces waiting for the writer thread, and the bound |
| `redline_traces_saved_total` | traces persisted |
| `redline_traces_dropped_total{reason=...}` | traces lost: `queue_full`, `write_failure`, `closed`, `capture_failed`, plus rarer reasons (`enqueue_failure`, `lifecycle_write_failure`, `shutdown_timeout`, `writer_unavailable`) when they occur |
| `redline_write_failures_total` | writer batches that failed |

Suggested alerts: any increase of `redline_traces_dropped_total{reason="write_failure"}` or
`redline_write_failures_total` (disk full, permissions, store locked); a sustained queue depth
near capacity (the app produces traces faster than the store absorbs them: lower the sample
rate). See [HTTP API](http-api.md) for the exact format.

## Health and doctor

- `redline doctor` (add `--production` in staging/production) checks the store location,
  filesystem, WAL, UI bundle, access settings and capture settings from inside the process
  environment. Run it in the real container.
- `GET {mount}/api/meta` reports recording state and drop counters for the UI.
- `redline instrumentation --store PATH [--window SECONDS] [--json]` and
  `GET {mount}/api/instrumentation` (also on the Settings page) show what redline cannot see:
  installed integrations that are not instrumented, truncated traces, traces without a
  profile, dropped and failed writes. Counts come from a bounded sample of recent traces.
- `redline audit-store` counts possibly unmasked keys in a store without printing values.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/testing.md -->
<!-- page: Full-stack testing -->

# Full-stack release testing

The example projects share [`examples/compose.yaml`](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/blob/main/examples/compose.yaml).
It provisions disposable PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server and Redis services with health checks,
and an image containing all framework adapters, database drivers, Celery and Chromium.

From the repository root:

```bash
docker compose -f examples/compose.yaml up --build \
  --abort-on-container-exit --exit-code-from tests tests
```

The runner executes the complete package suites, including network tests, live database
request/transaction/privacy cases, plans and compile checks, a real Redis/prefork worker,
and browser tests of the built UI. It also checks demos, docs, lint, package metadata and
fresh wheel installation. Integration skips or missing reports fail the run.

The MySQL cases (pymysql, aiomysql and asyncmy drivers, EXPLAIN, index advice, killed
connections) also run on every push in the lightweight `mysql` CI job against a plain
`mysql:8.4` service, without the full Compose stack; a skipped test fails that job.

`examples/testing/results/summary.json` must show `qualified: true` for the current run,
and the Compose command must exit zero. Results are ignored by Git. Each run keeps
separate logs, JUnit reports and actual dependency versions. Browser screenshots support
review but do not replace a full accessibility audit or production load testing.

Interactive demo services are available through the `demos` profile with host loopback
ports 8011–8014 and disposable token authentication. The shops use SQLite; the integration
matrix separately exercises real databases. All database credentials/data are test-only.

SQL Server's image requires Linux amd64. Microsoft does not support emulation on Apple
Silicon; failures there remain failures. Native amd64 CI provides the supported environment.
The existing CI trigger remains **main pushes only**, with no PR/manual test trigger and
no implicit publishing authorization.

See the [complete test-project guide](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/blob/main/examples/testing/README.md)
for prerequisites, commands, demo URLs, driver coverage, cleanup and current verification
limits. A passing Compose baseline is one release gate; validate actual deployment
storage, concurrency, drivers, permissions and framework versions as described in
[Production](production.md).


## The query-count ratchet

A ratchet is a committed file of numbers that may only improve: a pull request that adds
queries to an endpoint or a test fails, one that removes queries tightens the file.

**Endpoints**, from a [refactor-check suite](refactor-check.md):

```bash
redline check ratchet checks/orders.toml --store .redline/check.db --update   # create it
redline check ratchet checks/orders.toml --store .redline/check.db           # CI: fail on regressions
redline check ratchet checks/orders.toml --store .redline/check.db --update   # after a green run: tighten
```

The file defaults to `<suite>.ratchet.json` (`--ratchet-file`). Per request it stores the
median query count (needs `--store`, see
[server-side metrics](refactor-check.md#server-side-metrics)) and the median latency.
Query counts are exact: one more query is a regression. A latency regression needs the median
to grow by more than both `--latency-pct` (30) and `--latency-ms` (20); `--no-latency` tracks
queries only. Without `--update` nothing is written (and the file must exist); with it, the
file is written only when nothing regressed: improvements lower the numbers, new endpoints
are added, nothing is ever raised. Keys are sorted, so diffs stay small. A request that is
broken (at least half of its calls failed) is reported and fails the run. `--json` and
`--markdown` write the verdict; the exit code is `1` on regressions.

**Tests**, with the pytest plugin (tests that use the `redline` marker or `--redline-all`):

```bash
pytest --redline-ratchet tests/queries.ratchet.json                          # fail on more queries than recorded
pytest --redline-ratchet tests/queries.ratchet.json --redline-ratchet-update # tighten / add, only if the whole session passed
```

Each test is keyed by its node id and records the query count of its busiest request. The
same file can hold both the `endpoints` and `tests` sections.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/security.md -->
<!-- page: Security -->

# Security

[← Index](index.md)

Redline records the most sensitive thing about your application: what it was asked to do
and what it said back. This page is the threat model, what is protected by default, what is
**not**, and how to expose the UI safely.

To report a vulnerability privately, see `SECURITY.md` in the repository.

## What Redline stores

For every kept request, on local disk, in `.redline/redline.db`:

| Data | Stored as | Redacted? |
|---|---|---|
| Request and response **headers** | name and value | values of `redact_headers`, and of any header whose name matches `redact_keys` (`X-Auth-Token`, `X-CSRFToken`, `X-Session-Id`…), are masked |
| **Query string** | key and value | values whose key matches `redact_keys` are masked |
| **Request body** | text, capped at `max_body_bytes` | JSON, form and multipart keys matching `redact_keys` are masked; multipart files become `[file: name, N bytes]`; any other text (plain, XML, GraphQL, JSON that does not parse) goes through the free-text rule |
| **Response body** | text, capped | JSON, form and multipart keys are masked; HTML and other text are **not** scanned (cost); only if `capture_response_body` is on |
| **SQL text** and **parameters** | controlled by `capture_sql_params` | `false` withholds values and normalizes literals; `reads_only` retains values only for recognized reads; otherwise configured column/table/profile patterns mask parameters |
| **Callsites** | file, line, function and optional **source line** | SQL capture/route restrictions remove associated source and generated fix snippets; other captured source can contain literals |
| **Tracebacks** and exception messages | text | the free-text rule (URL passwords, secret query values, `key=value` secrets, JWTs, card numbers), chained exceptions included |
| **Exception locals** (project frames: names and `repr` of variables) | text, at most 30 per frame, 300 characters each | variables whose **name** matches `redact_keys` are masked; containers have secret keys masked to a depth of 4, and the whole `repr` goes through the free-text rule (`key=value` pairs, URLs). Values under innocent names are **not** |
| **Log records** emitted during the request | level, logger, message (2,000 characters), callsite | the free-text rule: `key=value`, `key: value` and `"key": "value"` pairs whose key matches `redact_keys` are masked, and so are URL passwords and secret query values. Bare secrets in a sentence are not |
| **Normalised SQL summaries** (`trace_sql`) | statements with literals replaced by `?` | contains no parameter values |
| **Outbound URL and cache key patterns** | digit runs, UUIDs and long hex strings replaced by `*` | cache keys: the part after a session prefix (`django.contrib.sessions.cache`, `session:`, `sess:`) or a secret-looking word (`api_key:`) is masked; URLs as below |
| **Release name** | text | no |
| **Load-run definitions** | the scenario | secret-looking header values, body keys and URL secrets are masked |
| Outbound **URLs** (`http_out`) | URL | the password of `scheme://user:password@host` and query-string values whose key matches `redact_keys` are masked |
| The request **path** | text | values of route parameters named like a secret (`token`, `uidb64`, `key`, `signature`, `code`, or matching `redact_keys`); for unmatched routes (404), long token-like segments |
| Client address | `REMOTE_ADDR` / ASGI client | no |

Everything is JSON in a SQLite file readable by anyone who can read the file.

## Redaction

Redaction is **on by default** and cannot be turned off by accident: there is no
"disable redaction" switch. It runs on the trace before it is handed to the store, so values recognized by the configured rules are masked before persistence.
Unrecognized sensitive data can still reach disk. It is mostly **key-based**: it looks at the *name* of a field
(header, query key, JSON key, column, table, route parameter). Free text (log messages,
exception messages, tracebacks, text bodies) additionally has JWTs and Luhn-valid card
numbers masked by shape.

### Defaults

| Where | What is masked | Replaced with |
|---|---|---|
| Log messages, exception messages and tracebacks, non-JSON request bodies | `key=value`, `key: value`, `"key": "value"` pairs and `<key>value</key>` elements whose key matches `redact_keys`; URL passwords and secret query values inside the text; JWTs; Luhn-valid card numbers (13–19 digits, optionally grouped) | `[redacted]` |
| Exception locals | the value of a variable whose name matches `redact_keys`; secret keys of containers (4 levels deep); and the free-text rule over the whole `repr` | `[redacted]` |
| Headers | `authorization`, `cookie`, `set-cookie`, `x-api-key`, `proxy-authorization` (case-insensitive), and any header whose name matches `redact_keys` | `[redacted]` |
| Query strings, form bodies, multipart fields, JSON bodies (any depth, GraphQL `variables` included) | any key matching `(?i)pass(word)?\|secret\|token\|api[_-]?key\|(?<![a-z])auth(orization)?(?![a-z])\|session\|csrf\|card\|cvv\|ssn\|private[_-]?key\|access[_-]?key\|signature\|credential` | `[redacted]` |
| Outbound URLs | the same key rule on the query string, and the password in `user:password@host` | `[redacted]`, or `%5Bredacted%5D` in the userinfo so the URL still parses |
| SQL parameters | values bound to a column whose name matches the same pattern (`SET "password" = %s`, `INSERT ... ("token") VALUES (%s)`, `password = crypt(%s, ...)`, `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET api_key = %s`), or to a table whose name matches it (`"authtoken_token"."key" = %s`, `"django_session"."session_key" = %s`; an unqualified column in a statement on such a table is masked too). Django's `auth_` app prefix is ignored, so `auth_user` stays visible | `[redacted]` |
| Cache keys (Django cache, redis) | the rest of the key after `django.contrib.sessions.cache`, `django.contrib.sessions.cached_db`, `session:`, `sess:`, or after a word matching the key pattern | `django.contrib.sessions.cache[redacted]` (the prefix is kept, so hit rates still group) |
| URL path | the value of a route parameter named `token`, `uidb64`, `key`, `signature`, `code` or matching the key pattern (`/reset/<uidb64>/<token>/` → `/reset/[redacted]/[redacted]/`); on unmatched routes, segments of 20+ token characters that mix letters and digits | `[redacted]` |
| Multipart file parts | the content | `[file: name, N bytes]` |
| Bodies | cut at `max_body_bytes`, **after** masking, so a cut never exposes half a secret | |
| Binary bodies | replaced by `<N bytes binary>` | |

The `auth` rule is deliberate: it matches `auth` and `authorization` only as a **whole word**,
so `author`, `author_id`, `authenticated`, `authority` and `oauth_provider` stay visible,
which would otherwise hide half a blog's data.

### Customising

```python
REDLINE = {
    "REDACT_HEADERS": ["authorization", "cookie", "set-cookie", "x-api-key",
                       "proxy-authorization", "x-internal-token"],
    "REDACT_KEYS": [
        r"(?i)pass(word)?|secret|token|api[_-]?key|(?<![a-z])auth(orization)?(?![a-z])"
        r"|session|csrf|card|cvv|ssn|private[_-]?key|access[_-]?key|signature|credential",
        r"(?i)^iban$|national_id",
    ],
}
```

!!! danger "Your list replaces the default"

    `redact_headers` and `redact_keys` **replace** the built-ins, they do not add to them.
    If you set `redact_keys` to one pattern, the default pattern is gone. Copy the
    defaults into your list and add to them. There is no warning when you narrow the list.

### What redaction does NOT catch

Be clear-eyed about this. Anything not matched by **key name** is stored in clear.

| Not masked | Why | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| A secret in the **URL path** under an innocent parameter name (`/users/<email>/`, `/invite/<slug>/`) | Only parameters named like a secret are masked | Put the path in `ignore_paths`, or avoid secrets in paths |
| **Personal data** under ordinary keys (`email`, `name`, `address`, `phone`, `dob`) | They do not all match the default credential pattern | Add reviewed profiles/custom patterns, and keep bodies off in production |
| **Bare secrets in text request bodies**, and anything in **HTML or other non-JSON response bodies** | Text request bodies only get the free-text rule (`key=value`, `<key>`, JWTs, cards); response text is not scanned | Turn off `capture_request_body` / `capture_response_body`, or `ignore_paths` |
| **Literal values inlined in SQL text** when SQL value capture is enabled | Key masking does not identify arbitrary statement literals | Use bound parameters and `capture_sql_params = false` in production |
| **SQL parameters** bound to columns *and* tables whose names look innocent (`settings.value`, `kv.data`) | Matching is on the column and table name | Add patterns, or accept it |
| **Bare secrets in exception messages** (`ValueError: bad abc123`) | Only the free-text rule applies (`token=abc123` and `token: abc123` *are* masked) | Do not put secrets in exception messages |
| **Source lines** in callsites | They are your code | n/a, but note they land on disk |
| **Other headers** that carry secrets under innocent names (`Referer` with a token in the URL, `X-Signature`) | Only the listed names and names matching `redact_keys` are masked | Extend `redact_headers` |
| **Multipart field values** under innocent names, and **file names** | Fields are parsed and masked by name; Django and Flask do not read multipart bodies at all, FastAPI and Litestar store the parsed fields (files as `[file: name, N bytes]`) | Turn off request body capture for upload routes with `ignore_paths` |

!!! tip "Verify with your own traffic"

    Send a request containing a fake secret under each field name your app really uses,
    then open **Request / Response**. The demo does this: `POST /checkout` with
    `Authorization`, `card_number` and `password` shows all three redacted.

### Logs and locals

Two 0.2 features capture more of your application's internals than 0.1 did, so they deserve
the same scrutiny as request bodies.

- **Log messages** are formatted, redacted for `key=value` pairs, and capped at 2,000
  characters. A log line like `Created user alice@example.com with token=abc123` stores the
  email and masks the token. If your logs carry personal data, raise `log_level`, or set
  `capture_logs = False`.
- **Exception locals** are the values of variables in project frames when a request raised.
  A model instance's `repr`, a request object, a dict of form data: the value is stored as
  printed. Names that look secret are masked; **a secret under an innocent name is not**. The
  `staging` and `production` presets turn `capture_locals` off. The `logs` and `locals`
  [feature switches](access-control.md#feature-switches) are the access-side counterpart.

Neither feature is a place to put secrets, and neither is a reason to log them: redaction
is a safety net, not a licence.

### The SQL EXPLAIN consequence

Because masked parameter values are what is stored, EXPLAIN of a query filtered on a
secret column or table (every query on `django_session`, `authtoken_token`…) runs with `[redacted]`
as the value. The plan may differ from the real one.
See [EXPLAIN](explain.md#safety).

## Who can open the UI

The UI and API expose SQL, bodies, source lines and exception locals, and can run EXPLAIN.
Treat access to them as access to a database console with read-only privileges *and* to the
traffic.

From 0.2 there is **one access policy for every framework**, chosen with the `access`
setting: `local`, `token`, `basic`, `framework` (the adapter's native hook), `custom` or
`open`. On top of it you can add IP allow-lists, trusted proxies, a `read_only` mode and
per-feature switches. The full description, with recipes for a laptop, a VPN, staging,
production, a reverse proxy and Kubernetes, is on [Access control](access-control.md). The
sections below describe the defaults and the threats.

=== "Django"

    **Default: active superusers** (staff before 0.2: staff status is often handed out for
    one model's admin, and Redline shows every user's requests). The check is
    `request.user.is_active and request.user.is_superuser`.

    - An **anonymous** visitor to the page is redirected to the admin login (or
      `LOGIN_URL`).
    - A **signed-in non-superuser** (staff included) gets `403`.
    - The **API** answers `403` JSON `{"error": {"code": "forbidden", ...}}`.

    Change it with `REDLINE["PERMISSION"]`, a callable `(request) -> bool` or a dotted
    path to one:

    ```python
    # myproject/redline.py
    def is_performance_team(request):
        user = request.user
        return user.is_active and user.groups.filter(name="performance").exists()

    # settings.py
    REDLINE = {"PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.is_performance_team"}
    # the 0.1 rule: "django_redline.conf.staff_permission"
    ```

    The callable is wrapped: an exception in it denies access (it **fails closed**).

=== "FastAPI, Flask and Litestar"

    **Default: `local`, loopback only, and only in debug mode until you set `access`.**
    While `access` is not set anywhere and the app is not in debug mode (`app.debug`),
    every Redline URL answers `404` and an error is logged at startup: a reverse proxy on
    the same host that adds no `X-Forwarded-For` would otherwise make every visitor
    local. Set `access = "local"` to accept that risk on a development machine, or
    `token`/`basic` on a server.

    With `local` in force and without `dependencies` (FastAPI), `permission` (Flask) or
    `guards` (Litestar), a request is served only when **both** hold, and a warning is
    logged at startup:

    - the client is loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`; a unix-socket peer only with
      `trust_unix_socket = true`);
    - the `Host` header names loopback: `localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127.x.x.x` or
      `[::1]`, with any port. This defeats DNS rebinding (below).

    A loopback peer that sends `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Real-IP` or `Forwarded` without being
    in `trusted_proxies` is refused too (it is almost certainly a reverse proxy on the same
    host). Pass your own hook (it implies `access = "framework"`; an empty list is no hook),
    or set `access`, for anything else. `access = "framework"` with no hook attached
    refuses every request (`403`) in all four adapters: there is nothing to delegate to. A FastAPI dependency should raise
    `HTTPException` to refuse; one that returns `False` is refused with `403` as well. A refusal is `403` JSON `{"error": {"code": "forbidden", ...}}`. See
    [FastAPI](fastapi.md#access-control), [Flask](flask.md#access-control) and
    [Litestar](litestar.md#access-control).

### Cross-site request forgery

Reads are `GET`. Every other method (`DELETE` on traces and runs, `POST api/explain`,
`POST api/runs`, login and logout) is protected:

- **Django** runs Django's own CSRF machinery on every API request (token in the CSRF
  header, plus the Origin and Referer checks on HTTPS), even if `CsrfViewMiddleware` is not
  installed, and answers `403 csrf_failed` as JSON.
- The shared access gate (all four adapters) rejects `Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site` **and
  `same-site`**, and any `Origin` (including `null`) whose host and port differ from the
  host the request was addressed to, with `403 csrf_failed` in the same JSON shape. This
  applies whatever access policy you chose. A request with no `Origin` is not a browser and
  passes.
- **Token and basic access** use an HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict session cookie scoped to the
  mount (`Secure` over https, see `cookie_secure`), so a cross-site request does not carry
  it. Logging out revokes the session in that process (in memory).
- **Replay** sends the recorded request **without your cookies** unless you tick "Send my
  cookies": the method, path and body were chosen by whoever made the recorded request,
  and replaying them with your session would be a stored CSRF.

### Forcing capture

`?_redline=profile` and `X-Redline-Profile: 1` start the profiler and make Redline keep the
trace whatever `sample_rate` says. They are honoured only in framework debug mode or when
the request itself carries valid Redline credentials (a Bearer token or Basic
credentials, a client the `local` policy lets in, or `access_check`); anyone else
could make you profile and store their requests at will. The login cookie is scoped to
the mount, so the browser never sends it to application URLs. With `access = "framework"` (a
hook that only runs inside Redline's own routes) only debug mode honours them. The
`production` preset turns profiling off. `X-Redline-Run` (the load tester's header) and `X-Redline-Check` (the refactor check's) tag a
trace only when that run exists in the store and is running (a check also for a minute after it ends).

### DNS rebinding

A web page on `evil.example` can re-point its own DNS name at `127.0.0.1`. Your browser
then sends that page's requests to your local server, as same-origin requests, so CORS and
the CSRF checks do not stop it reading `GET` endpoints. What gives it away is the `Host`
header, which still says `evil.example`.

- **FastAPI, Flask, Litestar:** the default `local` policy refuses any `Host` that is not a
  loopback name or address (`403 forbidden`). If you reach the app through a hosts-file
  alias, allow it explicitly with `allowed_hosts=["devbox"]` in the settings.
  With your own `dependencies` (real authentication), the attacker's page has no
  credentials for your host (cookies are bound to `evil.example`), so it is refused too.
- **Django:** every Redline view calls `request.get_host()`, so `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is enforced
  on them even without `CommonMiddleware` (an unknown host gets Django's `400`). With
  `DEBUG = True` and an empty `ALLOWED_HOSTS`, Django only accepts `localhost`,
  `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]`. The admin session cookie is not sent to the attacker's host name
  either. Do not combine `ALLOWED_HOSTS = ["*"]` with a `PERMISSION` that returns `True`.

### Framing

The UI page is served with `X-Frame-Options: DENY` by every adapter, so another site
cannot frame it and trick a click on **Clear all**.

### Putting it behind a proxy

!!! warning "Loopback is not a security boundary behind a proxy"

    If a reverse proxy forwards to your app on `127.0.0.1`, every request would look local.
    Redline refuses a loopback peer that carries forwarding headers unless it is a trusted
    proxy, but a proxy that strips them is not detectable, so use `access = "token"` and set
    `trusted_proxies` so the real client address is taken from `X-Forwarded-For` **only**
    when the request comes from your proxy (read from the right, skipping trusted hops).
    Without `trusted_proxies` Redline ignores that header, so a client cannot spoof its
    address. See
    [Access control: behind a reverse proxy](access-control.md#behind-a-reverse-proxy).

### Badge, Server-Timing and CSP

- The **floating badge** adds one `<script src>` tag, from Redline's own mount, to HTML pages
  in debug mode (`badge = "auto"`). It is off in the `production` preset. Under a strict
  CSP that allows only nonced scripts Redline skips the injection; see
  [Server-Timing and the badge](server-timing-badge.md#content-security-policy).
- **Server-Timing** (`server_timing`, default `"auto"`: debug mode only) exposes timings, a
  query count and a trace id to anyone who can read the response, including anonymous
  clients and the browser, which can be a side channel (for example to tell which accounts
  exist from query counts). No SQL or data. Outside debug mode leave it off unless you want
  it, and Redline warns when it is forced on outside `dev`.
- The **trace id** in `Server-Timing` lets someone who already has UI access find the trace;
  it grants nothing by itself.
- **Snapshots** are files containing a full trace. Whoever has the file has the data.

### Load from the UI

Starting a load run from the UI is **off by default** (`load_from_ui = False`, `403
load_disabled`). When on, its safety rests on these rules:

1. The request list may contain only **paths** (each must start with a single `/`). A scheme
   or host is rejected with `400 invalid_body`. The target is the `base_url` setting, or
   else the URL the request was addressed to, accepted only for a loopback host or one in
   `allowed_hosts`; a forged `Host` header cannot aim a run at another machine, and other
   hosts need `base_url`. Runs are capped at one hour, 5 000 rps and 200 steps.
2. It is gated by the same access policy, by `read_only` and by the `load` feature switch.
3. It is a real load: a user who may start runs can make your instance slow. Enable it only
   in environments where that is acceptable, and not in production.

The `redline load` command line is a different matter: it runs on the machine you run it
on, against the URL you give it, with the rights you have there. Point it only at systems you
own or are authorised to test.

### Refactor checks

Starting a [refactor check](refactor-check.md) from the UI is opt-in too: `checks_from_ui`
defaults to `"auto"`, which means **debug mode only**, and the `production` preset sets it to
`false` (`403 checks_from_ui_disabled`). It is also refused under `read_only` and when the
`checks` feature is off. A check is sequential `GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests: a suite
containing any other method is rejected when it is loaded, saved or started. Runs started
from the UI are limited to 200 requests, 5 000 calls and 15 minutes, and aim at the
`base_url` setting or the server's own listening port, never at the `Host` header.

What the feature stores, and what it does not:

- **`${env:NAME}` placeholders are never expanded in anything stored.** A suite keeps the
  placeholder. The value is read from the environment of the process that runs the check. For a
  run started from the UI, the headers are handed to the background process in a file with mode
  `0600` that is deleted when the run ends.
- **Secret header values are masked** (`[redacted]`) in stored suites, in `api/checks` responses
  and in exported TOML, unless they are only a placeholder (optionally after a scheme such as
  `Bearer ${env:API_TOKEN}`). Saving a suite with `[redacted]` back keeps the stored value.
- **Baselines are redacted.** Response headers and bodies go through the redactor before they
  are written (JSON keys at any depth, text through the text redactor), and again when a
  baseline is imported through the API, along with suite headers, URLs and request paths. The
  same redaction is applied to both sides of a comparison, so a masked secret never shows as a
  difference. A baseline is still a copy of your responses: keep it as private as a trace.
- **The check tag cannot force storage.** Every check call carries `X-Redline-Check: <run
  id>;req=<i>;n=<k>`. Redline honours the tag only when `<run id>` belongs to a check run that
  exists in the store and is running (or ended less than a minute ago). The ids are random
  128-bit values known only to Redline users. For any other request carrying the header, the
  `check_*` tags are removed and its normal sampling decision stands; a request that sampling
  would have dropped and that was only provisionally kept for the tag is dropped entirely.
  Profiling is never started by the tag.

### If you must expose it

In order of preference:

1. **Do not.** Use it in development and staging, and look at production traces by tunnelling
   (`ssh -L`) to a loopback-only instance.
2. Put it behind your SSO or an authenticating proxy **in addition to** the application's
   check, restricted to a small group.
3. Serve it only on an internal network or a VPN.

Never expose it with a dependency or permission that lets everyone in, or `access = "open"`
(which Redline refuses without `REDLINE_ALLOW_OPEN=1` and warns about on every request).

## Data on disk

- The file is **not encrypted**. On POSIX systems the store directory Redline creates is
  `0700`, and the database, its `-wal`/`-shm` files and the load-run files (`runs/`) are
  `0600`, as is a page written by `redline export --html`. These files are never written
  through a symlink. An older, world-readable database is tightened when it is opened. A directory
  that already existed (for example when `storage_path` is in your project root) keeps its
  permissions. Nothing changes on Windows.
- **Never commit it.** A store directory Redline creates (and `.redline/`) gets a
  `.gitignore` containing `*`; an existing `.gitignore` is never overwritten. Check your
  Docker build context and your backups too.
- It is **not your application database**: separate file, separate lifetime. Deleting it is
  always safe (`manage.py redline_clear` or **Clear all** in the UI).
- Traces live as long as `max_age_days` and `max_rows` say, **and no longer**: retention is
  the main control on how much data you hold. Keep both low in production. The longer-lived
  [history](history.md) tables (`history_retention_days`, 90 by default) hold only
  **aggregates**: counts, latency histograms, normalised SQL and issue titles. They contain
  no request bodies, headers or parameter values, but an issue title can contain a
  table name or a route.
- It is a **GDPR-style** concern as much as a security one: recorded bodies may be personal
  data. Retention, access control and the redaction patterns are your levers. Redline has
  no per-user erase; the nearest equivalent is `DELETE api/traces/<id>` or clearing
  everything.

## Other surfaces

| Surface | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **Responses** | Every adapter: the page sets `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: same-origin`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY` and `Cache-Control: no-store`. API responses are `no-store` and `nosniff` |
| **Static assets** | Served through the same access check. Hashed asset names are cached for a year; the path is resolved (symlinks and `..` included) and refused unless it stays inside the bundle directory, so `assets/../../conf.py` is a `404` |
| **`X-Redline-Trace` header** | Django only, and only when `DEBUG` is true: the id of the trace is added to the response, so you can find it. It is not sent in production |
| **Rendering** | The UI renders stored text through React, which escapes it: there is no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` or `innerHTML` anywhere. The SQL highlighter returns tokens rendered as text nodes, the diff view renders each line as text, and a suggestion's docs link is only rendered when it is `http(s)` (never `javascript:`). Trace ids are URL-encoded in API calls |
| **Outbound network** | Recording starts no telemetry, update check or exporter. Explicit load/check, online SQL compilation and export operations contact their configured targets |
| **Dependencies** | `redline-core` has **no runtime dependencies** |
| **The profiler** | Optional; adds `pyinstrument` |

## Supply chain: published and source installs

Published prereleases are available from the project's PyPI packages; use the adapter
for your framework so its exact core dependency is resolved together. Pin the matching
adapter/core versions in a reviewed lock file. See [Getting started](getting-started.md#install).
For an unreleased source install, use adapter and core from the same reviewed Git commit,
not moving branches or unrelated versions. Verify package/project links and distribution
provenance rather than relying only on a similar package name.

## A short threat model
