The full, structured version (assets, trust boundaries, STRIDE table and a checklist for an
independent reviewer) is on [Threat model](threat-model.md).

| Attacker | Wants | Stopped by |
|---|---|---|
| Anonymous internet user | Read traces | Django: login and superuser check. Others: `404` until `access` is set (outside debug mode), the loopback policy, a token or your own hook. **Not stopped** if you expose it open |
| Anonymous internet user | Force profiling and storage of their requests | `X-Redline-Profile` / `?_redline=profile` honoured only in debug mode or with Redline credentials; `production` turns profiling off |
| Logged-in non-admin user | Read other users' request data | `PERMISSION`, `dependencies`, `permission`, `guards` or a token |
| A client that sends a made-up `X-Redline-Check` header | Make Redline store its requests, or tag them as part of a check | The tag is honoured only for a check run that exists in the store and is running; otherwise it is stripped, and a request that was only kept for the tag is dropped |
| A logged-in user who may start load runs | Make the server hit someone else (or another local service), or overload it | Paths only (no host); the target is the server's own listening port, never the `Host` header; `load_from_ui` off by default, `read_only`, the `load` switch |
| Someone who guesses or sniffs a token | Read everything | A long random token, HTTPS, login rate limit, constant-time comparison. Use a VPN as well |
| A malicious website the admin visits | Delete traces, trigger EXPLAIN | CSRF protections; `X-Frame-Options: DENY` |
| A malicious website (DNS rebinding) | Read `GET` endpoints of a local instance | FastAPI: the `Host` check of the loopback default, or real auth. Django: `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (enforced on Redline's views) and the session cookie |
| Someone with read access to the disk or backups | Everything stored | redaction, retention, file permissions. **Not** encryption |
| An admin with the UI | Run arbitrary SQL | Not possible: EXPLAIN takes a trace and span id, never SQL, and is limited to **recorded single read-only `SELECT`s** (no locking clause, no data-modifying CTE, no second statement; see [EXPLAIN: safety](explain.md#safety)), in a rolled-back transaction. They can read what was recorded and, if `explain_analyze` is on, make the server re-run recorded queries |
| Someone who can write the store file | Plant SQL for EXPLAIN | The same `is_explainable` check runs again before EXPLAIN, on the stored text; side-effecting *functions* in a planted `SELECT` would only run under `explain_analyze` (off by default), in a rolled-back transaction |


## Shared-environment controls in 0.4

The [real-world guide](real-world-workflows.md#safer-shared-development-recording) describes
`capture_sql_params`, profiles, table patterns, route modes, logger filters and redaction
preview. The production recipe additionally disables log capture and active tools explicitly.
Route rules are applied after the route template is known and before persistence; `values`
preserves JSON structure while masking values, and `body` removes body contents. They also
restrict SQL values, query values, source snippets, log messages and exception detail for
that recording. Review source/fix snippets and nested issue evidence as capture surfaces too.

A user resolver is an explicit synchronous callable returning an identifier. Request-ID
headers are configurable, can be redacted, and are not proof of identity or authorization.
Do not use a client-supplied request ID to choose a store, authorize access or attach a trace
to another tenant. A person ID can still be personal data even when it is not a name.

For multiple codebases, separate stores, credentials and processes are the initial isolation
boundary. Secondary stores deliberately expose those files to the same authorized UI users;
read-only file access does not create per-codebase authorization. Configure `extra_stores`
only when that sharing is intended.

## Explicit outbound operations

Recording does not start an exporter automatically. Existing load/check commands contact
their configured target. Online SQL checks contact an explicitly supplied development DSN.
`redline export` previews summary JSON by default; `--send` and an explicit collector URL
are required to transmit it. The initial format omits bodies, SQL and arbitrary tags/error
messages and does not follow redirects. It is not a full production telemetry pipeline.
See the repository's `SECURITY.md` data-egress statement.


For recording in shared or production environments, `capture_error_details = false`
keeps exception types and structured database codes while suppressing free-text
messages, formatted tracebacks and exception locals. Set `capture_logs = false` as
well: warning/error severity does not make a log message free of personal data. These
are defaults of both `shared-dev` and `production`; explicit configuration can override
them. SQL failure messages also require that statement's SQL parameter capture policy
to allow capture. Counts and structured error categories remain useful when text is off.


Capture byte budgets reduce the amount of SQL, span data and tag text retained. They do
not replace redaction: a secret can fit inside a short value. The bounded value converter
uses standard JSON primitives and avoids arbitrary application object conversion methods.
Oversized, deep, cyclic or unsupported metadata is incomplete evidence, never a clean bill
of health. Validate secret canaries separately from size-limit tests.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/threat-model.md -->
<!-- page: Threat model -->

# Threat model

[← Index](index.md) · [Security](security.md)

This is the structured threat model behind [Security](security.md). It exists so that a
reviewer (internal or an independent third party) can check each claim against the code.
[Security](security.md) explains the controls to users; this page lists assets, trust
boundaries, entry points and residual risks. Redline has **not** had an independent
security review yet.

## Scope and assumptions

- Redline runs **inside** the application process (middleware/plugin + database hooks) and
  serves its UI and JSON API under a mount path (default `/_redline/`) of the same server.
- It targets development and staging. Production use is limited to the recording-only
  preset in [Production](production.md).
- The host, its filesystem, the Python environment and the application code are trusted.
  An attacker who can change them owns the application anyway.

## Assets

| Asset | Where | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Captured request data: headers, query strings, bodies, SQL text and parameters, logs, exception locals | the trace store (SQLite file or shared PostgreSQL store) | Personal data, credentials and business data can leak through it |
| Source callsites and snippets | the store | Reveal code structure and literals |
| Access credentials: Redline token, basic-auth hashes, session cookie, `REDLINE_SECRET_KEY` | settings, environment, cookies | Grant UI/API access |
| Database connections of the app | in-process engines | EXPLAIN re-runs recorded reads on them |
| The app's availability | the process | Recording costs CPU, memory and disk |

## Trust boundaries and entry points

| # | Boundary | Entry points | Main controls |
|---|---|---|---|
| B1 | Browser / network → Redline UI and API | `GET/POST {mount}/api/*`, login, static assets, SSE stream | access policy (`local`, `token`, `basic`, framework hook, `open` only by opt-in), CSRF checks on mutations, `Host` check against DNS rebinding, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, rate-limited login, constant-time comparison, `read_only` and per-feature switches |
| B2 | Any client → recorded application | every request the app serves | redaction before persistence, capture byte budgets, sampling, route rules; profiling and check tags honoured only for authorised callers |
| B3 | Redline → the app's database | EXPLAIN, index advice, catalog reads | only recorded single read-only `SELECT`s, re-validated on the stored text; rolled-back transaction; `explain_analyze` off by default |
| B4 | Redline → disk | store file(s), WAL, profile blobs | private file permissions, retention/pruning, WAL check, network-filesystem refusal; **no encryption at rest** |
| B5 | Redline → other services | OTLP export, load and refactor-check targets, webhooks, the GitHub API (`redline check comment`), OpenAPI downloads | nothing is sent by default; every egress needs an explicit command or setting; load targets are path-only on the server's own port; credentials (GitHub token, webhook URL) go only over https (plain http only to loopback for the token), never across redirects; answers are size-capped |
| B6 | Developer machine / CI → Redline CLI | `redline check`, `check-sql`, `analyze`, `load` | static commands parse source and never import it; `check-imports` imports in an isolated subprocess only when asked |

## Threats (STRIDE) and mitigations

| Threat | Category | Mitigation | Residual risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unauthenticated read of traces | Information disclosure | access policy; `404` until configured outside debug; doctor `--production` flags `open` | an operator can still choose `access="open"` |
| Secrets stored in clear | Information disclosure | key-based redaction of headers, query, bodies, logs and locals; SQL parameter policies; route rules | free text and values under innocent names are not caught ([what redaction misses](security.md#what-redaction-does-not-catch)) |
| Cross-site request deletes or triggers EXPLAIN | Tampering | CSRF token / same-origin checks on every mutation | depends on the browser enforcing SameSite and Origin |
| DNS rebinding against a loopback instance | Spoofing | `Host` allow-list for the loopback policy; `ALLOWED_HOSTS` on Django | another app on the same origin is trusted |
| Forced recording of attacker requests | Tampering / DoS | profile and check headers honoured only for authorised callers; bounded queue drops instead of blocking | high-cardinality traffic still costs CPU before sampling |
| Arbitrary SQL through EXPLAIN | Elevation of privilege | EXPLAIN takes trace/span ids, never SQL; `is_explainable` on stored text; rolled back | under `explain_analyze` a planted `SELECT` calling a side-effecting function would run (in a rolled-back transaction) |
| Store file stolen from disk or backups | Information disclosure | redaction, retention, file permissions | no at-rest encryption |
| Crafted request data makes redaction slow | Denial of service | redaction patterns are linear-time; error, header and identifier texts are cut before they are scanned | free-text capture still costs CPU proportional to the capture budgets |
| Recorder exhausts memory/disk | Denial of service | span/SQL/body/trace byte budgets, bounded writer queue, retention | budgets do not bound total process memory; see [capacity](production.md#capacity-and-failure-behavior) |
| Exported telemetry leaks data | Information disclosure | OTLP export omits bodies, SQL text and free-text tags; preview by default | collector security is the operator's |
| Malicious dependency or tampered release | Tampering | trusted publishing, PEP 740 attestations, CI actions pinned to full commit SHAs, checkouts without persisted credentials, least-privilege workflow permissions, Dependabot, `pip-audit` / `zizmor` in review | users must verify attestations themselves |

## Review checklist for an independent reviewer

1. Access policy: every route under the mount goes through the same guard (`access.py`), including static assets, the SSE stream and the login form.
2. CSRF: every non-GET API route checks the token/origin (`access.py`, adapter routes).
3. EXPLAIN: `is_explainable` cannot be bypassed via comments, CTEs, multiple statements or vendor-specific syntax (`explain.py`, `explain_mssql.py`, `sql.py`).
4. Redaction runs before *every* persistence path, including jobs, logs, exception locals and refactor-check results (`redact.py`, `privacy.py`, `recorder.py`).
5. No egress without explicit opt-in (`otlp.py`, `load/`, `check/`, webhook commands).
6. File permissions and path placeholders of the store (`storage/safety.py`).
7. The bundled UI renders recorded data without HTML injection (React escaping; no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` on recorded values).

## Needs a human

- An independent third-party security review against the checklist above.
- Validation of the deployment topology (proxy, TLS, filesystem, process model) in each
  environment where Redline is enabled; `redline doctor --production` covers what can be
  checked from inside the process.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/storage.md -->
<!-- page: Storage -->

# Storage

[← Index](index.md)

Redline keeps traces in a **separate SQLite file** of its own, written by a background
thread. This page covers the design, the schema, retention, the failure modes, and how to
look inside. When several worker processes or hosts should share one store, point
`storage_url` at a PostgreSQL database instead: see
[A shared PostgreSQL store](#a-shared-postgresql-store).

## Why a separate file

Each choice fixes something that makes in-database profilers painful.

| Choice | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Its own file**, never your application database | Profiling data cannot bloat your database, you need no migrations, and Redline's writes can never be recorded as your queries (it is not a Django connection nor one of your SQLAlchemy engines) |
| **WAL mode** | The UI can read while the writer writes |
| **A bounded queue and a writer thread** | The request path only does a `put_nowait`; disk I/O happens elsewhere |
| **Stdlib `sqlite3`** | `redline-core` has no runtime dependencies |

## Where the file is

| | Default |
|---|---|
| Django | `<BASE_DIR>/.redline/redline.db` |
| FastAPI, Flask, Litestar | `.redline/redline.db`, relative to the **working directory** at start |
| Any | the `storage_path` setting. `":memory:"` works (nothing persists) |

Parent directories are created. Add `.redline/` to `.gitignore`. The `-wal` and `-shm`
files next to it belong to the database while it is open; do not delete them while the app
runs.

## The schema

Created on first open with `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`.

| Table | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `traces` | one row per trace: id, started_at, framework, method, path, route, view, status, duration_ms, query_count, query_ms, issue_count, issue_kinds, has_profile, tags, and `body` | `body` is the full trace as JSON (spans, issues, redacted request and response, **without** the profile). Indexed by start time and by `(route, method)` |
| `profiles` | one row per profiled trace: the speedscope JSON | Kept apart so lists never load it |
| `trace_tags` | `(trace_id, key, value)` | makes `tag=key:value` filters fast |
| `issues` | one row per issue per trace, with the issue as JSON | Indexed by issue id and time; this is what the Issues page aggregates |

### Schema version 3 (0.2)

Version 0.2 adds a `meta(key, value)` table holding `schema_version` (`3` in 0.2, `4` since 0.3; see below) and a set of
**derived tables** that are written in the same transaction as the trace, from the same
batch:

| Table | Holds | Lives |
|---|---|---|
| `trace_sql` | one row per (trace, SQL fingerprint): the normalised statement, execution count, total and max time, rows, vendor, db alias | with its trace |
| `trace_ext` | one row per (trace, outbound URL pattern): count, total and max time, errors | with its trace |
| `trace_cache` | one row per (trace, cache key pattern): gets, hits, misses, sets, deletes | with its trace |
| `rollups` | hourly per release, route and method: count, errors, summed duration, a latency **histogram**, summed queries and query time, issue count | `history_retention_days` |
| `issue_rollups` | hourly per release and issue: occurrences (for period comparison) | `history_retention_days` |
| `releases` | release name, first and last seen, request count | `history_retention_days` |
| `issue_index` | every issue ever seen: kind, severity, title, route, first and last seen, first and last release, occurrences | `history_retention_days` |
| `runs`, `run_steps` | [load-test](load-testing.md) runs and their per-step results and histograms | `history_retention_days` |

Version 3 also adds `saved_seq` to `traces`: an insertion-order sequence number (indexed,
`meta` keeps the high-water mark). The live stream uses it to resume exactly after the last
event a client saw (`after=` or `Last-Event-ID`), because traces are saved when they
*finish*, not when they start.

In the rollups and the issue index a request that matched no route (a 404, a scanner
probing random paths) is filed under the single route key `(unmatched)`, so the long-lived
history does not grow a row per random path.

The first three power the [Database](database.md), [Cache](cache-efficiency.md) and
[External calls](external-calls.md) pages and are pruned **with their trace**. The rest
power [History](history.md) and the Load page and outlive the traces.

A re-saved trace id replaces its trace-scoped rows and is **not** counted again in rollups,
releases or the issue index. History reflects **kept** traces, so [sampling](production.md#sampling)
applies to it.

### Schema version 4 (0.3)

Version 0.3 adds the [refactor check](refactor-check.md) tables. They are new tables only; no
existing table changes.

| Table | Holds | Lives |
|---|---|---|
| `check_suites` | a saved suite: id, name, the suite as JSON (secret header values redacted, `${env:NAME}` placeholders kept), created and updated time | until you delete the suite (which deletes its runs) |
| `check_runs` | one row per baseline or compare run: kind, status (`running`, `done`, `failed`, `stopped`), label, commit sha and branch, the baseline it was compared with, a summary, the redacted suite snapshot, base URL, release, progress and error | the 50 most recent per suite |
| `check_results` | one row per request of a run, `(run_id, idx)`: the baseline data or the comparison result as JSON | with its run |

Retention is by count, not age: whenever a run is created or a baseline is imported, each
suite keeps its **50 newest runs** (runs without a suite form one group). A run that is still
running is never removed, and neither is a baseline that a kept compare run refers to.
**Clear all** (`DELETE api/traces`) and `redline_clear` do not touch these tables. A `running`
row whose background process died becomes `failed` with the error `the check process exited
unexpectedly`. Redline checks this when runs are read, for runs older than 10 seconds, and only
where a `runs` directory sits beside the store file (as for load runs).

The tables are written synchronously, outside the trace writer's batches, because a check run
is a handful of writes and the report must be readable the moment the run ends.

### Migration

Migrations are additive and run when the store connects. A 0.1 file (no `schema_version`
row), a version 2 file and a version 3 file are migrated **in place**, inside one `BEGIN
IMMEDIATE` transaction that re-checks the version once it holds the lock, so several workers
starting at once migrate it exactly once.
The new tables are created and **backfilled from the traces already stored**. Traces
written by 0.1 still load: every new field has a default.

There is no downgrade. If you may need to roll back to 0.1, copy `.redline/redline.db`
first. The data is a cache of recent requests, so deleting the file is always an
acceptable fix for a store that will not open.

## Verifying the filesystem

`redline doctor` creates a temporary SQLite database in the nearest existing parent of the
store and requires `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL` to succeed there. It also reports a warning
for Linux mounts that commonly break SQLite's shared-memory file (`nfs`, `cifs`, `9p`,
`virtiofs`, `fuse` and similar). The probe never opens or initializes the configured store.
Run it in the same container, mount and working directory as the application. A successful
probe is necessary but not sufficient for concurrent containers; a named volume or local
disk is safer than a bind mount through a VM sharing layer.

## The writer thread

`SQLiteStore.save(trace)` puts the trace on a bounded queue (`writer_queue_size`, default
1000) and returns. A daemon thread named `redline-writer`, started on the first `save` in
each process:

1. takes one item, then drains up to **50** more that are already waiting (a batch);
2. writes the batch in **one transaction**, opened with `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (as are pruning
   and migrations), so concurrent worker processes take the write lock up front and wait
   instead of failing with a busy error halfway through;
3. every 200 saved traces, runs [retention](#retention);
4. survives errors: a failed batch is logged on the `redline` logger and the thread
   carries on.

### Overload

If the queue is full, `save` does not wait: the trace is **dropped and counted**. The
count is `store.dropped`, exposed as `storage.dropped` in `GET api/meta`. It means the
writer cannot keep up with the rate of kept traces. Lower `sample_rate`, turn off
body capture, or raise the queue bound (which only postpones the problem and uses memory).
`store.written` counts what was stored.

### Flushing and shutdown

`store.flush(timeout)` blocks until everything enqueued so far is written (it returns
`False` on timeout). `store.close()` flushes, stops the thread and closes the connection.
Both adapters call them at shutdown (FastAPI: the lifespan wrapper; Django: an `atexit`
hook). A hard kill loses whatever was still queued.

### Concurrency

One connection is shared behind a lock. SQLite serialises writers anyway, and the UI's
reads are small, but note:

- UI reads and the writer take turns. A long aggregate (a 7-day Endpoints page over many
  thousands of traces) delays the writer for its duration.
- Several **processes** on one host can share the file (WAL, 10-second busy timeout); for
  several hosts, or many busy workers, use the [shared PostgreSQL
  store](#a-shared-postgresql-store). The test suite
  opens one file from two independent OS processes (100 traces each) and checks the count;
  it does not use fork, so it exercises the same path as separate containers. See
  [Production: process models](production.md#process-models) for the caveats.
- After `fork()` (gunicorn `--preload`, uWSGI without `lazy-apps`) the store opens a
  new connection, queue and writer thread in the child; the parent's connection is never
  touched there. See [Production: process models](production.md#process-models).
- `SQLiteStore(background=False)` writes inline on the calling thread. That is for tests
  and short scripts, **not** for serving requests.

## Retention

Two rules, applied together.

| Rule | Setting | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Age | `max_age_days` (default 7) | delete traces whose start is older than this. `0` or `None` disables the age rule |
| Count | `max_rows` (default 10,000) | keep the newest N, delete the rest. `0` or `None` disables the row cap |

Zero means "no limit" for both rules, and a negative value is an error. Pruning never
deletes everything because of a zero; that is what **Clear all** is for.

Applied by the writer every 200 saved traces, by `manage.py redline_prune` (Django) on
demand, and when you call `store.prune(max_age_s=..., max_rows=...)`. Pruning removes the
trace and its profile, tags and issue rows together. **Clear all** (`DELETE api/traces`)
and `manage.py redline_clear` remove everything.

Because retention is checked per 200 writes, the store can briefly exceed `max_rows` by up
to roughly that many.

### History tables

The [history](history.md) tables have their own, longer clock.

| Setting | Default | Covers |
|---|---|---|
| `history_retention_days` | `90` | `rollups`, `issue_rollups`, `releases`, `issue_index`, and load `runs` with their steps. `0` or `None` keeps them forever |

When pruning runs it also calls `prune_history()`: rollup hours that ended before the
cutoff are deleted, as are releases and issue-index entries **last seen** before it, and
finished runs created before it. A run that is still `running` is never deleted. The trace
summary tables (`trace_sql`, `trace_ext`, `trace_cache`) follow their traces.

**Clear all** and `redline_clear` delete traces and **keep history**, so a clean-up does not
erase your release comparisons. `store.clear(history=True)` wipes history as well.

!!! note "Retention shapes the Issues and Endpoints pages"

    Both pages only know about traces that still exist. A 7-day window with
    `max_age_days = 2` shows two days. A `max_rows` that holds an hour of traffic makes a
    `24h` window show an hour.

## Size

Measured with `benchmarks/storage.py` on 2026-10-26 (Apple M2 Pro, Python 3.13.15), for a
`GET` with browser-like headers and a JSON response of about 1 KB, every query issued
from one loop line (so the 20- and 200-query traces carry an N+1 issue and its fix
suggestion). Bytes are the `.db` file after a WAL checkpoint, divided by the traces stored:

| Trace | On disk per trace |
|---|---|
| no queries | **1.6 KiB** |
| 20 queries | **31 KiB** |
| 200 queries | **261 KiB** |
| a pyinstrument profile of a ~20 ms request | **+1.6 KiB** (a profile grows with the number of distinct stacks sampled; deep, long requests reach hundreds of KiB) |

So each SQL span costs about **1.3 KiB** on disk, most of it the SQL text and the
callsite (file, line, source line and up to 12 stack frames). With the defaults
(`max_rows = 10,000`) a store of 20-query traces settles around **300 MiB**; a store of
plain requests around 16 MiB. `max_spans_per_trace` (default 2000) bounds the largest
single trace at roughly 2.6 MiB.

The factors, largest first:

- the number of SQL spans, and the length of your SQL;
- captured bodies (up to `max_body_bytes` each, request and response);
- **profiles**, which can dominate for long requests;
- headers and tags.

To measure your own app: after a representative run, `ls -lh .redline/` (include the
`-wal` file) and divide by `storage.rows` from `GET api/meta`. Reproduce the table with
`uv run python benchmarks/storage.py`.

Disk usage after pruning does not shrink on its own: SQLite reuses freed pages but does not
return them to the operating system. To reclaim space, stop the app and run
`sqlite3 .redline/redline.db 'VACUUM'`, or delete the file.

## Looking inside

It is an ordinary SQLite database:

```bash
sqlite3 .redline/redline.db
```

```sql
.tables
SELECT method, route, count(*) AS n, round(avg(duration_ms), 1) AS avg_ms
FROM traces GROUP BY method, route ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 10;

SELECT json_extract(body, '$.error.type'), count(*) FROM traces
WHERE json_extract(body, '$.error') IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1;
```

Treat the file as **read-only**: the schema and the JSON layout are not a public
interface. Use the [HTTP API](http-api.md) for anything you build on.

## Backup and copying

You usually do not need to back it up. To take a copy of a running database consistently
use SQLite's online backup: `sqlite3 .redline/redline.db ".backup copy.db"`. Copying only
the `.db` file while it is being written can miss data that is still in the `-wal` file.

## A shared PostgreSQL store

A SQLite file belongs to one host: it must sit on a local disk (WAL does not work reliably
over NFS/SMB), and every replica keeps its own. For several worker processes, containers or
hosts writing **one** store, use PostgreSQL:

```bash
pip install "redline-core[postgres]"            # psycopg 3 with its bundled libpq
export REDLINE_STORAGE_URL="postgresql://redline:secret@db.internal:5432/redline"
```

or `storage_url = "postgresql://..."` in `redline.toml` (Django: `REDLINE["STORAGE_URL"]`).
With `storage_url` set, every adapter builds `PostgresStore` instead of the SQLite file and
`storage_path` is not used. The SQLite file stays the default.

- **Same engine.** `PostgresStore` and `SQLiteStore` share one implementation
  (`redline_core.storage.sqlite.SQLStore`); a small dialect layer rewrites placeholders,
  `INSERT OR REPLACE` (into `ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE`) and the column types. Every page,
  aggregate and API route works the same; the live suite checks that endpoints, issues, the
  SQL workload, history and the issue index come out identical to SQLite on the same data.
- **Same write path.** `save()` only enqueues; the writer thread writes a batch per
  transaction. Each write transaction takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock first, so
  writers from all processes and hosts are serialized the way SQLite serializes them (the
  live-tail sequence and the merged hourly histograms stay exact). Reads take no lock. At a
  few hundred kept traces per second this is not a bottleneck; sample more aggressively if
  `storage.dropped` grows.
- **Schema versioning.** The `meta` table holds `schema_version` as in SQLite. The first
  process to connect creates the tables under the same lock, so workers starting together
  create them once; reopening is a no-op.
- **Connections.** One connection per process, opened lazily (a store built before `fork()`
  does not hand its socket to the workers) and reopened after the server drops it. Statements
  are not server-side prepared, so PgBouncer in transaction mode works. On macOS the GSSAPI
  probe is disabled (`gssencmode=disable`; it crashes forked children) unless the URL sets
  `gssencmode`.
- **Placement.** Use a dedicated database or schema and a role that owns it; Redline never
  writes your application database. `PostgresStore(url, schema="redline")` creates and uses
  that schema; from settings, add `?options=-csearch_path%3Dredline` to the URL (the schema
  must exist). Retention (`max_rows`, `max_age_days`, `history_retention_days`) is applied
  by whichever worker's writer prunes, to the whole shared store.
- **Secrets.** `redline config` and `GET api/config` show the URL with its password masked.

Load tests and refactor checks **started from the UI** need a SQLite store (their background
process writes into the store file), so those UI actions answer `501` with a shared store;
the CLI (`redline load`, `redline check`) still records into SQLite files. `redline doctor`
checks the driver and that the database answers.

## A different store

The `Store` protocol is public. To plug in your own, pass `install(store=...)` (FastAPI),
`Redline(store=...)` (Flask), `RedlinePlugin(store=...)` (Litestar) or set `REDLINE["STORE"]`
(Django); see [Extending](extending.md#the-store-protocol).

The 0.1 `Store` surface is unchanged, so a 0.1 custom store keeps working. The 0.2
features (history, the Database, Cache and External pages, load runs, live tail) live on an
**extended** protocol, `redline_core.storage.ExtendedStore`. A store that lacks a method, or
raises `NotImplementedError`, makes the matching API route answer `501 not_supported` and
the UI page say it is unavailable, while everything else works.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/performance.md -->
<!-- page: Performance and overhead -->

# Performance and overhead

[← Index](index.md)

A profiler that slows the thing it measures is worse than useless, so Redline is built to
keep its cost low and explainable. This page describes the **cost model** (where the time
goes and what you can do about it) and the [measured numbers](#measured-numbers).

!!! abstract "In one line"

    Measured on an Apple M2 Pro (Python 3.14, 2026-10-27, v0.2 development tree): recording
    every request costs about **0.04 to 0.09 ms per request plus 28 to 51 µs per SQL
    query**, depending on the framework; disabled, it is a few µs per request and under
    1 µs per query. The v0.1 figures (0.05 to 0.06 ms and 22 to 44 µs) are kept
    [below](#v01-numbers) for comparison. Details and how to reproduce are
    [below](#measured-numbers).

## Where the cost is

Work happens in four places. Each is controlled by a different setting.

### 1. Per request, always (unless ignored)

Starting and finishing a trace, creating the span list, the middleware's own bookkeeping,
and on FastAPI wrapping `receive` and `send` to copy body chunks (only up to
`max_body_bytes`).

Reduce it with `ignore_paths` (the request is not recorded at all) or `enabled: false`.

### 2. Per query, always (inside a recorded request)

For every SQL statement: two `perf_counter()` reads, the span object, the **SQL
fingerprint** (memoised, so repeated statements are cheap), a **stack walk** to find the
callsite (a cached filename verdict per frame, one `linecache` read for the innermost), and
**parameter redaction by column** (a regular expression over the statement).

This is the cost that **`sample_rate` does not reduce**: the decision to keep a trace is
made when the request ends, after these costs were paid. A request with 400 queries
pays 400 times. Hot, query-heavy endpoints are where Redline costs most, and also where
it is most useful.

### 3. Per kept trace

When the sampler keeps a trace: redaction of headers, query and bodies, running the
detectors, running the fix suggesters (the Django and SQLAlchemy ones parse source files
with `ast`, so they do real work per issue),
and JSON serialisation. Lowering `sample_rate` reduces this directly.

### 4. On the writer thread

SQLite inserts, with WAL. It competes for the GIL with your request threads, but it is off
the request path. The request only does a `put_nowait`.

### What 0.2 adds to the cost model

The 0.2 features were designed to cost nothing when idle. Their cost, by where it falls:

| Feature | When it costs | What it costs |
|---|---|---|
| Event-loop lag monitor ([Blocking in async](async-blocking.md)) | only while a request is in flight on a loop | a timer callback every 5 ms per busy loop; a watchdog thread that sleeps until a tick is overdue. Nothing in an idle process. `detect_blocking = False` removes it |
| Row counts and `has_limit` on SQL spans | per query | reading `rowcount` and one scan of the SQL text; no extra query |
| Transaction and pool-wait spans | per transaction / checkout | one span each |
| Log capture ([Logs](logs-and-exceptions.md)) | per log record inside a request | formatting, redaction and a callsite lookup; one `ContextVar.get()` outside a request |
| Exception locals | only when a request raises | walking the traceback once; nothing on the happy path |
| Derived tables (`trace_sql`, `trace_ext`, `trace_cache`, rollups, issue index) | per **kept** trace, on the **writer thread** | more rows per batch in the same transaction. The request thread is not involved |
| `Server-Timing` header | per recorded response | formatting one string |
| Badge injection | per recorded HTML response in debug mode | one string insert before `</body>` |
| Contrib integrations (`requests`, redis, asyncpg, psycopg) | per call inside a request | one `ContextVar.get()` outside a request; a span inside |
| The aggregate pages and History | when a page is opened | queries over small summary tables, not over trace bodies |
| Load testing | while a run is going | the generator runs in separate **processes**; run it from another machine if you want its CPU kept off the app under test |

The [measured numbers](#measured-numbers) below include v0.2 with all of the above active
(the harness exercises the recorder end to end). The individual additions are small
per-span or per-batch costs that were **not benchmarked one by one**. If you need a number
for your app, use [Measure it yourself](#measure-it-yourself).

### Plus, on demand

| Feature | Cost |
|---|---|
| Profiling a request | pyinstrument sampling every millisecond while the request runs; only for profiled requests |
| EXPLAIN | one query on your database, once, when someone clicks. `ANALYZE` runs the query for real |
| The UI polling | one `COUNT(*)` plus a page query every two seconds while a Requests page is open and Live mode is on polling (Live mode normally uses one open SSE connection instead) |
| `api/stream` | one open connection per viewer, closed after five minutes on ASGI servers and about 25 seconds on WSGI servers, where it holds a worker thread (the client reconnects and resumes by `seq`) |
| A snapshot download | building one HTML file (the UI bundle, inlined) |

## What the design avoids

- **No disk I/O on the request path.** Saving is a queue put.
- **No cost when idle.** Every hook is `ContextVar.get()` and a `None` check outside a
  recorded request: your management commands, tests and ignored paths pay almost nothing.
- **No extra queries.** Redline never queries your application database while recording.
  (EXPLAIN does, on demand.)
- **No unbounded buffering of bodies.** Request and response bodies are copied up to
  `max_body_bytes` and no further, streaming responses included.
- **No tracing of itself.** Its own mount is ignored and its store is not one of your
  connections.

## Memory

- Each in-flight SQL span costs about **1.5 KB** (measured, including its callsite stack).
  A request stores at most `max_spans_per_trace` spans (default **2000**, about 3 MB);
  beyond that spans are counted but not kept, so a runaway loop of 100,000 queries does
  not hold 150 MB. Query counts, query time, and the N+1 and slow-query issues still
  include the dropped spans (per fingerprint and callsite counters), and the trace is
  marked **truncated** in the UI. `0` or `None` removes the cap.
- A queue of up to `writer_queue_size` full traces in memory when the writer lags.
- Garbage: a span object and a dict per query (beyond the cap, a short-lived one).
- The callsite stack walk is a Python loop. Deep stacks cost more.

## How to keep it cheap

| Do | Effect |
|---|---|
| Ignore health checks, metrics and static assets | their requests are skipped entirely |
| Lower `sample_rate` | less analysis, serialising and disk; **not** less recording |
| Turn off `capture_response_body` | smaller traces, less redaction work, less memory |
| Lower `max_body_bytes` | less copying |
| Leave `profile` at `opt_in` | no profiler cost unless asked |
| Keep `max_rows` modest | a smaller file, and faster Issues and Endpoints queries |
| Set `project_root` correctly | callsite classification caches work; a wrong root means no callsites and wasted walks |

## Measured numbers

### v0.2 numbers

From `benchmarks/RESULTS.md`, measured on **2026-10-27** against the v0.2 development tree
(`redline-core 0.1.0a1` version string), Apple M2 Pro, Python 3.14.7 (CPython, macOS
arm64), Django 6.1.2, FastAPI 0.162.0, Flask 3.1.3, Litestar 2.25.0, SQLAlchemy 2.1.6,
pyinstrument 5.1.3. Method as in v0.1: 1500 timed requests per cell, three interleaved
rounds pooled, a fresh subprocess per cell, an in-process client, in-memory SQLite. The
`off` baseline is a bare view, so Redline's *share* looks larger than it would next to a
real database. The run was repeated back to back; the two runs agree within 2 to 4%, and
the table shows run 1 with run 2 where they differ visibly.

**Added time per request** (median, 0 queries) and **per SQL query**, recording with
`sample_rate = 1` (every trace kept), against Redline not installed:

| Framework | Per request (v0.2) | v0.1 | Per query (v0.2) | v0.1 | Disabled, per request / query |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Django | +0.071 ms | +0.063 ms | +28.0 µs | +22.4 µs | +0.004 ms / +0.4 µs |
| FastAPI | +0.089 ms | +0.048 ms | +50.1 µs | +44.1 µs | +0.007 ms / +0.4 µs |
| Flask | +0.038 ms | new | +28.2 µs | new | +0.001 ms / +0.2 µs |
| Litestar | +0.058 ms | new | +50.9 µs | new | about 0 / +0.3 µs |

Other modes (run 1): with `sample_rate = 0` (nothing kept) the per-request / per-query cost
is +0.042 ms / 14.8 µs (Django), +0.061 ms / 28.2 µs (FastAPI), +0.037 ms / 27.3 µs (Flask)
and +0.036 ms / 31.3 µs (Litestar). Profiling every request (`profile: "all"`) costs
+0.222 / +0.342 / +0.217 / +0.237 ms per request and +65 / +119 / +68 / +116 µs per query,
in that order.

Read the comparison with care. Django and FastAPI are somewhat more expensive than in v0.1
(FastAPI's fixed cost +0.089 vs +0.048 ms is the largest move). Part of it may be Python
3.14 against 3.13 and a shared machine (the `off` baselines drifted by a few microseconds),
but it is consistent across both runs, so treat it as a candidate regression until it has
been re-measured on 3.13. Flask is the cheapest adapter per request; Litestar and FastAPI
share the ASGI path and cost about the same.

Storage (`benchmarks/storage.py`, v0.2 against v0.1):

| Queries / trace | On disk per trace | v0.1 | Writer, traces/s | v0.1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 2.3 KiB | 1.6 KiB | about 29,000 to 32,000 | 53,600 |
| 20 | 31.5 KiB | 30.9 KiB | about 3,200 to 3,600 | 3,800 |
| 200 | 265.3 KiB | 260.9 KiB | about 400 | 440 |

A profile adds 1.8 KiB of speedscope JSON per profiled trace. An in-flight SQL span costs
1,549 bytes, so the default `max_spans_per_trace = 2000` caps a request at about 3 MiB of
spans. Tiny traces are about 0.7 KiB bigger and the writer is slower for them (not
investigated), still far above any realistic rate for one process.

**Load generator** (`redline load`, httpx, open model, against a hello-world ASGI app on
the same machine): about 1,300 requests per second per worker process without drops, scaling
less than linearly (about 1,600 to 1,800 with 2 workers, about 2,400 to 3,000 with 4).
Beyond a worker's capacity the open-model backlog never drains and the run collapses, which
`redline load` reports as a knee, so start a sweep low and step up. Repeat sweeps varied by
10 to 25% at the edge. For more than about 1,000 requests per second per process add
`--workers`.

### v0.1 numbers

From `benchmarks/RESULTS.md`, measured on **2026-10-26** against `0.1.0a1`, Apple M2 Pro, Python 3.13.15
(CPython, macOS arm64), Django 6.1.2, FastAPI 0.162.0, SQLAlchemy 2.1.6, pyinstrument
5.1.3. Each cell is 1500 timed requests after warm-up, in a fresh subprocess, through an
in-process client against in-memory SQLite. The baseline (`off`) is a bare view with no
middleware, so Redline's *share* looks larger than it would next to a real database and
templates; the absolute added time is what carries over.

**Added time per request** (median, 0 queries) and **per SQL query**, against Redline not
installed:

| Mode | Django / request | Django / query | FastAPI / request | FastAPI / query |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled: false` | +0.004 ms | +0.4 µs | +0.006 ms | +0.4 µs |
| recording, `sample_rate = 0` (nothing kept) | +0.039 ms | +12.5 µs | +0.028 ms | +25.6 µs |
| recording, `sample_rate = 1` (every trace kept) | +0.063 ms | +22.4 µs | +0.048 ms | +44.1 µs |
| `profile: "all"` (a flamegraph on every request) | +0.195 ms | +41.9 µs | +0.229 ms | +91.2 µs |

The FastAPI per-query figures include SQLAlchemy's event dispatch around a ~15 µs
`text()` query. A disabled FastAPI install adds no middleware and no SQLAlchemy listeners.

| Scenario | Result |
|---|---|
| Disabled vs not installed | a few µs per request, under 1 µs per query |
| Recording with `sample_rate = 0` | the per-query recording cost alone: 12.5 µs (Django), 25.6 µs (FastAPI) |
| Recording with `sample_rate = 1` | adds analysis, redaction and the enqueue: 22.4 µs / 44.1 µs per query |
| Query-heavy request | linear in query count: at the `sample_rate = 1` rates, 200 queries add about 4.5 ms (Django) or 9 ms (FastAPI); beyond `max_spans_per_trace` the cost per query drops (no redaction, no storage) |
| Profiled request | about 0.2 ms per request plus roughly double the per-query cost while pyinstrument samples |
| Writer saturation | the writer stores about **3,800 traces/s** of 20 queries each (about 440/s at 200 queries, 50,000/s with none) on the same machine; `dropped` only rises above that rate of *kept* traces (`benchmarks/storage.py`) |

The plan's target was "under 1 ms plus a few microseconds per query when not profiling".
The per-request part is met by a wide margin; the per-query part is **12 to 51 µs** across
both releases, more than "a few", mostly spent on fingerprinting, callsite capture and
parameter redaction.

### Reproduce

```bash
uv sync --all-packages
uv run python benchmarks/overhead.py     # about 4 minutes; --quick for a smoke run
uv run python benchmarks/storage.py      # about a minute: sizes and writer throughput
```

Absolute numbers are machine specific; compare modes on the same machine.

### Measure it yourself

The benchmark is a bare view. To know the cost in your application, A/B it with a
representative load:

1. Run the app with `enabled: false`, record requests per second and latency percentiles
   with a load tool you trust (`redline load`, Locust, k6, `wrk`, `hey`).
2. Run again with Redline on at the settings you intend for production.
3. Compare latency percentiles and CPU, not just the mean.
4. Check `storage.dropped` in `GET api/meta` after the run: it must be `0`.
5. Repeat with a query-heavy endpoint, since that is the worst case.

## Why this page exists anyway

The cost model tells you *which setting to reach for* when something is slow, which does
not depend on the numbers. The measurements say how much, on one machine; your own A/B
says how much on yours.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/settings.md -->
<!-- page: Settings reference -->

# Settings reference

[← Index](index.md)

Every setting, its type, default and effect. They are defined once, in
`redline_core.conf.Settings`, and shared by every adapter. Each adapter only chooses *how
you pass them*, and settings can also come from a [preset, a config file and `REDLINE_*`
environment variables](configuration.md), which this page's defaults sit underneath.

=== "Django"

    ```python
    # settings.py
    REDLINE = {
        "SAMPLE_RATE": 0.1,
        "SLOW_QUERY_MS": 50,
        "PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.can_view",   # Django-only
    }
    ```

=== "FastAPI"

    ```python
    install(app, engine=engine, settings={
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
        "slow_query_ms": 50,
    })
    ```

    or pass a `redline_core.Settings` instance.

=== "Flask"

    ```python
    app.config["REDLINE"] = {"sample_rate": 0.1, "slow_query_ms": 50}
    Redline(app, engine=engine)           # or Redline(app, settings={...})
    ```

=== "Litestar"

    ```python
    RedlinePlugin(engine=engine, settings={"sample_rate": 0.1, "slow_query_ms": 50})
    ```

=== "redline.toml"

    ```toml
    sample_rate = 0.1
    slow_query_ms = 50
    ```

## Rules that apply to every setting

- **Keys are case-insensitive.** `SAMPLE_RATE` and `sample_rate` are the same. The tables
  below use the lower-case names (Django: write them upper-case by convention).
- **Unknown keys are errors**, with a suggestion: `SettingsError: Unknown Redline
  setting(s): 'sampel_rate' (did you mean 'sample_rate'?). Valid settings: ...`. In
  Django this surfaces as `ImproperlyConfigured` and as the system check
  `django_redline.E001`.
- **Types are checked.** A string where an integer belongs, a negative number, or a
  `bool` where a number belongs is rejected. A float or int is fine for any number setting.
- **List settings** (`ignore_paths`, `redact_headers`, `redact_keys`) accept a list, tuple
  or a single string (treated as a one-element list).
- **Regular expressions are compiled at load time**, so an invalid pattern fails at
  startup, not on the first request.
- `Settings` is **immutable**. `settings.replace(...)` returns a changed copy.

!!! warning "A list you set replaces the default, it does not extend it"

    Setting `ignore_paths` or `redact_headers` or `redact_keys` discards the built-in
    list. If you set `"IGNORE_PATHS": ["^/health"]`, then `/static/`, `/media/` and
    `/favicon.ico` are **no longer ignored**. Include the defaults you want to keep. (The
    adapters still add Redline's own mount for you.) The same holds for `redact_keys`:
    overriding it with one pattern removes password, token and card masking unless
    your pattern includes them. See [Security](security.md#redaction).

## General

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `bool` | `True` | Master switch. When false nothing is recorded or stored. Django: the middleware stays installed but every request passes straight through. FastAPI: `install()` adds no middleware and no SQLAlchemy listeners. The UI still serves stored traces |
| `storage_path` | `str` or `os.PathLike` (converted to `str`) | `".redline/redline.db"` | The SQLite file. Parent directories are created. `":memory:"` works. **Django default:** `<BASE_DIR>/.redline/redline.db`. See [Storage](storage.md) |
| `storage_url` | `postgresql://` URL or `None` | `None` | Store traces in this shared PostgreSQL database instead of the SQLite file, so several workers and hosts write one store. Needs `redline-core[postgres]`. The password is masked wherever settings are shown. See [Storage: a shared PostgreSQL store](storage.md#a-shared-postgresql-store) |
| `project_root` | `str`, `os.PathLike` or `None` | `None` | Directory that marks "your code" for [callsite capture](how-it-works.md#callsites). `None` means the working directory. **Django default:** `BASE_DIR`. Also where [`redline.toml`](configuration.md#the-config-file) is looked for |
| `preset` | `"dev"`, `"shared-dev"`, `"staging"` or `"production"` | `"dev"` | A bundle of defaults. Explicit settings override it. See [Configuration](configuration.md#presets) |
| `release` | `str` or `None` | `None` (automatic) | Name stamped on each trace for [History](history.md#releases). Automatic: `REDLINE_RELEASE`, then `GIT_SHA` / `SOURCE_VERSION` / `RENDER_GIT_COMMIT` / `HEROKU_SLUG_COMMIT`, then `git rev-parse --short HEAD` in `project_root` (once, one-second timeout), else none |

## Sampling: what gets stored

See [How it works: sampling](how-it-works.md#sampling).

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sample_rate` | `float`, 0 to 1 | `1.0` | Fraction of requests kept at random. **Django default:** `1.0` when `DEBUG` is true and **`0.1` when `DEBUG` is false** (and the check `django_redline.W005` fires if you set `1.0` in production) |
| `always_keep_slower_than_ms` | `float`, 0 or more | `500` | A request at least this slow is kept regardless of the dice. `0` keeps everything |
| `always_keep_errors` | `bool` | `True` | Keep requests that returned status 500 or above, raised an unhandled exception, or contained an observed SQL/connection failure, regardless of the dice. A **4xx is never an error**, even when it was raised as an exception (Django's `Http404`, `PermissionDenied`): those traces have `error: null` and are kept only by the dice or the slow rule |
| `ignore_paths` | list of `str` | `["/static/", "/media/", "/favicon.ico"]` | Paths never recorded. An entry starting with `^` is a **regular expression** (matched with `re.search` on the path); anything else is a **path prefix**. Redline's own mount is always added |

## Capture and redaction

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `capture_request_body` | `bool` | `True` | Store request bodies (redacted, capped). When false, bodies are not read at all |
| `capture_response_body` | `bool` | `True` | Store response bodies (redacted, capped). Streaming and file responses are never captured |
| `max_body_bytes` | `int`, 0 or more | `20000` | Cap for a stored body. Longer bodies are cut and flagged `body_truncated`. Masking runs **before** the cut |
| `redact_headers` | list of `str` | `["authorization", "cookie", "set-cookie", "x-api-key", "proxy-authorization"]` | Header names (case-insensitive) whose values are replaced with `[redacted]` |
| `redact_keys` | list of regex | `["(?i)pass(word)?\|secret\|token\|api[_-]?key\|(?<![a-z])auth(orization)?(?![a-z])\|session\|csrf\|card\|cvv\|ssn\|private[_-]?key\|access[_-]?key\|signature\|credential"]` | Patterns matched with `re.search` against **key names** in query strings, form and JSON bodies (at any depth), outbound URLs, SQL parameter column names, log messages (`key=value` pairs) and the names of exception locals. A match masks the value. `auth` and `authorization` match only as a whole word, so `author`, `author_id`, `authenticated` and `oauth_provider` stay visible |
| `capture_logs` | `bool` | `True` | Keep the log records emitted during a request. See [Logs and exceptions](logs-and-exceptions.md) |
| `log_level` | `str` (`DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARNING`, `ERROR`, `CRITICAL`; case-insensitive) | `"INFO"` | An extra minimum level for records stored in a trace. Capture follows your application's own logger levels (Redline never adds a root handler or changes a level), so a record your logging configuration drops is never captured; `log_level` can only raise the bar further |
| `max_logs_per_trace` | `int` | `200` | Cap per trace; extras are counted, not stored |
| `auto_instrument` | `"off"`, `"warn"` or `"on"` | `"warn"` | Outbound-call integrations (httpx, requests, redis, boto3). `"warn"`: at install, log one warning naming installed but uninstrumented ones; `"on"`: instrument every installed one at install; `"off"`: neither. See [Integrations](integrations.md#zero-config-coverage) |
| `capture_locals` | `bool` | `True` | Keep the local variables of project frames in an exception (names matching `redact_keys` are masked). See [Logs and exceptions](logs-and-exceptions.md#exceptions-with-locals) |
| `capture_error_details` | `bool` | `True` | Capture exception messages and formatted tracebacks. When false, errors retain type/codes without formatting message or traceback text; exception locals are also disabled. SQL messages additionally require SQL parameter capture for that statement. Shared-dev and production default to false |

## Detectors

See [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md).

| Setting | Type | Default | Minimum | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `n_plus_one_threshold` | `int` | `5` | 2 | The same read from the same line at least this many times is an N+1 |
| `duplicate_threshold` | `int` | `2` | 2 | Identical SQL and params at least this many times is a duplicate |
| `sql_retry_storm_threshold` | `int` | `3` | 2 | Attempts after a transient SQL failure (same statement and callsite) before a `sql_retry_storm` finding |
| `slow_query_ms` | `float` | `100` | 0 | A query at least this slow is a slow query. `0` flags every query. It also feeds the N+1 and duplicate severity rules |
| `too_many_queries` | `int` | `50` | 0 | A request with at least this many queries is over budget. `0` disables the check |
| `blocking_ms` | `float` | `20` | 0 | A stall of the event loop of at least this long is reported. See [Blocking in async](async-blocking.md) |
| `large_result_rows` | `int` | `1000` | 0 | A SELECT returning at least this many rows is a [large result](result-size.md) |
| `unbounded_rows` | `int` | `200` | 0 | A SELECT with no `LIMIT` returning at least this many rows is [unbounded](result-size.md#unbounded-query) |
| `slow_serializer_ms` | `float` | `50` | 0 | A [serializer](serializers.md) at least this slow is reported |
| `long_transaction_ms` | `float` | `200` | 0 | A [transaction](transactions.md) open at least this long is reported |
| `slow_external_ms` | `float` | `500` | 0 | An [outbound call](external-calls.md) at least this slow is reported |

Two more switches belong here. `detect_blocking` (`bool`, default `True`) runs the
event-loop lag monitor in async adapters, only while a request is in flight; set it false to
remove it entirely.

## Profiling

See [Flamegraphs](flamegraphs.md). Needs `redline-core[profile]`.

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `profile` | `"off"`, `"opt_in"`, `"sampled"`, `"all"` | `"opt_in"` (`production` preset: `"off"`) | Who gets profiled. Anything else is an error. In `opt_in`/`sampled`, `?_redline=profile` / `X-Redline-Profile: 1` count only in framework debug mode or from a request with valid Redline credentials |
| `profile_sample_rate` | `float`, 0 to 1 | `0.0` | In `"sampled"` mode, the fraction of untriggered requests to profile |

## EXPLAIN

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `explain_analyze` | `bool` | `False` | Allow `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which **executes** the query. Off: `analyze: true` is refused with `403 analyze_disabled`. See [EXPLAIN](explain.md#safety) |

## Developer experience

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `editor` | `"vscode"`, `"cursor"`, `"pycharm"`, `"idea"`, `"sublime"`, `"none"`, or a template string | `"vscode"` | Where callsite links open. A template contains `{file}` (absolute path) and `{line}`. See [Open in editor](the-ui.md#open-in-editor) |
| `server_timing` | `"auto"` or `bool` | `"auto"` | Add a `Server-Timing` header (trace id, query count and time) to recorded responses. `auto` means on when the framework is in debug mode. See [Server-Timing and the badge](server-timing-badge.md) |
| `badge` | `"auto"` or `bool` | `"auto"` | Inject the floating badge into HTML responses. `auto` means on when the framework is in debug mode (FastAPI, Flask and Litestar: the app's `debug` flag) |
| `load_from_ui` | `bool` | `False` | Allow starting a [load run](load-testing.md#starting-a-run-from-the-ui) from the UI (`POST api/runs`). Needs `redline-core[load]`. Off whenever `read_only` is on or the `load` feature is off |
| `checks_from_ui` | `"auto"` or `bool` | `"auto"` | Allow starting [refactor-check](refactor-check.md) baseline and compare runs from the UI (`POST api/checks/runs`). `auto` means on only while the framework is in debug mode; `true` and `false` force it. Needs `redline-core[load]` (httpx). Off whenever `read_only` is on or the `checks` feature is off; the `production` preset sets it to `false`. Reading suites and reports is not affected |

## Storage and retention

See [Storage](storage.md).

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `max_rows` | `int` (0 or more) or `None` | `10000` | Keep at most this many traces; the oldest beyond it are pruned. **`0` or `None` disables the row cap** |
| `max_age_days` | `int` (0 or more) or `None` | `7` | Prune traces older than this. **`0` or `None` disables age-based pruning** |
| `max_spans_per_trace` | `int` (0 or more) or `None` | `2000` | Spans stored per request. Beyond it spans are **counted, not stored**; query totals are retained and the trace is marked `truncated`. Bounded overflow groups can preserve detector evidence, but byte limits may discard those groups too. Middleware/view spans bypass the count cap only while within the byte budget. **`0` or `None` disables this count cap**, not byte limits. See [Performance](performance.md#memory) |
| `history_retention_days` | `int` (0 or more) or `None` | `90` | How long hourly rollups, the issue index, releases and load runs are kept, independent of `max_age_days`. **`0` or `None` keeps them forever**. See [History](history.md#retention) |
| `writer_queue_size` | `int` | `1000` (minimum 1) | Bound of the in-memory queue between requests and the writer thread. When full, new traces are **dropped and counted** (`storage.dropped` in `api/meta`). SQLite writer failures also add lost batch traces to this counter |

For the optional retention/span count limits above, `0` and `None` mean "no limit";
negative values are errors. `writer_queue_size` always requires an integer of at least 1. To delete everything use **Clear all**, `DELETE api/traces` or
`manage.py redline_clear`, never a zero.

## Capture byte budgets

These positive integer settings complement span/log counts and body caps:

| Setting | Minimum | Default | Production preset | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `max_sql_bytes` | `256` | `65536` (64 KiB) | `16384` (16 KiB) | SQL text inspected/captured per execution; oversized text is incomplete evidence |
| `max_span_data_bytes` | `256` | `32768` (32 KiB) | `8192` (8 KiB) | Bounded JSON-safe data attached to an individual span |
| `max_tag_bytes` | `32` | `2048` (2 KiB) | `2048` (2 KiB) | Individual captured tag values; ordinary tags also have item/key limits |
| `max_trace_bytes` | `4096` | `1048576` (1 MiB) | `262144` (256 KiB) | Retained-span byte budget during recording and final serialized trace budget before saving |

These budgets cannot be disabled with `0` or `None`. They apply independently of the
older optional count/retention limits. Bounded capture limits traversal depth and total
items, handles cycles, shortens UTF-8 text safely, and substitutes unsupported application
objects without invoking their `str()`/`repr()` methods. This is an observation limit;
it does not constrain the application's original object allocations or database payload.

Per-value conversion uses bounded compact ASCII JSON; the final trace check measures
UTF-8 JSON with the storage serializer's default spacing, checking both profile-included
and profile-lookup shapes without arbitrary object conversion. It is a recording payload
budget, not a cap on SQLite indexes, history tables, WAL files or total disk space.

The production preset also reduces `writer_queue_size` to `64` and
`max_spans_per_trace` to `500`. Explicit settings override these defaults.

Truncation and dropped evidence must remain visible in a trace. A shortened statement
or omitted span cannot prove a query was safe or a request contained no failures.
Recorded SQL/connection error counts survive discarded span evidence. Altered captures
set `truncated.capture_limits` and `truncated.incomplete_evidence`. A total-size reduction
can set `reason = "trace_budget"` and dropped-span/issue counts. Incomplete SQL spans
withhold parameters and disable EXPLAIN. A privacy-processing failure produces only safe
minimal metadata with `reason = "privacy_failure"`; failure counts then live under
`truncated`, with no application tags or raw request content. See [HTTP API](http-api.md#capture-budgets-and-incomplete-evidence). A queue-length
limit also does not set a total process-memory bound: queued records, active requests,
analysis and the application have separate overhead. Measure the full process under load.

## Access control

Who may open the UI and API, and how. The policies, recipes and reasoning are on
[Access control](access-control.md); the table is the reference. Secrets (`token`,
`secret_key`, `basic_users`) are shown as `***` by `GET api/config` and `redline config`.

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `access` | `"local"`, `"token"`, `"basic"`, `"framework"`, `"custom"` or `"open"` | `"local"` (Django: `"framework"`, superusers) | The access policy. `"open"` is refused (`403 open_refused`) unless `REDLINE_ALLOW_OPEN=1` is set too. A native hook (non-empty FastAPI `dependencies=` / Litestar `guards=`, a Flask `permission=`) implies `"framework"` when you did not set `access` yourself. **Not set at all** (FastAPI, Flask, Litestar): `local` applies only in framework debug mode; otherwise every Redline URL answers `404` |
| `trust_unix_socket` | `bool` | `False` | Under `local`, count a unix-socket peer (no client address) as loopback. Off because a same-host reverse proxy is the usual such peer |
| `cookie_secure` | `"auto"`, `True` or `False` | `"auto"` | `Secure` attribute of the login cookie. `"auto"`: when the request is https (`X-Forwarded-Proto` counts only from `trusted_proxies`) |
| `access_check` | callable `(request_info) -> bool`, or a dotted path (`pkg.mod:fn` or `pkg.mod.fn`) | `None` | For `access = "custom"`. An exception counts as a refusal and is logged |
| `allowed_ips` | list of IPs or CIDRs (v4 or v6) | `[]` | With `local`: clients allowed **besides** loopback. With every other policy: when non-empty the client **must also** be in it (loopback is not implicit) |
| `allowed_hosts` | list of `str` | `[]` | Extra `Host` names accepted by `local`'s DNS-rebinding check (ports ignored). Also accepted as targets of UI-started load runs |
| `trusted_proxies` | list of IPs or CIDRs | `[]` | Only requests whose TCP peer is in this list have `X-Forwarded-For`, `-Proto` and `-Host` believed. A loopback peer sending forwarding headers without being listed is refused under `local` |
| `token` | `str` (secret) | `None` | The token for `access = "token"`: one string, no whitespace. Outside the `dev` preset it must be at least 24 characters. Prefer `REDLINE_TOKEN` |
| `token_file` | path | `None` | Read the token from a file once at startup (stripped). Not together with `token` |
| `basic_users` | table of user to hash (secret) | `{}` | For `access = "basic"`; hashes made by `redline hash-password` (`pbkdf2_sha256$...`). User names may not contain `:` |
| `secret_key` | `str`, 16 characters or more (secret) | `None` | Signs the login cookie. Unset: a random key per process, so with several workers a login only works on the worker that issued it, and every restart logs everyone out |
| `read_only` | `bool` | `False` | Refuse every non-GET `api/` call except `api/explain`, `api/login` and `api/logout` with `403 read_only`; `POST api/explain` with `analyze` is refused too |
| `features` | table of switch to `bool` | all `True` | Turn individual features off: `explain`, `profile`, `replay`, `replay_writes`, `snapshot`, `load`, `checks`, `logs`, `locals`, `sse`. An unknown name is an error. Merged per key across layers |
| `ui_enabled` | `bool` | `True` | `False`: every Redline URL answers `404` while capture continues |
| `mount_path` | `str` | `None` | Where FastAPI (`prefix`), Flask (`url_prefix`) and Litestar (`path`) serve the UI when that argument is not given; those arguments now default to `None`, and the final default is `/_redline`. Django ignores it (the URLconf decides). Also the default for `redline load --ui-url` |
| `session_ttl_s` | `int`, 1 or more | `43200` | Login cookie lifetime in seconds |
| `max_login_attempts` | `int`, 1 or more | `10` | Failed credential attempts per client IP per 300 seconds before `429 too_many_requests` |
| `base_url` | http(s) URL | `None` | Target of load runs and refactor checks started from the UI. Unset: `127.0.0.1` on the port the server listens on (ASGI `scope["server"]`, WSGI `SERVER_PORT`), never the `Host` header; required when that is unknown (a unix socket). `GET api/config` masks userinfo in it |

## Presets

`preset` only sets **defaults**. Anything you set elsewhere overrides it. The table is
exactly what `redline_core.conf.PRESETS` applies:

| | `dev` (default) | `shared-dev` | `staging` | `production` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sample_rate` | `1.0` | `1.0` | `0.25` | `0.05` |
| `capture_request_body` / `capture_response_body` | on | off | on | off |
| `capture_sql_params` | on | off | off | off |
| `capture_locals` | on | off | off | off |
| `capture_error_details` / `capture_logs` | on | off | on | off |
| `log_level` | `INFO` | `WARNING` | `INFO` | `WARNING` |
| `access` | `local` | `token` | `token` | `token` |
| `read_only` | off | on | off | on |
| `badge` / `server_timing` | `auto` | `auto` | `auto` | off |
| `load_from_ui` | off | off | off | off |
| `checks_from_ui` / `analysis_from_ui` | `auto` | off | `auto` | off |
| `explain_analyze` | off | off | off | off |
| `profile` | `off` | `off` | `off` | `off` |
| `writer_queue_size` | `1000` | `1000` | `1000` | `64` |
| `max_spans_per_trace` | `2000` | `2000` | `2000` | `500` |
| `max_sql_bytes` | `65536` | `65536` | `65536` | `16384` |
| `max_span_data_bytes` | `32768` | `32768` | `32768` | `8192` |
| `max_tag_bytes` | `2048` | `2048` | `2048` | `2048` |
| `max_trace_bytes` | `1048576` | `1048576` | `1048576` | `262144` |

`always_keep_errors` remains on in all presets. Shared-dev defaults retention to three
days. Shared-dev disables replay and replay writes. Staging disables replay writes.
Production disables the replay, replay writes, load, checks, explain and profile feature
gates as well as their UI opt-ins. Stored traces and their recorded analysis remain
available to authorized readers. Explicit settings override preset defaults; review
`redline config` after layering configuration.

Outside `dev` a token must be at least 24 characters, and `access = "token"` without a
`token` or `token_file` is always an error. Slow requests are kept in every preset
(`always_keep_slower_than_ms`, default `500`).

See [Configuration](configuration.md#presets) and [Production](production.md#start-with-recording-and-stored-data-inspection).

## Where a value comes from

Layers, last one wins: built-in defaults, the adapter's defaults, preset, config file
(`redline.toml` or `[tool.redline]`), `REDLINE_<SETTING>` environment variables, then the
framework's own settings. `redline config` prints the result and the layer of every value. See
[Configuration](configuration.md#layers-and-precedence).

## Django-only

| Setting | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `PERMISSION` | callable `(request) -> bool` or a dotted path to one | active superusers (`user.is_active and user.is_superuser`; staff before 0.2, kept as `django_redline.conf.staff_permission`). Used when `access = "framework"` | Who may open the UI and the API. See [Django: access control](django.md#access-control) |
| `STORE` | a `Store` instance, a callable (or class) taking the core `Settings` and returning one, or a dotted path to either | `None` (`SQLiteStore.from_settings(settings)`) | Where traces are kept: Django's counterpart of FastAPI's `install(store=...)`. See [Extending: the Store protocol](extending.md#the-store-protocol) |

`PERMISSION` and `STORE` are read by the Django adapter before the rest is handed to the
core, so they are not core settings and the other adapters do not accept them in `settings`.
Their counterparts are FastAPI's `dependencies` and `store=`, Flask's `permission=` and
`store=`, and Litestar's `guards=` and `store=`.

## Adapter defaults at a glance

| | Django | FastAPI | Flask | Litestar |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Passed as | `settings.REDLINE` dict | `install(settings=...)` | `app.config["REDLINE"]` or `Redline(settings=...)` | `RedlinePlugin(settings=...)` |
| `sample_rate` | `1.0` with `DEBUG`, else `0.1` | `1.0` | `1.0` | `1.0` |
| `storage_path` | `<BASE_DIR>/.redline/redline.db` | `.redline/redline.db` (working directory) | same as FastAPI | same as FastAPI |
| `project_root` | `BASE_DIR` | working directory | working directory | working directory |
| Mount prefix | wherever you `include()` the URLs (e.g. `/redline/`) | `prefix`, else `mount_path`, else `/_redline` | `url_prefix`, else `mount_path`, else `/_redline` | `path`, else `mount_path`, else `/_redline` |
| Access | `PERMISSION`, default superusers (`framework`) | `local` (loopback only, debug mode only while `access` is unset); `dependencies=` implies `framework` | `local` (same); `permission=` implies `framework` | `local` (same); `guards=` implies `framework` |

## A complete example

=== "Django"

    ```python
    REDLINE = {
        "ENABLED": True,
        "SAMPLE_RATE": 0.1,
        "ALWAYS_KEEP_SLOWER_THAN_MS": 300,
        "ALWAYS_KEEP_ERRORS": True,
        "IGNORE_PATHS": ["/static/", "/media/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health", "^/metrics"],
        "STORAGE_PATH": str(BASE_DIR / ".redline" / "redline.db"),
        "CAPTURE_REQUEST_BODY": True,
        "CAPTURE_RESPONSE_BODY": False,
        "MAX_BODY_BYTES": 10_000,
        "N_PLUS_ONE_THRESHOLD": 5,
        "SLOW_QUERY_MS": 50,
        "TOO_MANY_QUERIES": 40,
        "PROFILE": "opt_in",
        "EXPLAIN_ANALYZE": False,
        "MAX_ROWS": 5_000,
        "MAX_AGE_DAYS": 3,
        "PERMISSION": "myproject.redline.can_view",
    }
    ```

    `STORAGE_PATH` and `PROJECT_ROOT` accept a `pathlib.Path` (any `os.PathLike`) as well
    as a string; it is converted to `str`.

=== "FastAPI"

    ```python
    install(app, engine=engine, settings={
        "sample_rate": 0.1,
        "always_keep_slower_than_ms": 300,
        "ignore_paths": ["/static/", "/favicon.ico", "^/health", "^/metrics"],
        "storage_path": "/var/lib/myapp/redline.db",
        "capture_response_body": False,
        "max_body_bytes": 10_000,
        "slow_query_ms": 50,
        "too_many_queries": 40,
        "max_rows": 5_000,
        "max_age_days": 3,
    })
    ```


## v0.3 analysis settings

`analysis_from_ui` accepts `"auto"`, `true` or `false`. Auto enables source scans and
synthetic detector samples only in framework debug mode; the production preset sets it
to false. `read_only` still refuses these POST operations. Detector threshold settings,
model-count semantics and explicit cache-decode instrumentation are documented in
[Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md#additional-runtime-findings). Preview
controls do not change the server's effective configuration.


## v0.5 LLM-call and AI-diagnosis settings

| Setting | Default | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `llm_duplicate_threshold` | `2` | Identical prompts to one model in a request that raise `duplicate_llm_call`; `0` disables |
| `llm_serial_min` | `3` | Back-to-back LLM calls that raise `serial_llm_calls`; `0` disables |
| `llm_loop_calls` | `8` | LLM calls in one request that raise `llm_call_loop`; `0` disables |
| `llm_prompt_cache_chars` | `4000` | Anthropic prompt size that raises `uncached_large_prompt` without cache tokens; `0` disables |
| `ai_diagnosis` | `false` | Allows `redline diagnose --send` to contact the provider. Without it the command only previews |
| `ai_provider` | `"anthropic"` | Provider for diagnosis; the destination host is fixed per provider |
| `ai_model` | `"claude-sonnet-5-5"` | Model used for diagnosis |

The diagnosis API key is read from the `REDLINE_AI_API_KEY` environment variable only. It is not
a setting, so it never appears in `redline config`, the API or the UI. See
[LLM-call observability](llm.md) and [Working with AI agents](agents.md#ai-assisted-diagnosis).

## v0.4 database, privacy and job settings

These settings apply to the common recorder. Adapters resolve file/environment/framework
layers as described above. The [real-world guide](real-world-workflows.md) explains the
behavior and limitations; the [production recipe](production.md) deliberately disables
active tools and sensitive capture for its initial canary.

| Setting | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `capture_sql_params` | `bool` or `"reads_only"` | `True` (`False` in staging/shared-dev/production) | `False` withholds parameters and inline SQL literals, SQL source/fix snippets and potentially value-bearing SQL error messages. EXPLAIN is unavailable for that recording. `reads_only` retains values only for conservatively recognized reads |
| `instrument_engines` | `"explicit"`, `"all"` or `"flask_sqlalchemy"` | `"explicit"` | `all` enables process-level SQLAlchemy discovery for active opted-in recorders. Explicit engine registration is still supported; Flask-SQLAlchemy discovery remains available. It does not wrap arbitrary raw DBAPI connections |
| `ignore_sql` | list of regexes | session housekeeping (see below) | Statements whose every part matches one of these case-insensitive regexes (tested on the normalised statement: comments removed, keywords upper-cased) are not recorded as spans and do not count as queries. Default: `^(?:EXEC(?:UTE)?\s+)?(?:\[?sys\]?\.)?\[?sp_set_session_context\]?\b` and `^SET\s`, the session statements that run on pool checkout. Set `[]` to record everything. A failing statement is always recorded. Session-state tracking (`session_expected`) still sees ignored statements |
| `session_expected` | mapping of option name to SQL value spelling | `{"NOCOUNT": "OFF"}` | Baseline for observed session switches at pool checkin. SQL Server also observes isolation level, `IDENTITY_INSERT`, date/language/timeout/deadlock switches; PostgreSQL and MySQL observe session options, `set_config(x, y, false)` and MySQL user variables. Unknown changes are not invented. Generic string-valued options are compared by digest, so use the expected SQL value spelling |
| `session_expected_context` | list of strings | `[]` | SQL Server `sp_set_session_context` keys the application is expected to use. A remaining unnamed key is reported; an expected key is reported when it was set with `@read_only = 0` (lower severity). Values are never stored |
| `redact_profiles` | list of names | `[]` | Built-in pattern sets: `credentials`, `pii`, `health`, `payment`. They are starting points, not a privacy/compliance guarantee |
| `redact_tables` | list of regexes | `[]` | Additional table-name patterns for SQL parameter masking |
| `redact_routes` | mapping of `METHOD route-template` glob to mode | `{}` | `values` preserves JSON structure and masks values; `body` removes body contents. Also restricts that recording's SQL/query values, logs and exception/source detail before persistence |
| `capture_loggers` | list of logger-name globs | `[]` | Empty means no additional allowlist. A nonempty list captures only matching logger names; application level and `log_level` still apply |
| `ignore_loggers` | list of logger-name globs | `[]` | Matching loggers are excluded even if the allowlist matches |
| `request_id_headers` | list of header names | `["X-Request-ID", "X-Correlation-ID", "traceparent"]` | First configured request/response identifier becomes `request_id`; response takes precedence at completion. A valid `traceparent` also fills OTel trace/parent ids. Explicit header/key redaction still applies |
| `user_resolver` | synchronous Python callable or `None` | `None` | Called late with a framework request; return only an identifier string/integer. It is not a TOML string import path. Errors become a resolver-error tag rather than breaking the response |
| `storage_role` | simple role name | `"web"` | Substitution for `{role}` in `storage_path`. Use `worker` explicitly in a task worker; it is not inferred from Celery |
| `extra_stores` | list of existing file paths, at most 8 | `[]` | Read-only secondary request/job/profile browsing. It does not combine aggregates/history or permit secondary mutations/database execution |
| `allow_storage_in_repo` | `bool` | `False` | Non-dev presets refuse an in-repository store unless explicitly overridden. Prefer a private absolute path outside the checkout |

Nested `[redact]` configuration is equivalent to the flat fields:

```toml
[redact]
profiles = ["credentials", "pii", "health"]
tables = ["(?i)medical|clinical"]
routes = { "POST /private/*" = "values" }
```

Use either the nested spelling or its flat equivalent, not both for the same setting.
Ordinary key/header lists retain their replacement semantics. Enabling a profile does
not make arbitrary values in logs or exception text recognizable.

`storage_path` supports `{role}`, `{hostname}` and `{pid}`. Use an application/environment
prefix too, such as `/var/lib/redline/orders-production/{role}.db`. Templates do not make
remote filesystem storage safe and do not create per-application authorization.

### Production versus shared development

`shared-dev` disables request/response bodies, locals and SQL values; it enables token
access, read-only behavior, WARNING-level log capture and three-day trace retention. UI
load/check/source analysis and replay are off by default. It is useful for shared staging
work but is not a substitute for the stricter [production recipe](production.md).

An explicit setting overrides a preset, including sensitive capture switches. Inspect
`GET api/config` and recording health in the deployed process rather than assuming an
environment variable or configuration file was loaded by every worker.

### Job helpers and adapter options
