<!-- page: Roadmap -->

# Roadmap

[← Index](index.md)

Redline has four parts: **Profile**, **Analyze**, **Stress** and **Compare/CI**. Versions
0.1–0.3 implemented request analysis, load/history and comparison/test tooling. The 0.4
development release adds the database, job and privacy workflows described in
[Real-world workflows](real-world-workflows.md). The remaining roadmap is intent, not a
promise; production readiness still depends on the [deployment validation gate](production.md).

| Version | Theme | Status |
|---|---|---|
| **0.1** | Profile and Analyze: traces, N+1 with fix diffs, EXPLAIN, flamegraphs, UI, Django and FastAPI | **Built** |
| **0.2** | Analyze more, **Stress**, History: Flask and Litestar, a load tester, new detectors, release history, access control | **Built** (alpha) |
| 0.3 | **Compare / CI**: refactor checks, endpoint budgets, pytest and source analysis | Released; continued in 0.4 |
| **0.4** | Real-world SQL failures, jobs, privacy and bounded capture | Development; Compose qualification green, main CI and live deployment pending |
| 0.5 | Jobs, schema and the remaining report items | Planned; several items already landed in 0.4 |
| 0.6 | OpenTelemetry, more workers, Postgres store and AI policy | Planned; several items already landed in 0.4 |
| 1.0 | Hardened production mode and the long tail | Planned |

## The thesis

Load testers (Locust, k6, Gatling) only see an application from the outside. They tell
you the p95 doubled at 150 users. They cannot tell you **which query** went from 3 ms to
410 ms. Profilers like Redline see the inside but only one request at a time. No
open-source tool connected the two. 0.2 does: see [Load testing](load-testing.md).

## v0.2: what shipped

Everything below is built and documented. The [changelog](changelog.md) has the detail.

- **Five frameworks**: Django (and Ninja), FastAPI, [Flask](flask.md), [Litestar](litestar.md).
- **New analysis**: [blocking in async](async-blocking.md), [transactions and locks](transactions.md),
  [large and unbounded results](result-size.md), count/exists, [slow serializers](serializers.md),
  [external calls](external-calls.md), [cache efficiency](cache-efficiency.md),
  [logs and exception locals](logs-and-exceptions.md), [GraphQL](graphql.md) resolvers.
- **[Database](database.md)**: SQL search, a workload index advisor, unused indexes.
- **[Static N+1 scan](static-scan.md)** for templates and DRF serializers.
- **[Load testing](load-testing.md)**: `redline load`, an open-model scheduler corrected for
  coordinated omission, step ramps, knee detection, per-step bottlenecks, scenarios generated
  from OpenAPI or captured traffic.
- **[History](history.md)**: releases, hourly rollups, before/after compare, new and resolved
  issues, 90-day retention.
- **UI**: command palette, keyboard, open in editor, copy as cURL/HTTPie, replay, compare,
  Live mode, snapshots, the floating badge, Server-Timing.
- **[Configuration](configuration.md) and [access control](access-control.md)**: presets,
  `redline.toml`, `REDLINE_*`, tokens, basic auth, IP allow-lists, trusted proxies, read-only
  mode, feature switches.

## v0.3: Compare and CI

Make performance a thing you can regress-test.

- A **pytest plugin** (built in the development branch): `@pytest.mark.redline(max_queries=..., no_n_plus_one=True)`, so a
  test fails when a view regresses to an N+1.
- **`redline ci`** is available as `redline check compare/run`: **JUnit** output and a
  **Markdown PR comment** (`+queries`, `+p95`, the culprit line), comparing a run against a
  stored baseline. `--ruff` adds Ruff JSON to the same report; Redline does not become a
  linter.
- **Flamegraph diffs** between two requests or two releases are deferred to the next release.
- **OTLP export** is implemented in 0.4 as an explicit preview/send command: a root span,
  sanitized SQL spans, issue log records and W3C `traceparent` propagation. OTLP import
  remains unplanned.
- Baselines and diffs per endpoint in CI, building on the History comparison already in 0.2.
- **Refactor check** (**shipped in 0.3.0a1**, see [Refactor check](refactor-check.md)): pick a
  set of read-only endpoints, record a baseline before a refactor, run it again after, and
  get a per-endpoint report of performance changes (time, queries, issues, overall average)
  and of response changes (a diff that ignores fields that change on every call). From the UI
  and from the command line, with an exit code, JUnit and a Markdown PR comment for CI.
- **`redline analyze`**: a static analysis of the application's Python code (not only its
  templates) that finds likely bottlenecks before any request runs: queries inside loops
  (N+1), missing `select_related` / `prefetch_related` / `selectinload`, unbounded
  queries, blocking calls inside async views, and similar database and logic problems.
  Extends the template scan shipped in 0.2.

See [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) for the implemented UI, assertions, source analysis and detector additions. Two live targets, differential flamegraphs, serial-call concurrency advice and automated cold/warm scenarios are deferred to the next release.

## v0.5: Jobs, schema and the report's remaining 0.5 items

Most of this scope already landed in 0.4; the table records what is still open so it is
not silently treated as finished.

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| Celery task integration, request -> task stitching, jobs/stages/row outcomes and Jobs UI | **Landed in 0.4** |
| SQL Server online compilation (`sp_describe_*`, NOEXEC), schema snapshots and `schema-watch` | **Landed in 0.4** |
| Trigger-aware `OUTPUT` lint and schema metadata | **Landed in 0.4** |
| Multi-container storage: WAL probe, per-role files, `extra_stores`, two-process test | **Landed in 0.4** |
| FastAPI with mounted Flask in nested mode | **Landed in 0.4** |
| SQL Server actual plans and STATISTICS IO | **Landed in 0.4** |
| `check-imports` lazy imports and `--ruff` pass-through | **Landed in 0.4** |
| Error fingerprinting and a cross-deploy regression view | Open |
| RQ and Dramatiq adapters on the Celery contract | Moved to 0.6 |

## v0.6: OpenTelemetry, more workers and the 0.6 items

| Item | State |
|---|---|
| OTLP span/log export with explicit SQL opt-in | **Landed in 0.4** |
| Raw-SQL N+1 batching advice | **Landed in 0.4** |
| Log capture allowlist (`capture_loggers` / `ignore_loggers`) | **Landed in 0.4** |
| RQ and Dramatiq integrations | Open |
| `redline_core.dbapi.wrap` for non-SQLAlchemy projects | Open |
| Postgres store (`storage_url = "postgresql://..."`, see [Storage](storage.md)) | **Landed in 0.5** |
| AI-diagnosis policy, as a separate package if built | Open; never sends trace data without explicit opt-in |

## v1.0

The long tail.

- **Hardened production mode** beyond the SQLite store, including the Postgres store from
  0.6.
- **Distributed worker trace stitching** beyond the explicit Celery job recordings and
  parent/request ID labels added in 0.4.
- A **memory-per-request** extra (tracemalloc or memray).
- In-process **fault injection**: latency or errors per endpoint or query.
- **Index what-if** through HypoPG: test a suggested index without creating it.
- **Lock-wait detection** from `pg_locks`, and deeper pool and threadpool saturation signals.
- **Folding `django-signal-tracer` in** as a panel.

## What is likely to be missing for a while

Be realistic about gaps that are not on the list above:

- Frameworks other than Django, FastAPI, Flask and Litestar (Falcon, Sanic, Pyramid).
- ORMs other than the Django ORM and SQLAlchemy (you can write a
  [FixSuggester](extending.md#fixsuggester)).
- Non-SQL data stores beyond Redis and Django's cache API (MongoDB).
- Cross-service distributed tracing.
- Alerting.
- Distributed load generation, browsers and WebSockets in the load tester.

## How the roadmap is decided

Each version gets its own detailed plan before work starts, and each stays small. The
outline above is from the project plan; details, ordering and scope inside each version may
change. Issues and ideas are welcome on the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/issues).

## 0.4 development release

Database failures, SQL Server plan tooling, offline/online SQL checks, jobs, privacy,
storage probes and shared-environment controls are described in
[Real-world workflows](real-world-workflows.md). Driver and worker support distinguish
local fixtures from live deployment validation. The 0.4 branch also carries several
items the report scheduled for 0.5/0.6 (OTLP, schema watch, raw-SQL advice, import smoke
tests, MSSQL unused indexes); the tables above keep the genuinely open items visible.

A green local validation run is not a claim that every report requirement is complete.
The open rows in 0.5/0.6 are the remaining gaps, alongside deployment-specific evidence
that no test suite can supply.

---

<!-- source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/main/docs/api-stability.md -->
<!-- page: API stability -->

# API stability and deprecation policy

[← Index](index.md)

Redline is **beta** (`0.x`). This page says which names you can build on, how they may
change before 1.0, and how a change is announced. It is the authoritative list; older
design notes cited in code comments describe how features were specified and are not a
compatibility promise.

## Versioning

The five distributions (`redline-core`, `django-redline`, `fastapi-redline`,
`flask-redline`, `litestar-redline`) are released **in lockstep**: one version number, and an
adapter only supports the `redline-core` of the same release. Mixing versions is
unsupported (`scripts/check_versions.py` enforces it in CI).

Before 1.0:

- A **minor** bump (`0.5` → `0.6`) may change or remove public API, but only after the
  deprecation period below, and every such change is listed under **Changed** or
  **Removed** in the [changelog](changelog.md).
- A **pre-release** (`0.6.0a1`, `a2` …) may change anything that was *added* in the same
  pre-release series. Things that shipped in a final or earlier minor release follow the
  deprecation rule.
- Patch releases (`0.5.1`) fix bugs only.

From 1.0, the project follows semantic versioning for everything listed as public below.

## What is public

Public means: importable from the names below, documented on this site, and covered by the
deprecation rule. Everything else is **internal**, including any module or name starting
with `_`, and any module not listed here, even if it is importable.

| Surface | Public names |
|---|---|
| `redline_core` | everything in `redline_core.__all__`: `configure`, `get_recorder`, `Recorder`, `Settings`, `SettingsError`, `span`, `record_span`, `record_query`, `tag`, `job`, `stage`, `row_outcome`, `start_trace`, `finish_trace`, `current`, the model types (`Trace`, `Span`, `SpanContext`, `TraceBuilder`, `Issue`, `Suggestion`, `Callsite`, `Frame`) and the extension points `Detector`, `FixSuggester`, `GenericSuggester` |
| `redline_core.testing` | the pytest helpers documented in [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| `redline_core.contrib.*` | the `instrument_*` / `uninstrument_*` functions of each integration documented in [Integrations](integrations.md) |
| `redline_core.storage` | `SQLiteStore` construction from a path and the `Store` protocol for custom stores ([Storage](storage.md)); the SQL schema itself is internal |
| `django_redline` | the app label, the URL include, the settings documented in [Django](django.md), `span` |
| `fastapi_redline` | everything in `fastapi_redline.__all__` (`install`, `Redline`, `RedlineMiddleware`, `instrument_engine`, guards) |
| `flask_redline` | everything in `flask_redline.__all__` (`Redline`, `RedlineMiddleware`, `instrument_engine`, guards) |
| `litestar_redline` | everything in `litestar_redline.__all__` (`RedlinePlugin`, `RedlineMiddleware`, `instrument_engine`, guards) |
| Settings | every key documented in [Settings](settings.md), its environment variable and its `redline.toml` / `[tool.redline]` spelling |
| CLI | `redline` subcommands, their documented flags and **exit codes** ([CLI](cli.md)). Human-readable output is *not* stable; use `--json` / JUnit / Markdown outputs for machines |
| HTTP API | the endpoints documented in [HTTP API](http-api.md) under the UI mount. Fields may be *added* to responses at any time; clients must ignore unknown fields |
| Pytest plugin | the fixtures and markers documented in [Performance workflows](performance-workflows.md) |
| Files | the refactor-check baseline and suite formats, the load `scenario.toml` format |

Not public, and free to change in any release: the bundled UI's HTML/JS, log message text,
the SQLite schema (it is migrated automatically, see below), detector heuristics and
thresholds (an issue may appear or disappear when detection improves), fix-suggestion text,
and anything under `redline_core.ui`, `redline_core.storage.sqlite` internals,
`redline_core.check.*` internals and `redline_core.load.*` internals.

## Deprecation rule

A public name, setting, flag or endpoint is removed or changed incompatibly only after:

1. It has emitted a `DeprecationWarning` (Python API, settings) or a `deprecated:` line on
   stderr (CLI) naming the replacement, for **at least one minor release**; and
2. The deprecation is listed under **Deprecated** in the changelog of the release that
   introduced the warning, and the removal under **Removed** in the later release.

Settings keep their old spelling as an alias during the deprecation period.

Security fixes are the one exception: a default may tighten immediately (for example a
capture setting turning off) when keeping it would expose data. The changelog marks such
changes **Security**.

## Stored data

The trace store carries a schema version and is migrated forward in place when a newer
release opens it (additive migrations, one transaction, safe across processes). Every
published release's store format is opened by the current code in CI
(`scripts/check_store_upgrade.py`, the *Compatibility* workflow). Opening a store with an
**older** release than the one that last wrote it is not supported. The store is a
development artifact: there is no promise to keep its contents across a major version, but
a breaking store change would be announced one minor release ahead.

---

<!-- page: FAQ -->

# FAQ

[← Index](index.md)

## How finished is this?

**Beta, and open source.** This checkout develops `0.5.0b1` under the
`Development Status :: 4 - Beta` classifier and MIT licence. Published prereleases are
available on PyPI; they may lag this branch. [Getting started](getting-started.md#install)
covers both published and local workspace installs. Profile, Analyze, Stress and Compare/CI
have implementations. The [real-world guide](real-world-workflows.md) covers SQL failures,
jobs and shared-environment additions, including their support boundaries.

What that means in practice:

- **What is built.** Request tracing with span timelines; SQL, cache, template, serializer,
  transaction, GraphQL resolver and outbound HTTP spans; N+1, duplicate, slow-query,
  query-budget, blocking-in-async, transaction, result-size, count/exists, serializer and
  external-call detectors; fix suggestions for Django and SQLAlchemy; EXPLAIN with plan
  analysis for PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite; opt-in flamegraphs; logs and exception locals;
  redaction; a SQLite store with release-aware history; a load tester with knee detection
  and per-step bottlenecks; a static N+1 scan; one access-control model for all frameworks;
  a JSON API; the web UI; adapters for **Django (including Ninja), FastAPI, Flask and
  Litestar**, with demo apps.
- **It is tested.** The repository has a large test suite across the five packages,
  including concurrency tests for the `contextvars` recorder, redaction, and the fix
  suggesters against real models. CI covers Python 3.10 to 3.14 and Django 5.2, 6.0 and 6.1.
  PostgreSQL EXPLAIN tests skip when no server is available.
- **The API may still move.** Setting names, the JSON API shape and the extension protocols
  are not frozen. Pin an exact version or commit.
- **Upgrades are best-effort.** The SQLite store migrates itself in place and a 0.1 file is
  backfilled (see [Storage](storage.md#migration)), but there is no deprecation cycle yet.
- **Measured on one machine.** Overhead benchmarks exist (`benchmarks/`) and were run on an
  Apple M2 Pro against 0.1; see [Performance and overhead](performance.md#measured-numbers).
  Your application is not that benchmark, so A/B it.
- **Not yet proven in production.** It is designed to be usable there with the
  [production preset](production.md#the-production-preset), but multi-process behaviour in
  particular has had little real-world exercise.
- **Development additions.** Pytest budgets, refactor-check CI reports and explicit summary export
  exist; 0.4 adds job/Celery recording and database/privacy workflows. Live MySQL/SQL Server,
  broker/prefork and deployment load qualification remain pending. A shared Postgres store,
  distributed tracing and RQ/Dramatiq integrations are not implemented.

Use it in development and staging first, and on an internal service second.

## Can I install it from PyPI?

Yes. Install the published prerelease adapter for your framework, such as
`pip install --pre django-redline`; the matching core is an exact dependency.
[Getting started](getting-started.md#install) lists all four adapters and optional extras.
A published version may not include this checkout's unreleased features. Use a reviewed
local workspace or matching Git commit to test those changes.

## How is it different from django-silk?

django-silk is the best-known self-hosted Django profiler. Redline aims at the same job and
differs in the following, which are design choices, not criticism of a project that
solved a harder problem first.

| | django-silk | Redline |
|---|---|---|
| Frameworks | Django | Django (and Ninja), FastAPI, Flask, Litestar |
| Async | no async support | recorded through `contextvars`; ASGI and WSGI, sync and async views |
| Where traces live | your application database | a separate SQLite file |
| Secrets | request data is stored as captured | masked before storage, by default |
| N+1 | you compare query counts | detected, grouped, with the line that causes it |
| Fix | none | a unified diff for Django and SQLAlchemy |
| EXPLAIN | none | one click, safe by default, with index suggestions |
| Flamegraphs | cProfile call tree | pyinstrument, async-safe, exportable to speedscope |

What silk has that Redline does not: a longer history, a larger user base, and
Django-specific features this beta lacks. If silk does what you need and your data is not
sensitive, it may be enough.

## How is it different from django-debug-toolbar?

The toolbar is a superb **in-page, per-request, development** tool: you see one request's
panels inside the page you are looking at. Redline is a **persistent record** with a UI of
its own: it works for requests that are not HTML pages (APIs, JSON, htmx, background
calls), keeps the last few thousand, aggregates across them (Endpoints, Issues) and groups
repeated problems. They are complementary and can both be installed. The toolbar's
interactive panels (templates, settings, signals, headers) are things Redline does not try
to replicate.

## How is it different from Sentry or Logfire?

Those are **hosted observability platforms**: distributed tracing across services,
alerting, fleet-wide dashboards, retention measured in weeks, and a vendor to pay and trust
with your data. They are the right tool for **production** monitoring across a system.

Redline is **self-hosted and local**: the data never leaves your disk, it knows your ORM
well enough to say which line to change, and it costs nothing to run. It does **not** do
cross-service tracing, alerting or long-term retention. Used together, the APM tells you a
route got slow and Redline tells you the query behind it.

## How is it different from Locust or k6?

Load testers generate traffic and see the application from outside. Redline's profiler
sees inside one request at a time. Since 0.2 Redline also has a **load tester**
(`redline load`) that joins the two: it drives your app at a controlled rate with an open
model, corrects for coordinated omission, finds the knee, and shows which query or endpoint
got slower at each step. See [Load testing](load-testing.md).

It is deliberately smaller than Locust or k6: HTTP only, scenario files instead of
scripting, no distributed generators, no browsers or WebSockets. If you need those, use them
and tag the requests with `X-Redline-Run` so Redline can still correlate.

## Does it slow my application down?

It adds work: on an Apple M2 Pro, about **0.04 to 0.09 ms per request plus 28 to 51 µs
per SQL query** while recording every request (a few µs in total when disabled), measured
on v0.2 (v0.1: 0.05 to 0.06 ms and 22 to 44 µs). The 0.2 features add small per-span or
per-batch costs and are idle when unused. See
[Performance and overhead](performance.md) for the measurements, the cost model and what
each setting controls. The headline facts are that disk I/O is off the request path, the
cost when nothing is recording is a `ContextVar.get()`, and **`sample_rate` reduces analysis
and disk but not the per-query recording cost**.

## Is it safe to run in production?

It can be, with the `production` preset (sampling, token access, read-only, no bodies, no
locals), `explain_analyze` off, and retention limits. It is a beta, and not hardened. Read
[Production](production.md), [Access control](access-control.md) and
[Security](security.md) first. The safest posture is to run it in development and staging
and tunnel to a loopback-only or token-protected instance when you need to look at
production.

## Does it touch my database?

It **never writes** to it and never runs migrations. It reads from it only when you click
**Explain**: one `EXPLAIN` of a recorded `SELECT` (or `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` if you enabled it),
in a transaction that is always rolled back.

## Where does the data go?

To `.redline/redline.db` in a SQLite file, on the machine running your app. Nothing is sent
anywhere. See [Storage](storage.md).

## Can I use it with Flask / Litestar / Falcon?

Flask and Litestar: yes, since 0.2. See [Flask](flask.md) and [Litestar](litestar.md). Django
Ninja is served by the Django adapter ([Django Ninja](django-ninja.md)). Falcon and others
have no adapter. The `redline-core` engine is framework-free and you can drive it yourself
([Extending: Using the core directly](extending.md#using-the-core-directly)), but the web UI
is served by an adapter. A plain-Starlette entry point is not offered; Starlette apps work
through `fastapi-redline` if you can call `install()` on a FastAPI app.

## Can I use it with another ORM?

Recording works for any **SQLAlchemy** engine and any **Django database connection**, and
for raw **asyncpg** and **psycopg 3** through [integrations](integrations.md). Fix
suggestions exist for the Django ORM and SQLAlchemy. For other ORMs you still get detection
and the SQL if the driver is instrumented, and you can write a
[FixSuggester](extending.md#fixsuggester). Tortoise and Peewee are not instrumented, because
nothing hooks their cursors.

## Does it work with async Django?

Yes. The middleware is both sync and async capable, SQL goes through
`connection.execute_wrapper`, and context propagates through `sync_to_async`. There are
tests for async views. See [Django](django.md#async-views).

## Does it work with Django REST Framework?

Yes: requests are traced like any other. For N+1s, the fix suggester knows serializers: if a
serializer reads a relation for every object, the diff targets the view's `queryset` or
`get_queryset()`. See [Django: Django REST Framework](django.md#django-rest-framework).

## Does it work with Celery, Django-Q, RQ or other background workers?

Only if you drive the recorder yourself (see
[Extending](extending.md#using-the-core-directly)). Celery and RQ stitching, so a request
and its tasks appear together, is planned for [v1.0](roadmap.md).

## Does it support GraphQL, gRPC or WebSockets?

**GraphQL:** yes, with Strawberry and Graphene. Each field resolution is a span, and an N+1
is reported against the resolver path (`orders.*.customer`). See [GraphQL](graphql.md).
Without the extension, a GraphQL endpoint is recorded like any POST (one route).
**WebSockets are not recorded.** gRPC is not supported.

## Why does my N+1 show no diff?

The suggester found the relation but not the source expression: it lives in another module,
is built dynamically, or `project_root` is wrong. You still get a code hint at lower
confidence. See [N+1 detection: when the suggester cannot help](n-plus-one.md#when-the-suggester-cannot-help).

## Why is something reported as an N+1 that is not?

The detector counts the same read from the same line at least `n_plus_one_threshold`
(default 5) times. A loop that runs 5 legitimately different-by-design lookups, or a
cache-warming loop, looks identical. Raise the threshold, or accept the report as a
prompt to check. Tuning is in [N+1 detection](n-plus-one.md#tuning).

## Why are there no requests in the UI?

See the checklist in [Getting started](getting-started.md#look-at-it): ignored path, a
missing middleware or `install()`, a sample rate below 1, or the writer lagging a second.

## Why do I see no SQL?

FastAPI: the engine was not passed to `install()` or `add_engine()`. Django: the
database connection was opened before Redline was installed in a way that bypassed
`connection_created` (unusual; Redline also instruments connections already open at
startup). In both: the work ran in a bare thread, which is not attributed to a request.

## Can I turn it off without removing it?

Yes: `enabled: false` (`REDLINE["ENABLED"] = False`). On Django the middleware stays but
passes every request straight through; on FastAPI `install()` then adds no middleware and
no SQLAlchemy listeners at all. Measured, a disabled install costs a few µs per request and
under 1 µs per query. The UI still shows what is already stored.

## Can I record only some requests?

Yes: `ignore_paths` excludes by prefix or regex, and `sample_rate` samples. There is no
per-user or per-header filter in this version.

## Does it work on Windows?

The code is pure Python and uses no platform-specific calls that we know of, but CI runs on
Linux and the project has been developed on macOS. Treat Windows as untested.

## Does it support PostgreSQL / MySQL / SQLite?

Recording works with any database SQLAlchemy or Django can talk to. EXPLAIN and plan
analysis support **PostgreSQL, MySQL (including MariaDB) and SQLite**; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
only on PostgreSQL. Other databases record SQL but cannot be explained.

## Does it work with Django Ninja?

Yes, through `django-redline`. Ninja's per-path view is resolved to the real operation, so
the trace shows your endpoint function and the route aggregates per method. See
[Django Ninja](django-ninja.md).

## How does it find blocking calls in an async app?

An event-loop lag monitor runs only while a request is in flight, and a watchdog thread samples
the loop's stack when a tick is late. The issue names the call (`time.sleep`, `requests.get`,
sync ORM). See [Blocking in async](async-blocking.md).

## Can I compare two releases?

Yes: hourly rollups and an issue index are kept for 90 days, and the History page compares
any two releases or time ranges with a per-endpoint verdict. See [History](history.md).

## Is the load tester safe to point at production?

No. It is an attack tool by nature. Run it against your own staging or local environment.
Starting runs from the UI is off by default and can only target the app serving the UI. See
[Load testing](load-testing.md) and [Security](security.md#load-from-the-ui).

## Can I put it behind a reverse proxy or in Kubernetes?

Yes, with a token and `trusted_proxies`. See the recipes in
[Access control](access-control.md#recipes).

## How do I configure it per environment?

Presets (`dev`, `staging`, `production`), a `redline.toml`, `REDLINE_*` environment
variables, and your framework's settings are layered. `redline config` shows the result.
See [Configuration](configuration.md).

## How do I delete everything?

**Clear all** in the UI, `DELETE api/traces`, `manage.py redline_clear` (Django), or delete
the `.redline/` directory while the app is stopped.

## What is the licence?

MIT, copyright 2026 Mahmoud Ahmed. See `LICENSE` in the repository.

## Where do I report a bug or a security problem?

Bugs: the repository's [issue tracker](https://github.com/Pythondeveloper6/redline/issues).
Security: privately, see `SECURITY.md`. Contributing is in [Contributing](contributing.md).
